Use this prompt if you want ChatGPT to teach you Agile comprehensively. It is designed for your background (39 years old, pharmacy domain, transitioning toward Business Analyst/Product Manager, beginner in Agile, prefers practical learning over theory).

Act as a Senior Agile Coach, Scrum Master, Product Manager, and Business Analyst with 20+ years of industry experience.

Your task is to teach me Agile completely from absolute beginner to advanced level as if I am preparing for a Business Analyst, Product Analyst, Product Manager, or AI Product Manager role.

About Me:

- I have a Pharmacy background.

- I am transitioning into IT.

- I am a beginner in Agile.

- I learn best through practical examples.

- I want industry-level knowledge, not just certification knowledge.

- Assume I know nothing about Agile.

Your teaching style:

- Explain every concept in very simple English.

- Use real-world analogies before technical explanations.

- Use healthcare/pharmacovigilance examples whenever possible.

- Explain why something exists before explaining how it works.

- Never skip foundational concepts.

- Teach like a mentor, not like a textbook.

- Ask me small quizzes after each lesson.

- Give assignments and mini projects.

- Don\'t move to the next topic until the current topic is understood.

Cover everything from beginner to expert level.

Agile Masterclass

Module 1 -- Introduction to Agile

Lesson 1: What is Agile?

1. Concept

Agile is a mindset and a way of working that helps teams build products by delivering small pieces frequently, learning from feedback, and continuously improving.

Many beginners think Agile is:

❌ A software development process

❌ Scrum

❌ Jira

❌ Daily Standup meetings

These are not Agile.

Agile is a philosophy.

Everything else (Scrum, Kanban, Jira, Sprint, User Stories) comes later.

Think of Agile as the operating system of product development.

2. Why Agile Exists

Before understanding Agile...

You first need to understand the problem.

Imagine you want to build a house.

Traditional Method

You spend six months creating drawings.

Then another six months constructing.

After one year...

Customer says:

\"I don\'t like the kitchen.\"

Too late.

Everything is already built.

Huge money wasted.

Now imagine building room by room.

After building the kitchen...

Customer says:

\"I want a bigger window.\"

You change it immediately.

Then build the bedroom.

Again get feedback.

Then bathroom.

Again improve.

This is Agile.

Instead of building everything first...

You build...

Learn...

Improve...

Repeat.

3. Simple Explanation

Imagine you\'re cooking for guests.

Traditional Way

Cook 25 dishes.

Guests arrive.

Nobody likes spicy food.

Everything is wasted.

Agile Way

Prepare one dish.

Serve.

Ask feedback.

Improve.

Cook next dish.

Again improve.

Eventually every dish matches guests\' tastes.

Agile works exactly like this.

4. Real-life Analogy

Imagine writing a book.

Waterfall

Write all 500 pages.

Then show publisher.

Publisher says:

\"Wrong audience.\"

Start over.

Agile

Write first chapter.

Publisher reviews.

Improve.

Write second chapter.

Improve.

Continue.

Much safer.

5. Technical Explanation

Traditional software development assumed:

\"We know every requirement from Day 1.\"

Reality says:

Customers change.

Business changes.

Technology changes.

Competitors change.

Regulations change.

Users change.

Therefore...

Requirements also change.

Agile accepts change instead of fighting it.

That is Agile\'s biggest strength.

Agile Formula

Build Small\ \ ↓\ \ Get Feedback\ \ ↓\ \ Improve\ \ ↓\ \ Repeat\ \ ↓\ \ Deliver Value

Another way to visualize it:

Idea\ \ ↓\ \ Small Feature\ \ ↓\ \ Customer Feedback\ \ ↓\ \ Improvement\ \ ↓\ \ Next Feature\ \ ↓\ \ Feedback\ \ ↓\ \ Better Product

Instead of:

Idea\ \ ↓\ \ 12 Months Development\ \ ↓\ \ Launch\ \ ↓\ \ Failure

6. Industry Example

Suppose a company wants to build a food delivery app.

Traditional approach:

6 months planning\ \ ↓\ \ 8 months coding\ \ ↓\ \ Launch\ \ ↓\ \ Customers hate UI

Entire project must be redesigned.

Agile approach:

Week 1

Login

Customer feedback

Week 2

Restaurant list

Feedback

Week 3

Cart

Feedback

Week 4

Payment

Feedback

Week 5

Tracking

Feedback

By launch...

The product has already been improved based on real user input.

7. Healthcare Example

Suppose a hospital wants software for patient appointments.

Traditional approach:

Develop entire hospital system for one year.

After launch...

Doctors say:

Appointment workflow doesn\'t match real practice.

Expensive redesign.

Agile approach:

Sprint 1

Appointment booking

Doctors test.

Suggestions collected.

Sprint 2

Patient registration

More feedback.

Sprint 3

Prescription module

Again improved.

Eventually software matches real hospital workflow.

8. AI Product Example

Let\'s use your future project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform

Instead of building all modules:

  • Login

  • Dashboard

  • MedDRA Coding

  • Signal Detection

  • Literature Screening

  • Duplicate Detection

  • Reports

all together...

Agile would build:

Sprint 1

✅ Login

✅ Dashboard

Users test.

Sprint 2

ICSR Management

Users test.

Sprint 3

AI Data Extraction

Users test.

Sprint 4

MedDRA Coding

Users test.

Sprint 5

Signal Detection

Users test.

Every sprint improves the product based on actual user feedback from pharmacovigilance professionals.

9. Common Mistakes

❌ Thinking Agile means \"no planning.\"

Reality:\ Agile plans continuously.

❌ Thinking Agile means \"work faster.\"

Reality:\ Agile focuses on delivering value, not simply increasing speed.

❌ Thinking Scrum = Agile.

Reality:

Agile → Philosophy

Scrum → Framework implementing Agile principles

❌ Thinking Agile has no documentation.

Reality:

Agile values necessary documentation, avoiding unnecessary paperwork.

10. Best Practices

  • Deliver small, usable increments.

  • Gather customer feedback early and often.

  • Be open to changing requirements.

  • Collaborate across roles.

  • Continuously inspect and improve your process.

  • Focus on customer value rather than just completing tasks.

11. Interview Questions

Q1: What is Agile?

Answer:\ Agile is a mindset and set of values and principles for developing products iteratively, delivering value in small increments, and adapting based on customer feedback.

Q2: Is Agile a methodology?

A better answer is:\ Agile is primarily a mindset. Frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban help teams apply Agile principles.

Q3: Why was Agile introduced?

To overcome the limitations of traditional development by embracing changing requirements, reducing risk through frequent delivery, and improving customer satisfaction.

12. Mini Quiz

Answer these without looking back:

  1. Is Agile a framework or a mindset?

  2. Why was Agile created?

  3. What is the biggest advantage of Agile?

  4. Name one real-life example where Agile is useful.

  5. Is Scrum the same as Agile?

13. Practical Assignment

Imagine you\'re building your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

Write down:

  1. Why would building everything at once be risky?

  2. Which module would you build first?

  3. Which module would you build second?

  4. Why?

  5. What feedback would you collect after the first release?

Don\'t worry about perfect answers---we\'ll refine them together.

14. Jira Example

Imagine your Jira backlog contains:

Epic\ AI Pharmacovigilance Platform\ \ ↓\ \ Story 1\ User Login\ \ ↓\ \ Story 2\ Dashboard\ \ ↓\ \ Story 3\ Create ICSR Case\ \ ↓\ \ Story 4\ AI Extract Source Document\ \ ↓\ \ Story 5\ MedDRA Coding

In Agile, the team might choose only Story 1 and Story 2 for the first sprint, deliver them, gather feedback, and then plan the next sprint.

15. Diagram

Traditional Development\ \ Requirements\ │\ ▼\ Planning\ │\ ▼\ Development\ │\ ▼\ Testing\ │\ ▼\ Deployment\ │\ ▼\ Customer Feedback

Agile Development\ \ Idea\ │\ ▼\ Small Feature\ │\ ▼\ Customer Feedback\ │\ ▼\ Improve\ │\ ▼\ Next Feature\ │\ ▼\ Feedback\ │\ ▼\ Continuous Improvement

16. Summary

  • Agile is a mindset, not a tool or framework.

  • It emphasizes delivering value in small increments.

  • Customer feedback drives continuous improvement.

  • Change is expected and welcomed.

  • Scrum and Kanban are ways to practice Agile, but they are not Agile itself.

17. Key Takeaways

  • Agile = Mindset

  • Deliver small, valuable increments

  • Get feedback early

  • Improve continuously

  • Accept change instead of resisting it

  • Focus on customer value

Revision Cheat Sheet

Term Meaning

Agile A mindset for iterative, adaptive product development

Iteration A short cycle of work that produces something usable

Feedback Input from users or stakeholders to improve the product

Increment A working piece of the product delivered after each cycle

Continuous Regularly refining both the product and the Improvement team\'s process

14. Jira Example

Imagine the Jira board for Sprint 1 of the ADR platform:

+-----------+-------------+-----------+---------+

| To Do | In Progress | In Review | Done |

+-----------+-------------+-----------+---------+

| Login | | | |

| Register | | | |

| Dashboard | | | |

+-----------+-------------+-----------+---------+

As work progresses, cards move from left to right.

We\'ll learn Jira in depth later, but this gives you the basic idea.

15. Diagram

CUSTOMER

│

▼

Build Small Feature

│

▼

Release to Users

│

▼

Collect Feedback

│

▼

Improve the Product

│

▼

Build Next Small Feature

│

└──────────────► Repeat

This continuous loop is at the heart of Agile.

Module 1 -- Introduction to Agile

Lesson 2: Why Agile Was Created

1. Concept

Agile was created because traditional software development was failing to deliver what businesses and customers actually needed.

The problem wasn\'t that developers couldn\'t write code. The problem was that the world changes faster than long projects can keep up.

Imagine you\'re driving to a destination using a map printed 10 years ago. Roads have changed, traffic patterns have changed, and new highways exist. Even if you follow the map perfectly, you may still end up in the wrong place.

Traditional development assumed the \"map\" (requirements) would never change.

Agile accepts that the map will change---and plans for it.

2. Why It Exists

Before Agile, most software projects followed a sequential model (later known as Waterfall):

Requirements\ ↓\ Design\ ↓\ Development\ ↓\ Testing\ ↓\ Deployment

Each stage had to finish before the next one began.

This looked organized---but it created serious problems.

For example:

  • Requirements written in January

  • Development started in March

  • Testing in October

  • Product launched next January

By launch, customer needs might already have changed.

3. Simple Explanation

Imagine you\'re tailoring a suit.

Traditional Approach

  • Customer gives measurements.

  • Tailor works for two months.

  • Suit is delivered.

  • Customer has lost 8 kg.

The suit no longer fits.

Agile Approach

The tailor schedules fittings every week.

Week 1: Check measurements.

Week 2: Adjust sleeves.

Week 3: Adjust shoulders.

Week 4: Final fitting.

The finished suit fits perfectly because adjustments were made throughout the process.

That\'s Agile.

4. Real-Life Analogy

Suppose you open a restaurant.

Traditional thinking:

  • Design a menu with 200 dishes.

  • Spend ₹20 lakh on equipment.

  • Hire staff.

  • Open after one year.

Customers arrive and only order 20 dishes.

Most of your investment was unnecessary.

Agile thinking:

Week 1:

  • Launch with 15 dishes.

Collect customer feedback.

Week 3:

  • Add popular items.

Week 6:

  • Remove dishes nobody orders.

Your menu evolves based on real customer behavior.

5. Technical Explanation

During the 1980s and 1990s, software projects became increasingly large and complex.

Common issues included:

1. Changing Requirements

Businesses frequently changed their priorities while projects were still underway.

Example:

A bank initially requests online fund transfers.

Six months later, regulations require two-factor authentication.

The original requirements are now incomplete.

2. Late Customer Feedback

Customers often didn\'t see the software until it was almost finished.

By then, changing it was expensive and time-consuming.

3. High Failure Rates

Many projects experienced:

  • Budget overruns

  • Schedule delays

  • Missing features

  • Low customer satisfaction

4. Poor Communication

Business teams wrote long requirement documents.

Developers interpreted them.

Testers interpreted them again.

Important details were often misunderstood.

5. High Cost of Change

In traditional development:

Requirement Change\ \ ↓\ \ Rewrite Design\ \ ↓\ \ Rewrite Code\ \ ↓\ \ Retest Everything\ \ ↓\ \ Delay Project\ \ ↓\ \ Increase Cost

The later a change happened, the more expensive it became.

Agile reduces this risk by encouraging small, frequent adjustments.

6. Industry Example

Imagine an e-commerce company building a shopping app.

Traditional

12-month project.

After launch, users complain:

  • Search is confusing.

  • Checkout takes too many steps.

  • Wishlist is missing.

Major redesign required.

Agile

Month 1:

  • Product search.

Users provide feedback.

Month 2:

  • Shopping cart.

Feedback incorporated.

Month 3:

  • Checkout.

Improved based on real user testing.

The product becomes better every month instead of waiting until the end.

7. Healthcare Example

A hospital wants an Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system.

Traditional

After 18 months, doctors say:

  • Too many clicks.

  • Prescription workflow is incorrect.

  • Emergency cases are difficult to record.

The software technically works---but doesn\'t fit daily clinical practice.

Agile

Sprint 1:

  • Patient registration.

Doctors test it.

Sprint 2:

  • Appointment scheduling.

Feedback collected.

Sprint 3:

  • Prescription module.

Improved after physician review.

The system evolves around real healthcare workflows.

8. AI Product Example

Let\'s use your future AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform.

Initial assumption:

Users want AI to extract adverse event data from source documents.

After the first sprint, users say:

\"The extracted information is good, but we need confidence scores and highlighted source text.\"

With Agile:

  • Add confidence scores.

  • Highlight extracted text.

  • Improve the AI prompt.

  • Release an updated version.

Without Agile:

That feedback might only arrive after the full platform is finished, making changes much more expensive.

9. Common Mistakes

❌ \"Agile was created to make development faster.\"

Not exactly.

Its primary goal is to deliver the right product, not merely to increase speed.

❌ \"Planning isn\'t important in Agile.\"

Agile still plans---but planning happens continuously rather than only once at the beginning.

❌ \"Requirements don\'t matter.\"

Requirements are essential.

Agile simply recognizes that they may evolve.

❌ \"Change means poor planning.\"

Not always.

Markets, regulations, customer expectations, and technology all change.

Agile prepares teams to respond effectively.

10. Best Practices

  • Expect requirements to evolve.

  • Deliver usable software early.

  • Involve customers regularly.

  • Break large projects into smaller increments.

  • Learn from every release.

  • Improve continuously based on evidence.

11. Interview Questions

Q1. Why was Agile created?

Answer:

Agile was created to address the limitations of traditional software development by enabling teams to adapt to changing requirements, deliver value incrementally, collaborate closely with customers, and reduce project risk.

Q2. What problem does Agile solve?

It helps organizations respond effectively to changing business needs instead of relying on fixed assumptions made at the start of a project.

Q3. What are the biggest drawbacks of traditional development?

  • Fixed requirements

  • Late feedback

  • High cost of change

  • Long delivery cycles

  • Increased risk of building the wrong product

12. Mini Quiz

Try answering these without looking back:

  1. Why did traditional software projects often fail?

  2. What is the biggest assumption made by traditional development?

  3. Why is customer feedback important in Agile?

  4. Does Agile eliminate planning?

  5. Why is changing requirements less expensive in Agile?

13. Practical Assignment

Imagine your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

The client initially requests these modules:

  • Login

  • Dashboard

  • ICSR Management

  • AI Data Extraction

  • MedDRA Coding

  • WHO Drug Coding

  • Duplicate Detection

  • Signal Detection

  • Reports

After Sprint 1, users say:

  • \"We don\'t need WHO Drug Coding yet.\"

  • \"AI Data Extraction is our highest priority.\"

  • \"The Dashboard needs more case statistics.\"

Write down:

  1. Which modules would you reprioritize?

  2. What would move into the next sprint?

  3. What would you postpone?

  4. Why is Agile better suited to handling this change than a rigid plan?

14. Jira Example

Imagine your backlog starts like this:

Epic: AI Pharmacovigilance Platform\ \ Story 1: Login\ Story 2: Dashboard\ Story 3: ICSR Management\ Story 4: WHO Drug Coding\ Story 5: AI Data Extraction\ Story 6: Reports

After Sprint 1, the Product Owner updates priorities:

Story 1: AI Data Extraction\ Story 2: Dashboard Improvements\ Story 3: ICSR Management\ Story 4: Login Enhancements\ Story 5: Reports\ Story 6: WHO Drug Coding

Notice that nothing is \"wrong\" with the original plan---the priorities simply changed based on new information.

15. Diagram

Traditional Development

Requirements\ │\ ▼\ Design\ │\ ▼\ Development\ │\ ▼\ Testing\ │\ ▼\ Customer Feedback\ │\ ▼\ Expensive Changes

Agile Development

Plan\ │\ ▼\ Build Small\ │\ ▼\ Customer Feedback\ │\ ▼\ Improve\ │\ ▼\ Build Next Feature\ │\ ▼\ Repeat

16. Summary

Agile was created because long, rigid projects often produced software that no longer matched customer needs by the time it was delivered. Instead of assuming requirements remain fixed, Agile embraces change through short development cycles, regular customer feedback, and continuous improvement.

17. Key Takeaways

  • Traditional development assumed requirements would stay the same.

  • Real-world requirements frequently change.

  • Agile was designed to manage change rather than resist it.

  • Early and frequent feedback reduces risk.

  • The goal of Agile is building the right product, not just building it quickly.

Revision Cheat Sheet

Problem Traditional Agile Approach Approach

Changing requirements Difficult and Expected and manageable expensive

Customer feedback At the end Throughout the project

Risk High Reduced through small releases

Planning Mostly upfront Continuous

Delivery One large release Frequent small releases

Module 1 -- Introduction to Agile

Lesson 3: Problems with Traditional Waterfall

Learning Objective

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to answer:

  • What is Waterfall?

  • Why was Waterfall successful for many years?

  • Why does it struggle in software development?

  • When should Waterfall still be used?

  • How does Agile solve Waterfall\'s biggest problems?

1. Concept

Before Agile existed, almost every software project followed the Waterfall Model.

The name \"Waterfall\" comes from the idea that work flows downward, like a waterfall.

Requirements\ ↓\ Design\ ↓\ Development\ ↓\ Testing\ ↓\ Deployment\ ↓\ Maintenance

Each phase must be completed before moving to the next.

You do not go back unless absolutely necessary.

Think of climbing down a waterfall---you can\'t easily climb back up.

2. Why Waterfall Was Created

In the 1960s and 1970s, software was:

  • Smaller

  • Less complex

  • Built for governments and large organizations

  • Used on mainframe computers

  • Rarely changed after deployment

Projects needed:

  • Heavy planning

  • Detailed documentation

  • Strict approvals

Waterfall worked well because requirements changed very little.

3. Simple Explanation

Imagine building a bridge.

Before construction begins, engineers know:

  • Length

  • Height

  • Materials

  • Budget

  • Safety standards

You cannot build half a bridge and ask:

\"Would you like it longer?\"

Everything must be planned first.

Waterfall is perfect here.

Now imagine building a social media app.

You don\'t know:

  • Which features users will love

  • What competitors will launch next month

  • What regulations will change

  • How user behavior will evolve

This uncertainty makes Waterfall much less suitable.

4. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine ordering a custom wedding cake.

Waterfall

You choose:

  • Flavor

  • Size

  • Design

  • Decoration

The baker spends two weeks making it.

When you see it:

\"Actually, I\'d like it to be chocolate instead of vanilla.\"

The baker has to start over.

Agile

The baker first creates a small sample.

You taste it.

Adjust sweetness.

Try frosting.

Choose decorations.

The final cake matches your expectations because you gave feedback throughout.

5. Technical Explanation

Waterfall follows a linear sequential model.

Phase 1 → Phase 2 → Phase 3 → Phase 4

Each phase depends on the previous one being completed.

For example:

Requirements\ ↓\ System Design\ ↓\ Coding\ ↓\ Testing\ ↓\ Release

Testing only begins after coding is complete.

If testers discover a major issue, developers may need to revisit earlier work, causing delays and increased costs.

6. Why Waterfall Worked in Other Industries

Waterfall is still excellent when requirements are stable.

Examples:

Building a Hospital

You cannot:

  • Build ICU first

  • Design the foundation later

Everything must be planned.

Manufacturing an Aircraft

Changing the wing design after production starts could be dangerous and extremely expensive.

Highway Construction

Road dimensions, bridges, and materials are determined before construction.

Frequent changes would waste enormous amounts of money.

7. Why Waterfall Fails in Software

Software is different because it is easy to change technically---but difficult to change late in a project if everything depends on earlier decisions.

Here are the biggest challenges.

Problem 1 -- Requirements Change

Month 1:

Customer wants Feature A.

Month 8:

Customer now needs Feature B instead.

Waterfall assumes requirements remain fixed.

Reality rarely works that way.

Problem 2 -- Late Feedback

Customers may not see the product for many months.

By then, they often discover that the solution doesn\'t meet their real needs.

Problem 3 -- Expensive Changes

Imagine:

100,000 lines of code written\ \ ↓\ \ Customer requests a major workflow change\ \ ↓\ \ Architecture changes\ \ ↓\ \ Code rewritten\ \ ↓\ \ Testing repeated\ \ ↓\ \ Documentation updated

Late changes affect the entire project.

Problem 4 -- Long Delivery Cycles

Customers wait many months before receiving anything usable.

If the product is wrong, they only find out after significant time and investment.

Problem 5 -- High Risk

If a project lasts two years:

  • Technology may change.

  • Competitors may release better products.

  • Business priorities may shift.

  • Regulations may evolve.

The final product can already be outdated.

The Birth of Agile (2001)

In 2001, 17 experienced software practitioners met in the mountains of Utah, USA.

They had different backgrounds but shared a common frustration:

  • Too much paperwork

  • Too little customer collaboration

  • Long delivery cycles

They created what became known as the Agile Manifesto.

This document changed software development worldwide.

Important: The Agile Manifesto did not invent Agile.

It summarized ideas that experienced practitioners had already been using successfully.

We\'ll study the Manifesto in detail in the next lessons.

Lesson 5 -- The Agile Manifesto

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

1. Concept

The Agile Manifesto is a short document created in 2001 that defines the core values of Agile software development.

It does not tell you:

  • How to run meetings

  • How long a Sprint should be

  • How to write User Stories

  • Which tool to use

Instead, it answers a more fundamental question:

\"What should we value when building software?\"

That is why it\'s called a manifesto, not a process manual.

2. Why It Exists

By the late 1990s, many software teams were frustrated.

Projects often had:

  • Hundreds of pages of documentation

  • Months of planning

  • Long approval chains

  • Very little customer interaction

  • Software delivered too late

The process became more important than the product.

Developers began asking:

\"Why are we spending more time writing documents than solving customer problems?\"

3. The Story Behind the Agile Manifesto

In February 2001, 17 experienced software practitioners met at a ski resort in Utah, USA.

Although they used different development methods, they agreed on one thing:

Traditional software projects focused too much on rigid processes and not enough on delivering value.

Together they created the Agile Manifesto, a one-page document that transformed software development.

4. The Agile Manifesto

The Agile Manifesto says:

We are uncovering better ways of developing software by doing it and helping others do it.

It continues:

Through this work we have come to value:

Value 1

Individuals and interactions

over

Processes and tools

Value 2

Working software

over

Comprehensive documentation

Value 3

Customer collaboration

over

Contract negotiation

Value 4

Responding to change

over

Following a plan

Important

Notice that the Manifesto does not say:

  • Processes are bad

  • Documentation is useless

  • Contracts are unnecessary

  • Planning should be ignored

Instead, it says:

While the items on the right have value, we value the items on the left more.

This distinction is frequently asked in interviews.

Value 1: Individuals and Interactions over Processes and Tools

Why?

Processes and tools cannot solve problems by themselves.

People solve problems.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a hospital.

Would you rather have:

  • The world\'s best hospital software

  • Poor communication between doctors and nurses

OR

  • Good communication between healthcare professionals

  • Average software

Most people would choose the second option.

Good teamwork often produces better outcomes than perfect tools alone.

Software Example

Two developers using only email to communicate may misunderstand requirements.

Two developers discussing the work directly for ten minutes can often solve the issue immediately.

Pharmacovigilance Example

Suppose an AI incorrectly extracts an adverse event.

A pharmacovigilance specialist, developer, and Product Owner discuss the issue together.

Within minutes they identify the cause and improve the extraction logic.

The conversation creates more value than simply following a predefined process.

Interview Tip

Agile values people first, while still recognizing that processes and tools are important.

Value 2: Working Software over Comprehensive Documentation

This value is often misunderstood.

It does not mean:

\"Don\'t write documentation.\"

Instead, it means:

Documentation should support the product---not replace it.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine buying a new washing machine.

Which is more valuable?

  • A 500-page manual

  • A washing machine that actually works

The manual has value.

But the working machine provides the real value.

Software Example

Traditional approach:

  • 300-page requirement document

  • No usable software for a year

Agile approach:

  • Essential documentation

  • Working software delivered every few weeks

Healthcare Example

Imagine a hospital receives:

  • A detailed system specification

  • No working patient registration module

The document doesn\'t help patients.

A functioning registration system does.

AI Pharmacovigilance Example

Would your users prefer:

  • A 200-page AI design document

or

  • An AI that correctly extracts adverse event information from PDF reports?

The second option delivers immediate value.

Value 3: Customer Collaboration over Contract Negotiation

Traditional projects often treated the signed contract as the final authority.

Agile treats the customer as an ongoing partner.

Real-Life Analogy

Imagine hiring an architect.

Traditional approach:

Sign the contract.

No further discussions.

Receive the completed house a year later.

Agile approach:

Review progress regularly.

Adjust room sizes.

Improve the layout.

Refine the design together.

The customer remains involved throughout the project.

Healthcare Example

Doctors test each release and suggest improvements.

The software evolves around real clinical workflows instead of assumptions.

AI Product Example

Users say:

\"We need confidence scores for AI-extracted adverse events.\"

The Product Owner updates priorities.

The team delivers this improvement in a future sprint.

Value 4: Responding to Change over Following a Plan

This is one of Agile\'s defining characteristics.

Plans are useful.

But plans should evolve when reality changes.

Real-Life Analogy

You\'re driving from Ahmedabad to Mumbai.

Your GPS reports:

\"Accident ahead.\"

Would you continue on the original route because that was the plan?

Of course not.

You choose a better route.

Agile works the same way.

Healthcare Example

A new regulatory guideline requires additional safety reporting fields.

An Agile team updates the backlog and implements the change in upcoming iterations.

AI Example

A significantly better AI model becomes available.

Instead of ignoring it because it wasn\'t in the original plan, the team evaluates whether adopting it provides more customer value.

Agile Values More... Than...

Individuals and interactions Processes and tools

Working software Comprehensive documentation

Customer collaboration Contract negotiation

Responding to change Following a plan

The items on the right still matter.

The items on the left matter more when trade-offs arise.

Lesson 7: Agile Mindset

This lesson will help you move from knowing Agile terminology to thinking like an Agile professional.

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What an Agile mindset means.

  • How Agile thinking differs from traditional thinking.

  • Why mindset is more important than simply following Scrum rituals.

  • How an Agile mindset applies to Business Analysts, Product Managers, and AI product development.

  • How to apply this mindset to healthcare and pharmacovigilance projects.

What is an Agile mindset?

An Agile mindset is a way of thinking that values:

  • Customer value over simply completing tasks.

  • Learning and adaptation over rigidly following a plan.

  • Collaboration over working in silos.

  • Continuous improvement over assuming the first solution is perfect.

  • Experimentation and feedback over making assumptions without validation.

Simple definition: Agile mindset means focusing on delivering value, learning quickly, adapting to change, and continuously improving.

Why mindset matters more than process

A team can:

  • Hold Daily Scrums.

  • Use Jira.

  • Write User Stories.

  • Run Sprint Reviews.

But if they still:

  • Ignore customer feedback,

  • Resist change,

  • Work in silos, or

  • Focus only on finishing tasks,

then they are doing Agile without being Agile.

Real-life analogy

Imagine two doctors treating patients.

  • Doctor A follows a checklist exactly, even when the patient's condition changes.

  • Doctor B follows medical guidelines but also observes the patient, adjusts treatment, and learns from the outcome.

Doctor B demonstrates an Agile mindset: use a process, but adapt based on real evidence.

Agile mindset vs traditional mindset

Traditional mindset Agile mindset

Requirements are fixed. Requirements can evolve.

Follow the original plan. Adapt based on feedback.

Success means completing scope. Success means delivering customer value.

Changes are problems. Changes are opportunities to improve.

Teams work in separate silos. Teams collaborate closely.

Learning happens at the end. Learning happens continuously.

Core elements of an Agile mindset

1. Customer-centric thinking

Agile teams constantly ask:

"How does this feature help the customer?"

Example: In an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, a Product Manager should ask:

"Will this AI feature make case processing faster, more accurate, or more compliant for pharmacovigilance professionals?"

2. Embracing change

Agile professionals understand that change is natural.

  • Customer needs change.

  • Business priorities change.

Lesson 8: Agile vs Waterfall

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • The fundamental differences between Agile and Waterfall.

  • When each approach is most appropriate.

  • The advantages and limitations of both models.

  • How to explain Agile vs Waterfall in interviews.

  • How these approaches apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What is Waterfall?

The Waterfall model is a linear and sequential approach to project management and software development.

In Waterfall, work flows through predefined phases:

Requirements

↓

Design

↓

Development

↓

Testing

↓

Deployment

Each phase is usually completed before the next phase begins. This makes Waterfall structured and predictable when requirements are stable.

What is Agile?

Agile is an iterative and incremental approach. Instead of completing the entire project before delivery, Agile teams build and deliver the product in small increments.

Plan Small Feature

↓

Build

↓

Test

↓

Get Feedback

↓

Improve

↓

Repeat

This allows teams to learn from feedback and adapt the product continuously.

Aspect Waterfall Agile

Approach Linear and sequential Iterative and incremental

Simple real-life analogy

Waterfall analogy: building a bridge

When building a bridge, engineers must know the exact:

  • Length

  • Height

  • Materials

  • Budget

  • Safety requirements

Changing the bridge design after construction starts can be extremely expensive and dangerous. Therefore, Waterfall works well for projects with stable requirements.

Agile analogy: creating a mobile app

When building a mobile app, customer preferences may change frequently:

  • Users may want a simpler interface.

  • Competitors may introduce new features.

  • Market trends may shift.

  • Technology may evolve.

In this situation, Agile is more suitable because the team can release features incrementally and adapt based on user feedback.

Waterfall advantages

  • Clear structure: Each phase has defined deliverables and milestones.

  • Predictable scope: Requirements are documented upfront.

  • Strong documentation: Useful for regulatory and compliance-heavy projects.

  • Easier budgeting: Costs and timelines can be estimated more clearly when requirements are stable.

  • Suitable for fixed-scope projects: Works well when changes are unlikely.

Waterfall limitations

  • Inflexible to change: Modifying requirements later can be costly.

  • Late feedback: Customers may not see the product until late in the project.

  • Higher risk: If requirements are misunderstood, the final product may not meet user needs.

  • Long delivery cycles: Customers wait longer to receive usable value.

Agile advantages

  • Flexibility: Requirements can evolve as the project progresses.

  • Early value delivery: Customers receive usable features sooner.

  • Continuous feedback: Regular input improves product quality.

  • Reduced risk: Problems are identified and corrected early.

  • Better collaboration: Cross-functional teams work closely together.

Agile limitations

  • Less predictability: Scope may change during the project.

  • Requires active customer involvement: Stakeholders must provide regular feedback.

  • Can be challenging for fixed contracts: Flexible scope may conflict with rigid contractual agreements.

  • Needs strong team discipline: Agile works best when teams are collaborative and self-organized.

When to use Waterfall

Waterfall is most appropriate when:

  • Requirements are clear, stable, and unlikely to change.

  • The project involves physical construction or manufacturing.

  • Regulatory compliance requires detailed upfront documentation.

  • The project scope, budget, and timeline are fixed.

  • Examples include bridges, buildings, aerospace systems, and some highly regulated healthcare systems.

When to use Agile

Agile is most appropriate when:

  • Requirements are expected to change.

  • Customer feedback is essential.

  • The project involves software, AI, or digital products.

  • Innovation and rapid learning are priorities.

  • Examples include mobile apps, web platforms, AI systems, and evolving healthcare software.

Healthcare example

Waterfall in healthcare

A hospital building project may use Waterfall because:

  • The architectural design must be approved upfront.

  • Safety regulations require detailed planning.

  • Changes during construction can be costly.

Agile in healthcare software

A Hospital Management System may use Agile because:

  • Doctors and nurses can test modules early.

  • Workflows can be refined based on real usage.

  • Features such as appointment scheduling, prescription management, and billing can be released incrementally.

Pharmacovigilance example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform:

Waterfall approach

  • Gather all requirements upfront.

  • Design the complete system.

  • Develop all modules over many months.

  • Release the entire platform at the end.

Agile approach

  • Sprint 1: Login and Dashboard.

  • Sprint 2: ICSR Management.

  • Sprint 3: AI Data Extraction.

  • Sprint 4: MedDRA Coding.

  • Gather feedback after each sprint and adjust priorities.

The Agile approach is better suited here because pharmacovigilance regulations, user needs, and AI capabilities may change during development.

AI product example

Imagine building an AI Medical Chatbot.

  • Waterfall risk: The chosen AI model may become outdated before the product launches.

  • Agile benefit: The team can release a basic chatbot, collect user feedback, improve prompts, and integrate better AI models over time.

Common misconceptions

  • "Waterfall is bad." Waterfall is effective for projects with stable requirements and strong regulatory needs.

  • "Agile means no planning." Agile involves continuous planning and prioritization.

  • "Agile is always better." The best approach depends on the project context.

  • "Waterfall has no customer involvement." Customers are involved, but feedback is typically less frequent than in Agile.

Best practices

  • Choose Waterfall when requirements are fixed and compliance demands detailed documentation.

  • Choose Agile when requirements are evolving and customer feedback is critical.

  • Use a hybrid approach when some parts of the project require strict planning while software components benefit from iterative delivery.

  • Always evaluate the project's risk, complexity, regulatory requirements, and customer involvement before selecting an approach.

Interview questions

Q1. What is the main difference between Agile and Waterfall?

Answer: Waterfall is a linear, sequential approach where each phase is completed before the next begins, while Agile is an iterative, incremental approach that delivers value in small increments and adapts based on feedback.

Q2. When would you choose Waterfall over Agile?

Answer: Waterfall is preferred when requirements are clear, stable, and unlikely to change, such as in construction, manufacturing, or highly regulated projects requiring detailed upfront documentation.

Q3. Why is Agile often preferred for software development?

Answer: Agile is preferred because software requirements often change, customer feedback is important, and iterative delivery reduces the risk of building the wrong product.

Agile is an iterative, flexible approach best suited for projects where requirements may change and customer feedback is essential.

For software, AI, healthcare software, and pharmacovigilance platforms, Agile is often more suitable because it allows teams to adapt to evolving user needs, regulations, and technological advancements.

Key takeaways

  • Waterfall = linear, sequential, fixed requirements, one final release.

  • Agile = iterative, incremental, flexible requirements, frequent releases.

  • Waterfall works well for stable, fixed-scope projects.

  • Agile works well for dynamic, customer-driven software projects.

  • The choice between Agile and Waterfall depends on project context, risk, regulatory requirements, and the likelihood of change.

What is Lean?

Lean is a management philosophy focused on maximizing customer value while minimizing waste.

It originated in Toyota's manufacturing system, where the goal was to produce high-quality products efficiently by eliminating activities that did not add value.

Lean means: Deliver more value to the customer with less waste.

Core Lean principles

  • Identify value -- Understand what the customer truly values.

  • Map the value stream -- Analyze all steps required to deliver that value.

  • Create flow -- Ensure work moves smoothly through the process.

  • Establish pull -- Produce work only when there is demand.

  • Pursue perfection -- Continuously improve the process.

What is waste in Lean?

Lean identifies activities that consume time, effort, or resources without adding customer value.

What is Kanban?

Kanban is a workflow management method that helps teams visualize work, limit work in progress (WIP), and improve the flow of tasks through a process.

The word Kanban comes from Japanese and means "visual signal" or "card".

Simple definition

Kanban means: Visualize work, limit work in progress, and continuously improve flow.

Core principles of Kanban

  • Visualize workflow -- Display work items on a Kanban board.

  • Limit work in progress (WIP) -- Prevent the team from taking on too many tasks at once.

  • Manage flow -- Ensure tasks move smoothly from one stage to another.

  • Make process policies explicit -- Clearly define how work moves through the system.

  • Implement feedback loops -- Use regular feedback to improve the process.

  • Improve collaboratively -- Encourage the team to continuously optimize the workflow.

Key Kanban practices

1. Visualize work

A Kanban board makes all work visible. Team members can quickly see:

  • What work is pending.

  • What work is in progress.

  • What work is completed.

  • Where bottlenecks exist.

2. Limit work in progress (WIP)

WIP limits prevent the team from starting too many tasks simultaneously.

Example: If the "In Progress" column has a WIP limit of 2, the team cannot start a third task until one of the current tasks is completed.

3. Manage flow

Kanban focuses on keeping work moving smoothly through the system. The team monitors:

  • Cycle time -- Time taken to complete a task once work begins.

  • Lead time -- Time taken from request to completion.

  • Throughput -- Number of tasks completed in a given period.

In a Hospital Management System, Kanban can help manage:

  • Bug fixes.

  • Feature enhancement requests.

  • Support tickets from hospital staff.

  • Integration tasks with laboratory or billing systems.

A Kanban board allows the team to prioritize urgent healthcare issues and ensure work flows efficiently.

Kanban helps the team manage this continuous flow without waiting for the next sprint.

Advantages of Kanban

  • Improves visibility of all work.

  • Reduces multitasking through WIP limits.

  • Identifies bottlenecks quickly.

  • Supports continuous delivery.

  • Flexible because work can be reprioritized at any time.

  • Simple to implement without major process changes.

Limitations of Kanban

  • May provide less predictability than time-boxed Scrum sprints.

  • Requires discipline in maintaining WIP limits.

  • Can become overloaded if priorities are constantly changing.

  • May not provide enough structure for teams that need defined roles and ceremonies.

When to use Kanban

Kanban is particularly useful for:

  • Support and maintenance work.

  • Continuous flow of tasks.

  • Teams that receive frequent change requests.

  • Operational and service teams.

  • Bug fixing and enhancement requests.

  • AI model improvement pipelines.

Common misconceptions

  • "Kanban is not Agile." Kanban can be used within an Agile environment because it supports continuous improvement and customer value delivery.

  • "Kanban means no planning." Kanban still requires prioritization and workflow management.

  • "Kanban and Scrum cannot be combined." Many teams use Scrumban, which combines Scrum's structure with Kanban's flow management.

Best practices

  • Keep the Kanban board simple and easy to understand.

  • Set realistic WIP limits.

  • Review the board regularly to identify bottlenecks.

  • Use metrics such as cycle time, lead time, and throughput.

  • Continuously improve the workflow based on feedback and data.

Q2. What is the main difference between Scrum and Kanban?

Answer: Scrum uses fixed-length sprints and defined roles, while Kanban uses continuous flow, visual workflow management, and WIP limits.

Q3. What is a WIP limit?

Answer: A WIP limit restricts the number of tasks that can be in a particular stage of the workflow at the same time, helping reduce multitasking and improve flow.

Scrum analogy: a specific fitness plan

Scrum is like a specific workout program that helps someone apply the healthy living philosophy.

  • It defines workout schedules.

  • It defines roles such as trainer and participant.

  • It defines progress reviews and improvement cycles.

So, Agile is the philosophy; Scrum is one structured method for applying it.

Key Scrum components

1. Scrum roles

Role Responsibility

Product Owner Defines and prioritizes the Product Backlog.

Scrum Master Facilitates Scrum and removes impediments.

Developers Build and deliver the product increment.

2. Scrum events

  • Sprint -- A fixed-length iteration, usually 1--4 weeks.

  • Sprint Planning -- Team plans the work for the Sprint.

  • Daily Scrum -- Short daily meeting to inspect progress.

  • Sprint Review -- Demonstrate the completed work to stakeholders.

  • Sprint Retrospective -- Reflect on the process and identify improvements.

3. Scrum artifacts

Artifact Purpose

Product Backlog Prioritized list of all desired work.

Sprint Backlog Work selected for the current Sprint.

Increment Working product delivered at the end of the Sprint.

How Scrum implements Agile principles

Agile principle Scrum practice

Deliver value Scrum delivers increments at the end of each frequently. Sprint.

Respond to change. Product Backlog can be reprioritized.

Collaborate closely. Daily Scrum and cross-functional teamwork.

Continuous improvement. Sprint Retrospective.

Customer feedback. Sprint Review with stakeholders.

Healthcare example

Imagine developing a Hospital Management System.

Agile approach

  • Focus on delivering value to doctors, nurses, and patients.

  • Adapt requirements based on user feedback.

  • Improve the product continuously.

Scrum implementation

  • Sprint 1: Patient registration module.

  • Sprint 2: Appointment scheduling module.

  • Sprint 3: Prescription management module.

  • Sprint Review: Hospital staff provide feedback after each Sprint.

Pharmacovigilance example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform:

Agile mindset

  • Prioritize features that improve case processing efficiency.

  • Adapt to changing pharmacovigilance regulations.

  • Gather feedback from pharmacovigilance professionals.

Scrum execution

Sprint Increment delivered

Sprint 1 Login and Dashboard.

Sprint 2 ICSR Management module.

Sprint 3 AI Data Extraction feature.

Sprint 4 MedDRA Coding module.

AI product example

In an AI Medical Chatbot project:

  • Agile mindset: Continuously improve chatbot responses based on user feedback.

  • Scrum framework: Plan AI improvements in Sprints, review results with stakeholders, and refine the backlog.

Advantages of Scrum

  • Clear structure through defined roles and events.

  • Frequent delivery through Sprints.

  • Transparency through backlog visibility and reviews.

  • Continuous improvement through retrospectives.

  • Better collaboration through cross-functional teamwork.

Limitations of Scrum

  • May feel too structured for some teams.

  • Requires commitment to Scrum roles and events.

  • Can be difficult if stakeholders are not actively involved.

  • May not suit teams with highly unpredictable support work.

When to use Scrum

Scrum is particularly useful when:

  • The project has complex and evolving requirements.

  • The team can work in fixed-length iterations.

  • Regular stakeholder feedback is available.

  • The team benefits from defined roles and ceremonies.

  • The goal is to deliver incremental value frequently.

Common misconceptions

  • "Agile and Scrum are the same." Agile is the broader mindset; Scrum is one framework within Agile.

  • "Using Scrum automatically means the team is Agile." Scrum practices must be supported by an Agile mindset.

  • "Agile requires Scrum." Agile can also be implemented through Kanban, XP, Lean, and other frameworks.

Best practices

  • Understand Agile values and principles before applying Scrum.

  • Use Scrum when the team needs structure and regular feedback cycles.

  • Keep the Product Backlog prioritized and transparent.

  • Use Sprint Reviews to gather stakeholder feedback.

  • Use Sprint Retrospectives to improve team performance.

Interview questions

Q1. What is the difference between Agile and Scrum?

Answer: Agile is a mindset and set of values and principles for iterative, customer-focused development. Scrum is a specific Agile framework that provides defined roles, events, artifacts, and Sprints to implement Agile principles.

Q2. Is Scrum part of Agile?

Answer: Yes. Scrum is one of the most widely used frameworks for implementing Agile principles.

Q3. Can a team be Agile without using Scrum?

Answer: Yes. Teams can follow Agile principles using other frameworks such as Kanban, XP, Lean, or custom Agile approaches.

Mini quiz

Try answering these without looking back:

  • Is Agile a framework or a mindset?

  • Is Scrum a mindset or a framework?

  • Name the three Scrum roles.

  • Name the five Scrum events.

  • Why is Scrum considered an Agile framework?

Practical assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

  • Identify which Agile values would guide the product vision.

  • Define the Scrum roles for the project.

  • Create a simple Product Backlog with at least five items.

  • Plan the first Sprint by selecting a small set of backlog items.

  • Explain how the Sprint Review would help improve the platform.

Summary

Agile is a mindset and philosophy that emphasizes customer value, adaptability, collaboration, and continuous improvement.

Scrum is a specific Agile framework that provides roles, events, artifacts, and Sprints to help teams apply Agile principles in a structured way.

A simple way to remember this:

Agile is the philosophy; Scrum is one practical framework for applying that philosophy.

Key takeaways

  • Agile = mindset, values, and principles.

  • Scrum = framework with defined roles, events, and artifacts.

  • Scrum helps teams implement Agile in a structured, iterative manner.

  • Agile can also be implemented through Kanban, XP, Lean, and other frameworks.

  • For AI, healthcare, and pharmacovigilance projects, Scrum is useful when regular feedback and incremental delivery are important.

Lesson 12: Agile Myths

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • Common misconceptions about Agile.

  • The difference between Agile myths and Agile reality.

  • Why these myths can cause Agile implementations to fail.

  • How to explain Agile accurately in interviews and professional discussions.

  • How Agile myths apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

Why Agile myths exist

Agile is often misunderstood because people may:

  • Focus only on Scrum ceremonies.

  • Assume Agile means "faster development."

  • Think Agile removes planning and documentation.

  • Use Agile terminology without adopting the Agile mindset.

Important insight: Agile is not just a set of meetings or tools. It is a mindset focused on delivering customer value, adapting to change, and continuously improving.

Myth 1: Agile means no planning

Reality

Agile requires continuous planning, not the absence of planning.

  • Product Backlog refinement.

  • Sprint Planning.

  • Release planning.

  • Roadmap planning.

Difference:

Traditional planning Agile planning

Most planning happens at the beginning. Planning happens continuously.

Requirements are fixed upfront. Requirements can evolve.

Healthcare example: A Hospital Management System team may plan the overall roadmap, but adjust priorities after doctors test each release.

Myth 2: Agile means no documentation

Reality

Agile values working software over comprehensive documentation, but it does not reject documentation.

  • Agile teams create necessary documentation.

  • Documentation should provide value.

  • Excessive documentation that delays delivery is discouraged.

Pharmacovigilance example: Your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform would still need:

  • Regulatory documentation.

  • User stories and acceptance criteria.

  • Validation records.

  • Release notes.

Agile would simply avoid creating unnecessary documents that do not help users or compliance.

Myth 3: Agile means no deadlines

Reality

Agile projects still have deadlines, release targets, and business commitments.

  • Sprints are time-boxed.

  • Releases can have target dates.

  • Roadmaps provide long-term direction.

  • Priorities may change, but commitments still matter.

AI product example: An AI Medical Chatbot team may have a target release date for the first version, while still refining features based on user feedback.

Myth 4: Agile means changing requirements every day

Reality

Agile welcomes change, but changes are evaluated, prioritized, and managed.

  • Not every request is accepted immediately.

  • The Product Owner prioritizes the Product Backlog.

  • The team focuses on delivering the highest-value work first.

Healthcare example: If a new pharmacovigilance regulation requires additional reporting fields, the Product Owner would prioritize that change in the backlog rather than disrupting all ongoing work.

Myth 5: Agile means working faster

Reality

Agile is primarily about delivering the right value efficiently, not simply working faster.

  • Agile can reduce waste and improve focus.

  • Agile helps teams detect problems earlier.

  • Agile improves customer alignment.

  • However, quality and sustainability should not be sacrificed for speed.

Pharmacovigilance example: It is more valuable to deliver an accurate AI extraction feature incrementally than to rush a large release with poor data quality.

Myth 6: Agile is only for software development

Reality

Agile principles can be applied in many industries, including:

  • Healthcare.

  • Pharmacovigilance.

  • Marketing.

  • Product management.

  • Research and development.

  • AI product development.

Healthcare example: A hospital improvement initiative can use Agile by testing small workflow changes, collecting feedback from staff, and continuously improving patient care processes.

Myth 7: Agile means no management

Reality

Agile changes the role of management, but does not eliminate it.

Traditional management Agile leadership

Directs and controls work. Enables and supports the team.

Focuses on task assignment. Focuses on removing impediments.

Measures activity. Measures customer value and outcomes.

Product Manager example: In Agile, a Product Manager guides product vision, prioritization, and stakeholder alignment rather than micromanaging every task.

Myth 8: Agile means no fixed scope

Reality

Agile projects can have a defined scope or roadmap, but the scope may be refined as the team learns more.

  • The overall product vision can remain stable.

  • Specific features and priorities may evolve.

  • Scope is managed through backlog prioritization.

AI Pharmacovigilance example: The platform's overall scope may include ICSR management, AI extraction, MedDRA coding, and reporting. However, the order and detail of these features may change based on user feedback and regulatory priorities.

Myth 9: Agile is just Scrum

Reality

Scrum is one Agile framework, but Agile includes many approaches.

Agile framework Primary focus

Scrum Structured iterations and roles.

Kanban Continuous flow and WIP limits.

Extreme Programming (XP) Technical excellence and engineering practices.

Lean Eliminating waste and improving flow.

Interview tip: A common interview question is "Is Scrum the same as Agile?" The correct answer is No. Scrum is one framework used to implement Agile principles.

Myth 10: Agile guarantees success

Reality

Agile does not automatically guarantee success. Success depends on:

  • A genuine Agile mindset.

  • Strong collaboration.

  • Clear product vision.

  • Active stakeholder involvement.

  • Continuous improvement.

  • Technical quality.

Healthcare example: A hospital software project using Scrum ceremonies but ignoring doctor feedback would not truly be Agile, and the project could still fail.

Agile myths vs reality summary

Myth Reality

Agile means no planning. Agile uses continuous planning.

Agile means no documentation. Agile values necessary documentation.

Agile means no deadlines. Agile still has time-boxes and release goals.

Agile means constant uncontrolled Changes are evaluated and change. prioritized.

Agile means working faster. Agile means delivering value effectively.

Agile is only for software. Agile principles apply across industries.

Agile means no management. Agile requires supportive leadership.

Agile is just Scrum. Scrum is one Agile framework.

Agile guarantees success. Success depends on proper implementation.

Why these myths are dangerous

  • Teams may stop planning effectively.

  • Important documentation may be neglected.

  • Stakeholders may expect unlimited changes.

  • Managers may misunderstand their role.

  • Organizations may adopt Agile ceremonies without adopting Agile values.

Interview questions

Q1. Does Agile mean no documentation?

Answer: No. Agile values working software over comprehensive documentation, but it still requires necessary documentation that provides value and supports compliance, communication, and maintenance.

Q2. Does Agile mean no planning?

Answer: No. Agile involves continuous planning through backlog refinement, Sprint Planning, release planning, and roadmap adjustments.

Q3. Is Scrum the same as Agile?

Answer: No. Agile is a mindset and set of values and principles, while Scrum is one framework used to implement Agile principles.

Mini quiz

Try answering these without looking back:

  • Does Agile eliminate planning?

  • Does Agile reject all documentation?

  • Is Scrum the same as Agile?

  • Does Agile guarantee project success?

  • What is the main focus of Agile?

Practical assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

  • Identify three Agile myths that stakeholders might believe.

  • Write a correct explanation for each myth.

  • Explain how misunderstanding these myths could affect:

    • Regulatory compliance.

    • AI feature quality.

    • Stakeholder expectations.

    • Project planning.

Summary

Agile is often misunderstood because people focus on surface-level practices instead of the underlying mindset. In reality, Agile:

  • Requires continuous planning.

  • Values necessary documentation.

  • Manages changes through prioritization.

  • Focuses on customer value.

  • Requires collaboration, leadership support, and continuous improvement.

Understanding these myths is important for interviews and for applying Agile effectively in real projects, especially in healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

Key takeaways

  • Agile does not mean no planning.

  • Agile does not mean no documentation.

  • Agile does not mean uncontrolled changes.

  • Agile does not mean simply working faster.

  • Scrum is one Agile framework, not Agile itself.

  • Agile success depends on mindset, collaboration, customer focus, and continuous improvement.

Lesson 13: Where Agile Should and Shouldn't Be Used

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • The characteristics of projects that are well suited for Agile.

  • The characteristics of projects where Agile may not be the best choice.

  • How to evaluate project context before choosing a methodology.

  • How Agile applies to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

  • How to explain methodology selection in interviews and professional discussions.

The key principle

Agile is most effective when requirements are uncertain, likely to change, or need continuous customer feedback.

Traditional approaches such as Waterfall are often more suitable when requirements are stable, fixed, and well understood upfront.

Where Agile should be used

1. Software and digital product development

Agile is highly effective for software projects because requirements often evolve as users interact with the product.

  • Mobile applications.

  • Web applications.

  • SaaS platforms.

  • Enterprise software.

  • Cloud-based services.

Why Agile works:

  • Customer feedback can be gathered frequently.

  • Features can be released incrementally.

  • Priorities can change based on market needs.

  • Bugs and usability issues can be addressed quickly.

2. AI and machine learning projects

AI projects are particularly well suited for Agile because they involve experimentation and continuous learning.

  • AI medical chatbots.

  • Predictive analytics systems.

  • Natural language processing tools.

  • Computer vision applications.

  • AI pharmacovigilance platforms.

Why Agile works:

  • Model performance improves through iterative testing.

  • Data quality issues can be discovered and corrected early.

  • User feedback helps refine AI features.

  • Technology and algorithms evolve rapidly.

3. Healthcare software projects

Agile can be very effective for healthcare software when user workflows need continuous refinement.

  • Hospital Management Systems.

  • Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems.

  • Telemedicine platforms.

  • Patient portals.

  • Clinical decision support systems.

Why Agile works:

  • Doctors, nurses, and administrators can test features early.

  • Workflows can be improved based on real usage.

  • Regulatory and operational changes can be incorporated incrementally.

4. Pharmacovigilance and drug safety platforms

Your AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform is a strong example of a project well suited for Agile.Reasons:

  • Regulatory requirements may change.

  • AI extraction models need continuous improvement.

  • Pharmacovigilance professionals can provide ongoing feedback.

  • Features such as MedDRA coding and duplicate detection can be enhanced iteratively.

5. Innovation and research-driven projects

Agile is useful when the final solution is not fully known at the beginning.

  • New product development.

  • Research and development initiatives.

  • Startup product development.

  • Experimental technology projects.

Where Agile may not be the best choice

1. Construction and physical infrastructure projects

Projects involving physical construction often require detailed upfront planning.

  • Bridges.

  • Buildings.

  • Roads and highways.

  • Hospital construction.

Why Agile is less suitable:

  • Requirements are usually well defined before construction begins.

  • Changes after construction starts can be very costly.

  • Safety and engineering standards require detailed planning.

2. Manufacturing projects with fixed specifications

Manufacturing projects often depend on precise specifications and repeatable processes.

  • Automobile manufacturing.

  • Medical device manufacturing.

  • Pharmaceutical production lines.

Why Agile is less suitable:

  • Product specifications are usually fixed.

  • Changes can disrupt production and increase costs.

  • Quality and regulatory requirements may require strict process control.

3. Projects with stable, fixed requirements

If requirements are fully understood and unlikely to change, a predictive approach may be more efficient.

  • Simple payroll system migration.

  • Standard reporting system implementation.

  • Infrastructure upgrade with fixed scope.

Why Agile may not add much value:

  • The main advantage of Agile is adaptability.

  • If little change is expected, extensive iterative feedback may not be necessary.

4. Highly regulated projects requiring extensive upfront documentation

Some projects require detailed documentation and approval before development can proceed.

  • Aerospace systems.

  • Certain medical device software.

  • Government defense systems.

  • Safety-critical embedded systems.

Important note: Agile can still be used in these environments, but it often needs to be adapted with stronger documentation and compliance controls.

Agile vs non-Agile suitability

Project Agile is suitable Agile may be less characteristic suitable

Requirements Unclear or evolving. Fixed and well understood.

Customer feedback Frequent feedback needed. Limited feedback required.

Change Changes are expected. Changes are rare and costly.

Delivery Incremental delivery Final deliverable needed at possible. once.

Risk Risk reduced through early Risk managed through detailed feedback. upfront planning.

Examples Software, AI products, Construction, manufacturing, healthcare applications. fixed-scope systems.

Healthcare example

Agile is suitable: Hospital Management System

  • Doctors and nurses can test modules early.

  • Workflows can be refined based on real usage.

  • Features such as appointment scheduling and prescription management can be delivered incrementally.

Agile may be less suitable: Hospital building construction

  • Architectural designs must be approved upfront.

  • Safety regulations require detailed planning.

  • Changes during construction can be extremely costly.

Pharmacovigilance example

Agile is suitable: AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

  • AI extraction models require continuous improvement.

  • Regulatory requirements may evolve.

  • Users can provide feedback on extraction accuracy and workflow efficiency.

  • Features such as MedDRA coding and signal detection can be improved iteratively.

Agile may need adaptation: Regulatory submission system

  • Strict compliance documentation may be required.

  • Validation and audit trails are critical.

  • A hybrid approach combining Agile development with rigorous compliance processes may be more appropriate.

AI product example

Agile is suitable: AI Medical Chatbot

  • User feedback helps improve responses.

  • AI models can be updated iteratively.

  • Features such as symptom checking and appointment scheduling can be released incrementally.

Agile may be less suitable: Fixed AI hardware device

  • Hardware specifications may need to be finalized before production.

  • Manufacturing constraints may limit iterative changes.

Decision framework

Before choosing Agile, ask these questions:

Question If yes, Agile is more suitable

Are requirements likely to change? Yes.

Is customer feedback needed frequently? Yes.

Can the product be delivered incrementally? Yes.

Is innovation or experimentation involved? Yes.

Can the team collaborate closely with Yes. stakeholders?

If most answers are yes, Agile is likely a good fit. If most answers are no, a more predictive approach may be appropriate.

Common misconceptions

  • "Agile can be used for every project." Agile is powerful, but not always the best choice.

  • "Waterfall is outdated." Waterfall is still effective for projects with stable requirements and strong regulatory constraints.

  • "Agile and Waterfall are mutually exclusive." Many organizations use hybrid approaches, especially in regulated industries.

Best practices

  • Evaluate requirement uncertainty before choosing Agile.

  • Assess the need for customer feedback.

  • Consider regulatory and documentation requirements.

  • Determine whether incremental delivery is possible.

  • Use hybrid approaches when both flexibility and strict compliance are needed.

Interview questions

Q1. When should Agile be used?

Answer: Agile should be used when requirements are uncertain or likely to change, customer feedback is important, incremental delivery is possible, and the project benefits from adaptability and continuous improvement.

Q2. When may Agile not be the best choice?

Answer: Agile may not be the best choice for projects with fixed requirements, physical construction, manufacturing constraints, or extensive upfront regulatory documentation needs.

Q3. Can Agile be used in regulated industries?

Answer: Yes. Agile can be used in regulated industries such as healthcare and pharmacovigilance, but it may need to be adapted with stronger documentation, validation, and compliance controls.

Mini quiz

Try answering these without looking back:

  • What type of projects are best suited for Agile?

  • Why is Agile suitable for AI projects?

  • Give one example where Waterfall may be more appropriate.

  • What factors should be evaluated before choosing Agile?

  • Can Agile be adapted for regulated healthcare projects?

Practical assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

  • Explain why Agile is suitable for this project.

  • Identify three project characteristics that support the use of Agile.

  • Identify two regulatory or compliance considerations that may require adaptation of Agile practices.

  • Describe whether a pure Agile approach or a hybrid approach would be most appropriate, and explain why.

Summary

Agile is most effective for projects where requirements are evolving, customer feedback is valuable, and incremental delivery is possible. This makes Agile particularly suitable for software, AI, healthcare applications, and pharmacovigilance platforms.

However, Agile may be less suitable for projects with fixed requirements, physical construction constraints, manufacturing dependencies, or extensive upfront regulatory documentation needs. In such cases, Waterfall or a hybrid approach may be more appropriate.

Key takeaways

  • Use Agile for software, AI, healthcare applications, and projects with changing requirements.

  • Use Waterfall or predictive approaches for construction, manufacturing, and fixed-scope projects.

  • Evaluate requirement uncertainty, customer feedback, incremental delivery, and regulatory constraints before choosing a methodology.

  • Hybrid approaches are often useful in regulated industries such as healthcare and pharmacovigilance.

  • Your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform is well suited for Agile because it involves evolving requirements, AI improvement, and continuous user feedback.

MODULE 10 -- PRODUCT MANAGEMENT IN AGILE

Lesson 1: Product Management Fundamentals

1. What is Product Management?

Product Management is the discipline of:

Identifying customer problems, creating solutions, delivering value, and continuously improving the product.

A Product Manager (PM) acts as the connection between:

Customers

↓

Business Goals

↓

Product Strategy

↓

Development Team

↓

Product Release

↓

Customer Feedback

A Product Manager asks:

  • What problem should we solve?

  • Who are we solving it for?

  • Why is this important?

  • What should we build?

  • How will we measure success?

2. What is a Product?

A product is anything that provides value to users.

It can be:

Physical Product

Example:

  • Smartphone

  • Medical device

Digital Product

Example:

  • Mobile application

  • SaaS platform

  • Healthcare software

AI Product

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

A system that helps safety teams process adverse event cases faster using AI.

3. Product vs Project

A common interview question.

Project

A temporary effort to deliver something.

Example:

\"Build a hospital management application in 6 months.\"

Focus:

  • Timeline

  • Budget

  • Scope

Product

A continuous journey of creating value.

Example:

\"Continuously improve hospital management software based on user needs.\"

Focus:

  • Users

  • Value

  • Growth

  • Improvement

Comparison:

Project Product

Temporary Continuous

Has end date Evolves continuously

Deliver output Deliver value

Success = completion Success = user/business impact

4. Why Does Product Management Exist?

Without Product Management:

Companies may build:

❌ Features nobody needs\ ❌ Products without market demand\ ❌ Solutions without clear goals

Product Management ensures:

✅ Build the right product\ ✅ For the right users\ ✅ At the right time\ ✅ With measurable outcomes

5. Role of a Product Manager

A Product Manager is responsible for product success.

A PM does not usually:

❌ Write all code\ ❌ Design every screen\ ❌ Manage every task

Instead, PM:

✅ Defines direction\ ✅ Understands users\ ✅ Prioritizes problems\ ✅ Makes product decisions\ ✅ Aligns teams

6. Product Manager Responsibilities

A PM\'s work can be divided into five areas.

Area 1: Product Vision

Question:

\"Where do we want this product to go?\"

Example:

Vision:

\"Create the world\'s most intelligent pharmacovigilance assistant.\"

Area 2: Product Strategy

Question:

\"How will we achieve that vision?\"

Example:

Strategy:

  • Start with AI case extraction

  • Add automation gradually

  • Expand into predictive safety analytics

Area 3: Discovery

Question:

\"What problems should we solve?\"

Activities:

  • Customer interviews

  • Market research

  • User feedback

  • Competitor analysis

Area 4: Delivery

Question:

\"How do we build and launch it?\"

Activities:

  • Create roadmap

  • Prioritize features

  • Work with engineering

  • Manage releases

Area 5: Measurement

Question:

\"Did we create value?\"

Activities:

  • Analyze metrics

  • Track KPIs

  • Improve product

7. Product Manager Daily Activities

A typical PM day:

Morning

Review:

  • User feedback

  • Product metrics

  • Team updates

Meetings

Meet with:

  • Engineers

  • Designers

  • Customers

  • Business teams

Product Work

Activities:

  • Write requirements

  • Prioritize backlog

  • Review designs

  • Analyze data

Strategy Work

Activities:

  • Market research

  • Competitor analysis

  • Roadmap planning

8. Product Manager vs Business Analyst vs Product Owner

Very important for your career path.

Role Main Focus

Business Analyst Understand and document business needs

Product Owner Manage Agile backlog and maximize sprint value

Product Manager Define product vision, strategy, and success

Business Analyst

Question:

\"What does the business need?\"

Example:

\"Safety associates need faster case creation.\"

Product Owner

Question:

\"What should the team build next?\"

Example:

\"AI extraction feature should be prioritized in Sprint 3.\"

Product Manager

Question:

\"Why should we build this and what outcome do we want?\"

Example:

\"Reducing case processing time will improve regulatory compliance and customer value.\"

9. Product Manager and Agile

In Agile organizations:

PM works closely with:

  • Product Owner

  • Scrum Master

  • Development Team

Flow:

Product Manager

Defines Vision & Strategy

↓

Product Owner

Manages Backlog

↓

Development Team

Builds Product

↓

Users

Provide Feedback

10. Product Lifecycle

Every product goes through stages.

Stage 1: Discovery

Question:

\"Should we build this?\"

Activities:

  • Research

  • Customer interviews

  • Market analysis

Stage 2: Introduction

Product launch.

Focus:

  • Finding early users

  • Collecting feedback

Stage 3: Growth

Focus:

  • More users

  • Better features

  • Market expansion

Stage 4: Maturity

Focus:

  • Optimization

  • Retention

  • Efficiency

Stage 5: Decline or Transformation

Options:

  • Improve product

  • Change strategy

  • Replace technology

Example: AI Pharmacovigilance Product Lifecycle

Discovery

Problem:

Manual case processing is slow.

MVP

Build:

  • Document upload

  • AI extraction

Growth

Add:

  • Duplicate detection

  • Coding assistance

Maturity

Add:

  • Predictive safety signals

  • Advanced analytics

11. Product Thinking vs Feature Thinking

A beginner thinks:

\"What feature should we build?\"

A Product Manager thinks:

\"What problem should we solve?\"

Example:

Customer says:

\"I need a chatbot.\"

Feature thinking:

Build chatbot.

Product thinking:

Why?

Customer:

\"I cannot find safety information quickly.\"

Possible solutions:

  • Better search

  • Knowledge base

  • AI assistant

12. Product Manager Decision Framework

Before building anything, ask:

1. Is there a real problem?

Who has this problem?

2. Is it valuable?

Does solving it create impact?

3. Is it feasible?

Can we build it?

4. How will we measure success?

What metric improves?

13. Healthcare Product Manager Mindset

Healthcare products require additional thinking.

A PM must balance:

User Value

Does it help healthcare professionals?

Business Value

Does it create sustainable business impact?

Safety

Can it harm patients?

Compliance

Does it meet regulations?

Example:

AI recommendation system:

Normal product:

\"Make it faster.\"

Healthcare product:

\"Make it faster while ensuring safety and accuracy.\"

14. Your Career Alignment

Your background creates a unique product advantage.

Traditional PM:

Understands:

  • Software

  • Business

  • Users

You bring:

✅ Pharmacology knowledge\ ✅ Healthcare workflows\ ✅ Drug safety understanding\ ✅ AI interest\ ✅ Agile BA skills

Your possible niche:

Healthcare AI Product Manager

Examples:

  • AI Pharmacovigilance platforms

  • Clinical AI tools

  • Drug discovery AI

  • Healthcare analytics platforms
