5 Whys:

Why?

Doctor entered wrong dosage.

Why?

Selection list was confusing.

Why?

Similar drug names displayed together.

Why?

No medication safety design review.

Why?

UX validation was not part of development process.

Root Cause:

Poor medication interface design.

Solution:

Improve UX + validation workflow.

12. RCA in Agile

RCA is used during:

Sprint Retrospectives

Example:

Problem:

Team asks:

Why?

Action:

Example:

13. BA Interview Questions

Q1: What is RCA?

Answer:

\"Root Cause Analysis is a structured method used to identify the underlying reason behind a problem rather than only addressing symptoms.\"

Q2: Which RCA techniques have you used?

Answer:

\"I have used techniques such as 5 Whys, Fishbone Diagram, and Pareto Analysis to identify root causes and prioritize corrective actions.\"

Q3: Give a healthcare example.

Answer:

Lesson 7: Impact Analysis Masterclass

A BA does not only ask \"What should we change?\"

A senior BA asks:

\"If we make this change, what else will be affected?\"

This thinking prevents unexpected failures.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Impact Analysis is

  • Why BAs perform Impact Analysis

  • Types of impacts

  • Change Impact Assessment

  • Dependency Analysis

  • Risk Impact Analysis

  • Business, technical, and user impact

  • Impact Analysis document creation

  • Healthcare AI example

1. What is Impact Analysis?

Definition:

Impact Analysis is a technique used to identify the consequences, dependencies, risks, and affected areas of a proposed change.

Simple formula:

Change Request

↓

What will be affected?

↓

Impact Assessment

↓

Decision

↓

Implementation Plan

2. Why Impact Analysis Matters

Without Impact Analysis:

A small change can create unexpected problems.

Example:

Business request:

\"Add AI-generated medical summary.\"

Looks simple.

But impact includes:

  • Data privacy review

  • AI validation

  • User training

  • Regulatory approval

  • System integration

3. When Do BAs Perform Impact Analysis?

Impact Analysis is performed during:

Requirement Changes

Example:

New feature request.

System Changes

Example:

API modification.

Process Changes

Example:

New approval workflow.

Regulatory Changes

Example:

New compliance requirement.

Defect Fixes

Example:

Changing existing behavior.

4. Impact Analysis Process

A BA follows:

Understand Change

↓

Identify Affected Areas

↓

Analyze Impact

↓

Assess Risk

↓

Estimate Effort

↓

Recommend Action

Step 1: Understand the Change

Example:

Change:

\"AI should automatically classify adverse events.\"

Questions:

  • Why is this needed?

  • Who requested it?

  • What problem does it solve?

Step 2: Identify Affected Areas

A BA checks:

Business

Will business goals change?

Process

Will workflow change?

Users

Will users need training?

Technology

Will systems change?

Data

Will data requirements change?

Compliance

Will regulations be affected?

5. Types of Impact Analysis

1. Business Impact Analysis

Focus:

Business operations.

Questions:

  • Does revenue change?

  • Does cost change?

  • Does process change?

Example:

AI automation reduces manual review effort.

Impact:

Positive:

Lower operational cost.

2. User Impact Analysis

Focus:

People using the system.

Questions:

  • Will user workflow change?

  • Is training needed?

  • Will adoption be affected?

Example:

Reviewer moves from manual writing to AI-assisted review.

3. Technical Impact Analysis

Focus:

Technology changes.

Questions:

  • Which systems are affected?

  • Are APIs impacted?

  • Is database change required?

Adding RAG-based AI assistant.

Need:

  • Vector database

  • AI services

  • Security review

4. Data Impact Analysis

Focus:

Information changes.

Questions:

  • What data is required?

  • How is data stored?

  • Is privacy affected?

Impact:

Need:

  • Data cleaning

  • Access approval

5. Process Impact Analysis

Focus:

Workflow changes.

Example:

Current:

Future:

AI generates draft.

Very important in healthcare.

Questions:

  • Does regulation apply?

  • Is validation required?

  • Is audit trail needed?

  • Documentation

  • Validation

Lesson 8: Decision Analysis & Decision Matrix Masterclass

A BA is not only a requirement collector. A senior BA helps organizations make better decisions.

A BA uses Decision Analysis techniques to make decisions based on facts, not opinions.

1. What is Decision Analysis?

Definition:

Decision Analysis is a structured approach used to evaluate different options and select the best solution based on business objectives, constraints, risks, and value.

Simple formula:

Problem

↓

Possible Options

↓

Evaluate Criteria

↓

Compare Alternatives

↓

Select Best Decision

2. Why Decision Analysis Matters for a BA

Without structured analysis:

Decision becomes:

  • Based on personal preference

  • Influenced by seniority

  • Emotion-driven

Example:

Executive says:

\"Let\'s buy an AI tool.\"

Developer says:

\"Let\'s build ourselves.\"

Who is correct?

A BA analyzes:

  • Cost

  • Time

  • Risk

  • Capability

  • Business value

3. Decision Analysis Process

A BA follows:

Define Decision

↓

Identify Options

↓

Define Evaluation Criteria

↓

Collect Data

↓

Score Options

↓

Recommend Decision

↓

Document Decision

Decision:

\"How should we implement AI pharmacovigilance capability?\"

4. Decision Matrix

A Decision Matrix compares options using criteria.

Example:

Decision:

Criteria Build Buy Hybrid

Cost Medium High Medium

Speed Slow Fast Medium

Control High Low High

Compliance High Medium High

Problem:

Not all criteria have equal importance.

Weighted Decision Matrix.

5. Weighted Decision Matrix

This is a very common BA technique.

Formula:

Score = Weight × Rating

Example:

Selecting AI Solution.

Criteria:

Criteria Weight

Compliance 40%

Cost 20%

Speed 20%

Scalability 20%

Rating:

1 = Poor

5 = Excellent

Criteria Weight Rating Score

Cost 20 3 60

Speed 20 2 40

Scalability 20 5 100

400

Option B: Buy AI

Criteria Weight Rating Score

Compliance 40 3 120

Cost 20 2 40

Speed 20 5 100

Scalability 20 4 80

Total:

340

Decision:

Build wins.

6. Cost-Benefit Analysis

Used to compare:

Cost vs Expected Value.

Formula:

ROI = (Benefit - Cost) / Cost

Example:

AI Implementation

Investment:

₹1 crore

Expected yearly benefit:

₹2 crore

ROI:

(2 - 1) / 1

= 100%

7. Risk-Based Decision Analysis

Some decisions have higher risks.

BA evaluates:

Risk Probability

How likely?

Risk Impact

How serious?

Risk Score:

Probability × Impact

Example:

AI Auto Approval Feature

Probability:

High

Impact:

Very High

Risk:

Critical

Decision:

Require human approval.

8. Trade-off Analysis

Real projects always involve trade-offs.

Example:

You cannot maximize:

  • Speed

  • Cost

  • Quality

simultaneously.

Common trade-offs:

Speed vs Quality

Fast delivery may reduce testing time.

Cost vs Features

More features increase cost.

Automation vs Control

More automation may reduce human oversight.

Risks:

Option 2:

Benefits:

  • Faster

  • Safer

Risks:

  • Some manual effort remains

Decision:

Hybrid approach.

Why?

Best balance:

Speed + Safety.

Lesson 10: Requirement Engineering Fundamentals

Requirements are the bridge between a business problem and a successful solution.

A BA\'s main responsibility is not just writing documents.

A BA must ensure:

Business Need → Requirement → Solution → Business Value

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What requirement engineering is

  • Why requirement engineering matters

  • Requirement lifecycle

  • Types of requirements

  • Requirement hierarchy

  • Business vs Stakeholder vs Solution requirements

  • Functional vs Non-Functional requirements

  • Transition requirements

  • Healthcare AI examples

1. What is Requirement Engineering?

Definition:

Requirement Engineering is the systematic process of discovering, analyzing, documenting, validating, managing, and controlling requirements throughout a project lifecycle.

Simple:

It is the process of understanding:

  • What business needs

  • Why it needs it

  • What solution should provide

  • How success will be measured

Requirement Engineering Lifecycle

Business Need

↓

Elicitation

↓

Analysis

↓

Documentation

↓

Validation

↓

Management

↓

Solution Delivery

2. Why Requirement Engineering Is Important

Many project failures happen because requirements are unclear.

Example:

Business says:

\"We need AI automation.\"

Developer builds:

AI chatbot.

But business actually wanted:

AI-based adverse event extraction.

Problem:

Poor requirement understanding.

Good requirement engineering prevents:

❌ Wrong solution\ ❌ Rework\ ❌ Cost overruns\ ❌ Delayed delivery\ ❌ Stakeholder dissatisfaction

3. Requirement vs Feature vs Solution

Very important distinction.

Business Problem

Why change is needed.

Example:

Safety reviewers spend too much time processing cases.

Requirement

What capability is needed.

Example:

System should extract adverse event information automatically.

Feature

Product capability.

Example:

AI Document Extraction Module.

Solution

Implementation.

Example:

LLM + NLP pipeline integrated with safety database.

Flow:

Problem

↓

Requirement

↓

Feature

↓

Solution

4. Requirement Hierarchy

Professional BAs organize requirements in levels.

Level 1: Business Requirements

Question:

WHY?

Defines business objectives.

Example:

\"Reduce pharmacovigilance case processing time by 50%.\"

Created by:

  • Business owners

  • Executives

  • Product managers

Level 2: Stakeholder Requirements

Question:

WHAT do stakeholders need?

Defines user expectations.

Example:

\"Safety reviewers need faster case summarization.\"

Created from:

  • Interviews

  • Workshops

  • Research

Level 3: Solution Requirements

Question:

WHAT should the solution do?

Divided into:

  • Functional requirements

  • Non-functional requirements

Example:

\"The system should generate a case summary using AI.\"

Level 4: Transition Requirements

Question:

What is needed to move from current state to future state?

Example:

  • User training

  • Data migration

  • System integration

Requirement Hierarchy Diagram

Business Requirement

↓

Stakeholder Requirement

↓

Solution Requirement

↓

Functional + Non Functional

↓

Transition Requirement

5. Types of Requirements

A BA must understand four major categories.

1. Business Requirements

Explain business goals.

Example:

\"Reduce manual safety review effort.\"

Characteristics:

  • High level

  • Business focused

  • Outcome oriented

2. Stakeholder Requirements

Explain stakeholder needs.

Example:

\"Reviewer needs AI-generated summaries.\"

Characteristics:

  • User focused

  • Describes expectations

3. Solution Requirements

Describe solution capabilities.

Two types:

Functional Requirements

What the system should do.

Non-Functional Requirements

How the system should perform.

4. Transition Requirements

Temporary requirements needed during change.

Examples:

  • Data migration

  • Training

  • New SOP creation

6. Functional Requirements (FR)

Definition:

Functional requirements describe specific behaviors or capabilities that a system must provide.

They answer:

\"What should the system do?\"

Examples:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

FR1:

\"The system shall extract patient information from uploaded documents.\"

FR2:

\"The system shall generate an adverse event summary.\"

FR3:

\"The system shall allow reviewers to approve or modify AI suggestions.\"

Functional requirements usually start with:

\"The system shall...\"

7. Non-Functional Requirements (NFR)

Definition:

Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes and constraints of the system.

They answer:

\"How well should the system work?\"

Common NFR categories:

Performance

Example:

\"System response time should be less than 3 seconds.\"

Security

Example:

\"User authentication must use multi-factor authentication.\"

Reliability

Example:

\"System availability should be 99.9%.\"

Scalability

Example:

\"System should support 10,000 users.\"

Usability

Example:

\"Users should complete case review within 5 minutes.\"

Compliance

Example:

\"System must maintain audit logs.\"

Functional vs Non-Functional Example

Requirement:

\"AI summary should be generated.\"

Functional:

✅ System generates summary.

Non-functional:

✅ Summary generated within 5 seconds.

8. Transition Requirements

Transition requirements help move from current state to future state.

Example:

Implementing AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

Current:

Manual review.

Future:

AI-assisted review.

Transition needs:

Requirement Purpose

Data migration Move historical cases

User training Teach AI workflow

SOP update Define new process

Validation Ensure compliance

9. Requirement Quality Characteristics

Good requirements should be:

Clear

Easy to understand.

Complete

No missing information.

Consistent

No conflicts.

Testable

Can verify whether achieved.

Feasible

Can realistically be implemented.

Traceable

Can track from business need to solution.

10. Requirement Traceability

Traceability connects:

Business objective → Requirement → Feature → Test Case

Example:

Business Goal

Reduce review time

↓

Requirement

AI generates summaries

↓

Feature

Summary Engine

↓

Test Case

Verify summary accuracy

12. Interview Questions

Q1: What is requirement engineering?

Answer:

\"Requirement engineering is the process of eliciting, analyzing, documenting, validating, and managing requirements to ensure the solution meets business needs.\"

1. What is Requirement Elicitation?

Definition:

Requirement elicitation is the process of discovering, collecting, and understanding requirements from stakeholders, users, documents, systems, and business processes.

Simple:

Finding answers to:

  • What does the business need?

  • What problems do users face?

  • What capabilities are required?

2. Why Requirement Elicitation Matters

Poor elicitation causes:

❌ Missing requirements\ ❌ Wrong assumptions\ ❌ Scope changes\ ❌ Rework\ ❌ Failed products

Example:

A pharma company says:

\"We want AI automation.\"

Without elicitation:

Team builds:

AI chatbot.

After proper elicitation:

Discovery:

Actual need:

AI should extract adverse event data from reports.

3. Requirement Elicitation Process

A BA follows:

Prepare

↓

Identify Stakeholders

↓

Select Techniques

↓

Conduct Elicitation

↓

↓

Validate Requirements

Step 1: Prepare for Elicitation

Before meeting stakeholders:

BA understands:

  • Business objective

  • Existing documents

  • Current process

  • Stakeholder roles

Before interviewing safety reviewers:

Review:

Stakeholder Why involved

Step 3: Select Elicitation Technique

Different situations need different methods.

Technique 1: Stakeholder Interviews

Most common BA technique.

Definition:

A structured conversation to gather information.

Types:

Structured Interview

Fixed questions.

Example:

Survey style.

Semi-Structured Interview

Prepared questions + discussion.

Most commonly used.

Unstructured Interview

Open conversation.

Used during discovery.

For Safety Reviewer:

Interview Best Practices

Before:

✅ Prepare questions\ ✅ Understand stakeholder role

During:

✅ Listen more than talk\ ✅ Ask follow-up questions\ ✅ Capture examples

After:

✅ Confirm understanding\ ✅ Document findings

Technique 2: Workshops

Definition:

A collaborative session where multiple stakeholders discuss and define requirements.

Used when:

  • Many stakeholders exist

  • Conflicts need resolution

  • Process understanding is required

Example:

AI Workflow Workshop:

  • Safety reviewers

  • Medical experts

  • IT

  • Compliance

Technique 3: Brainstorming

Purpose:

Generate ideas.

Rules:

  • No immediate criticism

  • Encourage ideas

  • Group similar ideas

Example:

Question:

\"How can AI improve safety operations?\"

Ideas:

  • Auto-summary

  • Risk prediction

  • Duplicate detection

  • Document extraction

Technique 4: Observation

Definition:

BA watches users perform real work.

Why useful?

Example:

A reviewer says:

\"Case processing is simple.\"

Lesson 13: User Story Mastery for BA & Product Roles

A user story is not just a sentence. It is a bridge between user needs, business value, and development work.

In Agile organizations, BAs and Product Owners rarely hand over huge requirement documents to developers.

Instead, requirements are converted into:

  • Epics

  • Features

  • User Stories

  • Acceptance Criteria

  • Tasks

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What is a User Story

  • User Story structure

  • Epic vs Feature vs User Story

  • INVEST principle

  • How to write good user stories

  • Story splitting techniques

  • Acceptance criteria patterns

  • Definition of Ready (DoR)

  • Definition of Done (DoD)

  • AI Product user stories

1. What is a User Story?

Definition:

A User Story is a short description of a user\'s need written from the user\'s perspective, explaining what they want and why they need it.

Basic format:

As a \<user>

I want \<capability>

So that \<business value>

Example:

Weak requirement:

\"Create AI summary feature.\"

User Story:

As a pharmacovigilance reviewer,\ I want AI-generated case summaries,\ so that I can reduce manual documentation time.

2. Why User Stories Are Important

Traditional approach:

Business → Document → Developer

Problem:

  • Too much documentation

  • Less collaboration

  • Misunderstanding

Agile approach:

User Need → Conversation → User Story → Solution

Benefits:

✅ Focus on user value\ ✅ Better collaboration\ ✅ Easier prioritization\ ✅ Easier testing

3. Epic vs Feature vs User Story

Very important interview topic.

Epic

Large business capability.

Too big for one sprint.

Example:

Epic:

AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing

Contains:

  • Document upload

  • AI extraction

  • Summary generation

  • Review workflow

  • Reporting

Feature

A major capability inside an Epic.

Example:

Feature:

AI Case Summary Generation

User Story

Small piece of functionality deliverable in a sprint.

Example:

User Story:

As a reviewer, I want AI-generated summaries so that I can reduce review time.

Hierarchy:

EPIC

↓

FEATURE

↓

USER STORY

↓

TASK

Example:

Epic:

Online Banking

↓

Feature:

Fund Transfer

↓

User Story:

As a customer, I want to transfer money so that I can pay bills.

↓

Tasks:

  • Create transfer API

  • Build UI

  • Add validation

4. Anatomy of a Good User Story

A complete user story has:

1. Title

Short description.

Example:

Generate AI Case Summary

2. User Role

Who needs it?

Example:

Safety Reviewer

3. Goal

What capability is needed?

Example:

Generate summary

4. Business Value

Why?

Example:

5. Acceptance Criteria

How will we know it works?

5. INVEST Principle

A good user story follows INVEST.

Created by Bill Wake.

I -- Independent

Story should not depend heavily on another story.

Bad:

\"Complete checkout after payment system is built.\"

Good:

\"Validate payment details.\"

N -- Negotiable

Story is a discussion point.

Not a fixed contract.

V -- Valuable

Must provide user/business value.

Bad:

\"Create database table.\"

Good:

\"Store customer information securely.\"

E -- Estimable

Team should estimate effort.

S -- Small

Should fit within a sprint.

T -- Testable

Should have clear acceptance criteria.

6. Writing Good User Stories

A good user story answers:

Who?

User/persona

What?

Need/capability

Why?

Business value

Example:

Bad:

System should generate reports.

Better:

As a regulatory manager, I want automated safety reports so that I can submit compliance documents faster.

A story is Ready when:

Lesson 14: Advanced Requirement Techniques

Prioritization, MoSCoW, Kano Model, WSJF, Cost of Delay & Change Management

A BA\'s job is not to collect every requirement. A BA\'s job is to identify which requirements create the highest business value.

In real projects, stakeholders always say:

  • \"Everything is important.\"

  • \"This feature is critical.\"

  • \"We need this immediately.\"

But resources are limited:

  • Limited budget

  • Limited developers

  • Limited time

  • Limited capacity

A BA/Product Manager must answer:

\"What should we build first?\"

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • Requirement prioritization concept

  • MoSCoW technique

  • Kano Model

  • WSJF prioritization

  • Cost of Delay

  • Backlog refinement

  • Requirement Traceability Matrix (advanced)

  • Change management process

1. What is Requirement Prioritization?

Definition:

Requirement prioritization is the process of ranking requirements based on business value, urgency, risk, cost, and stakeholder needs.

Simple:

Not all requirements are equal.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Requirements:

  1. User login

  2. AI case summary

  3. Dashboard color theme

  4. Regulatory audit trail

Which comes first?

A BA evaluates:

  • Business value

  • Compliance importance

  • Risk

  • Effort

2. Why Prioritization is Important

Without prioritization:

❌ Team builds low-value features\ ❌ Important features delayed\ ❌ Budget increases\ ❌ Product loses focus

With prioritization:

✅ Faster value delivery\ ✅ Better MVP decisions\ ✅ Better stakeholder alignment

3. Requirement Prioritization Factors

A BA considers:

Business Value

Does it solve an important business problem?

Example:

Reduce case processing time.

Customer/User Value

Does it improve user experience?

Example:

AI-generated summaries.

Risk Reduction

Does it reduce business risk?

Example:

Audit trail capability.

Regulatory Need

Is it mandatory?

Example:

Compliance reporting.

Cost/Effort

How difficult is implementation?

Dependencies

Does another feature need to exist first?

4. MoSCoW Prioritization Technique

One of the most popular BA techniques.

MoSCoW:

Category Meaning

M Must Have

S Should Have

C Could Have

W Won\'t Have

M -- Must Have

Critical requirements.

Without them, solution fails.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance MVP:

✅ User authentication\ ✅ Case upload\ ✅ Security controls\ ✅ Human approval workflow

S -- Should Have

Important but not immediately critical.

Example:

  • Advanced analytics dashboard

  • Export reports

C -- Could Have

Nice-to-have features.

Example:

  • Custom themes

  • Additional charts

W -- Won\'t Have (Now)

Not planned in current release.

Example:

  • Fully autonomous AI approval

MoSCoW Example

AI Safety Platform:

Requirement Priority

Upload case documents Must

AI extraction Must

AI prediction model Should

Custom dashboard Could

Fully automated approval Won\'t

1. What is a Business Process?

Definition:

A business process is a sequence of activities performed to achieve a specific business outcome.

Who performs activities?

Business Process Model and Notation for Professional BAs

BPMN is the language that allows business people, BAs, developers, architects, and process teams to understand the same business process visually.

A senior BA is expected to convert business workflows into standardized process diagrams.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What BPMN is

1. What is BPMN?

BPMN stands for:

Business Process Model and Notation

Definition:

BPMN is a standardized graphical notation used to represent business processes and workflows.

The current widely used standard is managed by the Object Management Group.

Simple meaning:

BPMN is a visual language for showing:

  • Who performs an activity

  • What happens next

  • Where decisions occur

  • How systems communicate

2. Why BAs Use BPMN

A BA works between:

  • Business stakeholders

  • Product teams

  • Developers

  • QA teams

  • Compliance teams

Each group thinks differently.

BPMN creates a common language.

Example:

Business says:

\"The reviewer checks cases and sends approval.\"

Developer needs:

  • Who checks?

  • When?

  • What conditions?

  • What happens if rejected?

BPMN answers these questions.

3. BPMN vs Flowchart

Both represent processes, but BPMN is more powerful.

Flowchart BPMN

Simple diagrams Industry standard

Limited symbols Rich notation

Small processes Enterprise processes

|

Lesson 18: UML for Business Analysts

Understanding System Behavior Through UML Diagrams

BPMN explains how the business works. UML explains how the system behaves.

A professional BA often works between business processes and software solutions.

Example:

Business says:

\"We need an AI pharmacovigilance platform.\"

BPMN answers:

\"How does the safety workflow operate?\"

UML answers:

\"How should users interact with the system?\"

Learning Objectives

  • What UML is

  • Why BAs use UML

  • UML diagram categories

  • Healthcare AI examples

1. What is UML?

UML stands for:

Unified Modeling Language

Definition:

UML is a standardized visual modeling language used to describe software systems, their structure, behavior, and interactions.

Simple meaning:

UML helps describe:

  • Users

  • System functions

  • Data objects

  • System interactions

  • Object behavior

2. Why Does a BA Need UML?

A BA does not usually write code.

But a BA must communicate with:

  • Developers

  • Architects

  • QA Engineers

  • Product Teams

UML helps translate:

Business requirement

↓

System understanding

↓

Development solution

Example:

Business Requirement:

\"Reviewer should approve AI-generated case summaries.\"

Developer needs:

  • Who approves?

  • What happens before approval?

  • What data is involved?

  • What system response occurs?

UML helps define this.

3. BPMN vs UML

Very important interview question.

BPMN UML

Business process modeling Software/system modeling

Focus on workflow Focus on system behavior

Shows activities Shows objects and interactions

Business users understand Technical teams understand

Example:

BPMN:

\"How a safety case moves through the organization.\"

UML:

\"How reviewer interacts with AI system.\"

2. What is Workflow Design?

Definition:

Workflow design is the process of designing the sequence of activities, decisions, responsibilities, and system interactions required to complete a task.

A BA designs workflows to answer:

  • Who performs the task?

  • What happens next?

  • What decisions exist?

  • Where can automation help?

  • Where are bottlenecks?

3. Workflow Design Principles

Principle 1: Clear Ownership

Every activity should have an owner.

Bad:

\"Review case\"

Who reviews?

Better:

\"Safety reviewer validates extracted data.\"

Principle 2: Minimize Manual Work

Identify automation opportunities.

Example:

Manual:

Improvement:

Principle 3: Design Exception Handling

Real processes fail.

Example:

Missing information.

Workflow should define:

\"If data missing → request additional information.\"

Principle 4: Reduce Unnecessary Steps

Example:

Old:

System A

↓

Manual Copy

↓

System B

Better:

System Integration

Lesson 21: Solution Design & Requirements Validation

From Requirements to an Approved Solution

A BA\'s responsibility does not end after writing requirements. A BA ensures that the proposed solution actually solves the business problem.

Many projects fail because:

  • Requirements were misunderstood

  • Stakeholders were not aligned

  • Solution does not solve the real problem

  • Business rules were missed

  • Users reject the final product

Solution validation prevents this.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What is solution design

  • BA role in solution design

  • Functional solution design

  • Non-functional considerations

  • Business rules validation

  • Requirement walkthrough

  • Design review

  • Stakeholder approval

  • Prototype feedback loop

  • Healthcare AI solution example

1. What is Solution Design?

Definition:

Solution design is the process of defining how a proposed solution will meet business needs, user requirements, and technical constraints.

Simple:

Requirement:

\"Reduce pharmacovigilance processing time.\"

Solution design:

\"Create an AI-assisted workflow that extracts case data, generates summaries, and supports human validation.\"

2. Requirement vs Solution Design

Very important difference.

Requirement

Describes:

What the business needs

Example:

\"Reviewer should identify serious adverse events.\"

Solution Design

Describes:

How the solution will enable it

Example:

\"AI model analyzes event description and highlights potential seriousness indicators.\"

Comparison:

Requirement Solution

What How

Business need Implementation approach

User expectation System behavior

3. BA Role in Solution Design

A BA works between:

Business

↓

Business Analyst

↓

Product / UX / Development Team

↓

Solution

BA responsibilities:

✅ Understand problem\ ✅ Define solution options\ ✅ Validate requirements\ ✅ Identify gaps\ ✅ Ensure user needs are addressed\ ✅ Support design decisions

4. Solution Design Components

A BA considers:

1. Functional Design

What the system should do.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Functional requirements:

  • Upload documents

  • Extract information

  • Generate summary

  • Assign risk score

  • Allow approval

2. Non-Functional Design

How the system should perform.

Examples:

Performance

\"Dashboard loads within 3 seconds.\"

Security

\"Only authorized reviewers can access cases.\"

Reliability

\"System availability should be 99.9%.\"

Compliance

\"Maintain audit trail.\"

5. Business Rules Validation

Business rules define constraints.

Example:

Rule:

Serious adverse events must be submitted within 15 days.

BA converts this into system behavior:

IF:

Case seriousness = Serious

AND

Approval completed

THEN:

Submission deadline = 15 days

Business Rule Format

A BA often documents:

Field Example

Rule ID BR-001

Rule Name Serious Case Submission

Condition Serious event identified

Action Submit within 15 days

Exception Missing information

6. Requirement Validation

Before development starts, BA validates:

Is requirement complete?

Example:

\"System should generate reports.\"

Questions:

  • Which reports?

  • Who generates?

  • Format?

  • Frequency?

  • Data source?

Is requirement clear?

Bad:

\"System should be fast.\"

Good:

\"System response time should be below 3 seconds.\"

Is requirement testable?

Bad:

\"Easy to use.\"

Good:

\"User can complete case review within 5 steps.\"

7. Requirement Walkthrough

Definition:

A requirement walkthrough is a structured review session where stakeholders validate requirements before implementation.

Participants:

  • Business stakeholders

  • Product Owner

Lesson 23: Advanced User Stories & Acceptance Criteria Masterclass

Writing Requirements Like an Industry Business Analyst

A good BA does not write requirements as features. A good BA writes requirements as user problems and expected outcomes.

Many beginners write:

❌ \"Create AI dashboard.\"\ ❌ \"Add risk prediction button.\"\ ❌ \"Build report page.\"

These are system instructions.

An Agile BA writes:

✅ Who needs it?\ ✅ What do they want?\ ✅ Why do they need it?\ ✅ How do we know it works?

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • Epic → Feature → User Story hierarchy

  • User Story structure

  • Writing professional user stories

  • Acceptance Criteria

  • Given-When-Then format

  • AI product examples

1. Requirement Hierarchy in Agile

Large requirements are broken into smaller pieces.

Structure:

Product Vision

↓

Epic

↓

↓

2. What is a User Story?

Definition:

A user story is a short description of a user\'s need written from the user\'s perspective.

Standard format:

As a \<user>

I want \<goal>

So that \<benefit>

Example:

As a pharmacovigilance reviewer,

I want AI to generate case summaries,

So that I can review adverse events faster.

3. Three Important Parts

1. User (Who?)

Who needs this?

Examples:

  • Safety reviewer

  • Doctor

  • Patient

  • Administrator

2. Goal (What?)

What capability is needed?

Example:

Generate AI summary.

3. Benefit (Why?)

Why does it matter?

Example:

Reduce review time.

4. Bad vs Good User Stories

Bad:

\"Create AI module.\"

Problems:

❌ No user\ ❌ No purpose\ ❌ No value

Good:

\"As a safety reviewer, I want AI to identify potential safety risks so that I can prioritize urgent cases.\"

5. INVEST Principle

A professional user story should follow INVEST.

Created by:

Bill Wake

I -- Independent

Story should stand alone.

Bad:

\"Create approval button.\"

Depends on:

\"Create review screen.\"

Better:

\"Reviewer can approve validated cases.\"

N -- Negotiable

Story is not a fixed contract.

The team can discuss implementation.

V -- Valuable

Must provide user/business value.

Bad:

\"Add database field.\"

No user value.

E -- Estimable

Team should understand enough to estimate effort.

S -- Small

Should fit inside a sprint.

T -- Testable

Should have clear acceptance criteria.

6. User Story Example (Healthcare AI)

Story:

As a safety reviewer,

I want the system to highlight serious adverse events,

So that I can prioritize high-risk cases.

Acceptance Criteria:

Given a case is uploaded,

When AI analyzes the event,

Then serious indicators should be displayed.

Given a high-risk case,

When reviewer opens dashboard,

Then the case should appear as high priority.

7. Acceptance Criteria

Definition:

Acceptance criteria define the conditions that must be satisfied for a user story to be considered complete.

Simple:

User Story:

\"What user needs\"

Acceptance Criteria:

\"How we verify it works\"

Example:

Story:

AI generates summary.

Acceptance Criteria:

  • Summary generated after document upload

  • User can edit summary

  • System stores final version

  • Audit log is created

8. Given-When-Then Format

Most common Agile format.

Also called:

BDD (Behavior Driven Development)

Structure:

Given

(initial condition)

When

(action)

Then

(expected result)

Example:

Feature:

AI Risk Classification

Scenario:

High-risk case identification

Given a safety case contains serious adverse event indicators

When AI analyzes the case

Then the system should mark the case as high risk

9. Multiple Acceptance Criteria Example

User Story:

\"As a reviewer, I want AI-generated summaries so that I can reduce review time.\"

AC1: Generate Summary

Given a document is uploaded

When AI processing completes

Then a summary should be displayed

AC2: Confidence Score

Given AI generates a summary

When confidence is calculated

Then confidence percentage should be visible

AC3: Low Confidence

Given AI confidence is below threshold

When summary is generated

Then case should be flagged for manual review

10. Business Rules Inside User Stories

Business rules define restrictions.

Example:

Rule:

\"Only medical reviewers can approve serious cases.\"

User Story:

\"As a medical reviewer, I want to approve serious cases so that compliance requirements are followed.\"

Acceptance Criteria:

Given a serious case

When a safety reviewer attempts approval

Then approval option should not be available

Professional BAs always consider failures.

Normal:

Negative:

Expected:

\"Unable to process document. Upload valid file.\"

Edge cases are unusual situations.

Edge:

1000-page document.

  • Should processing continue?

  • Should user receive notification?

  • Should system split document?

2. BRD (Business Requirements Document)

What is BRD?

Definition:

3. FRD (Functional Requirements Document)

What is FRD?

Definition:

FRD describes what the system must do to satisfy business requirements.

Audience:

  • Developers

  • QA engineers

  • Architects

BRD says:

\"We need faster case processing.\"

FRD says:

\"System shall extract patient information automatically from uploaded documents.\"

FRD Structure

1. Functional Requirement ID

  • Event information

4. User Interaction

  3. Extracted information displayed

5. Business Rules

Example:

Only authorized reviewers can edit extracted data.

6. Acceptance Criteria

Example:

Given:

Document uploaded

When:

AI processing completes

Then:

Extracted fields should display.

4. SRS (Software Requirements Specification)

What is SRS?

Definition:

SRS describes complete software requirements including functional and non-functional requirements.

It is more technical than BRD/FRD.

Audience:

  • Developers

  • Architects

  • QA

  • Technical teams

SRS Includes:

Functional Requirements

What system does.

Example:

Login functionality.

Non-Functional Requirements

Example:

External Interfaces

  • Regulatory database

  • Drug database

Security Requirements

Example:

Role-based access control.

Data Requirements

Example:

  • Case ID

  • Patient information

  • Drug details

Why What How system behaves

High level Detailed Detailed + technical

↓

↓

Stakeholder management is the process of identifying, analyzing, communicating with, and managing people who influence or are affected by a project.

Simple:

A stakeholder is anyone who:

  • Wants something from the project

  • Can impact the project

  • Is affected by the outcome

Stakeholders can be:

Internal

Inside organization:

  • Product Owner

  • Business team

  • Developers

  • QA

  • Management

  • Compliance

External

Outside organization:

  • Customers

  • Regulators

  • Vendors

  • Partners

Step 4:

Situation 3:

Two stakeholders disagree.

BA approach:

Focus on:

  • Business objective

  • Data

  • User impact

Not personal opinions.

Avoiding

Accommodating

One side accepts.

Competing

Used for urgent decisions.

Lesson 26: Requirements Elicitation Masterclass (Advanced)

Discovering the Right Requirements from Stakeholders

A BA does not collect requirements. A BA discovers the real business need behind requirements.

A stakeholder may say:

\"We need an AI dashboard.\"

A beginner BA writes:

\"Create dashboard.\"

A senior BA asks:

  • Why do you need it?

  • What problem are you solving?

  • Who will use it?

  • What decisions will it support?

  • What happens today without it?

The difference between an average BA and a senior BA is the quality of questions asked.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What is requirement elicitation

  • Requirement elicitation vs requirement gathering

  • Elicitation techniques

  • Interview techniques

  • Workshop facilitation

  • Observation technique

  • Document analysis

  • Brainstorming

  • Prototyping as elicitation

  • Powerful BA questioning techniques

  • Healthcare AI example

1. What is Requirement Elicitation?

Definition:

Requirement elicitation is the process of discovering, understanding, and documenting stakeholder needs, expectations, problems, and business objectives.

Simple:

Finding:

\"What does the business actually need?\"

2. Requirement Gathering vs Requirement Elicitation

Important interview difference.

Requirement Gathering

Means:

Collecting information provided by stakeholders.

Example:

Stakeholder says:

\"We need faster reports.\"

BA writes it.

Requirement Elicitation

Means:

Investigating the real need.

BA asks:

Why are reports slow?

Answer:

Because analysts manually combine data from five systems.

Actual need:

Automated data integration.

Comparison:

Gathering Elicitation

Collect information Discover needs

Passive Active

Stakeholder-driven BA-driven

Surface requirement Root problem

3. Elicitation Process

A professional BA follows:

Prepare

↓

Identify Stakeholders

↓

Conduct Elicitation

↓

Analyze Information

↓

Validate Requirements

↓

Document

4. Elicitation Techniques

BABOK defines many techniques.

Most important for BAs:

  1. Interviews

  2. Workshops

  3. Observation

  4. Brainstorming

  5. Document Analysis

  6. Surveys

  7. Prototyping

  8. Focus Groups

5. Technique 1: Interviews

The most common technique.

Definition:

A structured conversation between BA and stakeholder to discover requirements.

Types:

Structured Interview

Fixed questions.

Example:

\"What fields are required?\"

Unstructured Interview

Open discussion.

Example:

\"Tell me about your current process.\"

Semi-Structured

Combination.

Most commonly used by BAs.

6. Effective BA Interview Questions

Weak question:

\"Do you need AI?\"

Better:

\"What challenges do you face while reviewing cases?\"

Powerful questions:

Current Process

\"How do you perform this activity today?\"

Problem Discovery

\"What is the biggest difficulty in this process?\"

Impact

\"What happens if this problem continues?\"

Frequency

\"How often does this occur?\"

Exceptions

\"What happens when something goes wrong?\"

Future State

\"What would an ideal process look like?\"

7. Healthcare AI Interview Example

Stakeholder:

Safety Reviewer

Bad BA:

\"Do you want AI summary?\"

Answer:

\"Yes.\"

Requirement:

Good BA:

Questions:

Current Process

Improvement

Actual requirement:

8. Technique 2: Workshops

Definition:

A workshop is a collaborative session where multiple stakeholders discuss, analyze, and define requirements.

Used when:

  • Many stakeholders involved

  • Requirements are complex

  • Decisions needed

Participants:

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance:

  • Safety reviewers

  • Medical experts

  • Compliance

  • IT team

  • Product owner

Workshop Agenda Example

Topic:

Step 1

Step 2

Step 3

9. BA Workshop Skills

A good facilitator:

✅ Controls discussion\ ✅ Encourages participation\ ✅ Avoids domination by one person\ ✅ Captures decisions\ ✅ Manages conflicts

10. Technique 3: Observation

Definition:

Observing users while they perform their actual work.

Why useful?

People often cannot explain their process accurately.

Example:

Reviewer says:

\"I review cases quickly.\"

Observation shows:

  • Opens multiple systems

  • Copies information manually

  • Searches databases

BA discovers:

Integration requirement.

11. Technique 4: Document Analysis

BA studies existing documents.

Examples:

  • SOPs

  • Policies

  • Reports

  • Existing systems

  • Regulations

Healthcare example:

Study:

Pharmacovigilance SOP

Discover:

  • Approval rules

  • Mandatory fields

  • Compliance requirements

12. Technique 5: Brainstorming

Definition:

A group technique to generate ideas and possible solutions.

Rules:

During idea generation:

❌ No criticism

✅ Encourage ideas

Example:

Question:

\"How can we reduce case review time?\"

Ideas:

  • AI summary

  • Automation

  • Better dashboard

  • Integration

13. Technique 6: Prototyping as Elicitation

Very powerful.

Sometimes users cannot describe what they want.

Show them something.

Example:

Ask:

\"What should dashboard contain?\"

User:

\"I don\'t know.\"

Show prototype.

User:

\"I need risk score here.\"

Prototype reveals hidden requirements.

14. Asking the 5 Whys Technique

Used for root cause discovery.

Example:

Problem:

Case processing is delayed.

Why?

Because reviewers spend too much time reading documents.

Why?

Because information is scattered.

Why?

Because systems are not integrated.

Root cause:

Lack of integrated information access.

Solution:

AI-assisted unified case view.

Challenge 1:

Lesson 27: Business Analysis Techniques Masterclass

The Core BA Toolkit for Problem Solving & Decision Making

A BA is not only a requirement writer. A BA is a problem solver who analyzes situations, identifies gaps, finds root causes, evaluates options, and recommends solutions.

In real projects, stakeholders rarely come with perfect requirements.

They come with problems:

  • \"Our process is too slow.\"

  • \"Users are unhappy.\"

  • \"The system has too many errors.\"

  • \"We need automation.\"

The BA applies analysis techniques to convert problems into solutions.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • SWOT Analysis

  • Gap Analysis

  • Root Cause Analysis (RCA)

  • Impact Analysis

  • Decision Matrix

  • MoSCoW Prioritization

  • Feasibility Analysis

  • Risk Analysis

  • Healthcare AI examples

1. SWOT Analysis

What is SWOT?

SWOT stands for:

Letter Meaning

S Strengths

W Weaknesses

O Opportunities

T Threats

Definition:

SWOT analysis evaluates internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats related to a business initiative.

Example: AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Strengths

Internal advantages:

✅ AI reduces manual work\ ✅ Faster case processing\ ✅ Better data organization

Weaknesses

Internal limitations:

❌ AI accuracy depends on data quality\ ❌ Initial implementation cost

Opportunities

External possibilities:

✅ Regulatory AI adoption\ ✅ Healthcare automation growth\ ✅ Global expansion

Threats

External risks:

❌ Regulatory restrictions\ ❌ Data privacy concerns\ ❌ Competitor solutions

SWOT Matrix

INTERNAL

Strengths Weaknesses

AI automation Data dependency

Fast processing Implementation cost

EXTERNAL

Opportunities Threats

Market growth Regulations

AI adoption Privacy risks

When BA Uses SWOT?

Use during:

  • New product analysis

  • Business case creation

  • Strategy discussions

  • Solution evaluation

2. Gap Analysis

One of the most important BA techniques.

Definition:

Gap Analysis identifies the difference between the current state (AS-IS) and desired future state (TO-BE).

Simple:

Where are we now?

↓

Where do we want to be?

↓

What is missing?

Example:

Current State (AS-IS)

Pharmacovigilance process:

  • Manual document review

  • 5 days processing

  • Multiple systems

Future State (TO-BE)

AI-assisted process:

  • Automated extraction

  • 2 days processing

  • Unified dashboard

Gap

Area Current Future Gap

Data Entry Manual Automated AI extraction needed

Review Slow Faster AI summary

Reporting Manual Automated Integration

BA Output:

Gap Register

Gap ID Gap Impact Solution

GAP-001 Manual extraction High effort NLP automation

3. Root Cause Analysis (RCA)

Problem:

A symptom is not always the real problem.

Definition:

Root Cause Analysis identifies the underlying reason behind a problem.

Example:

Problem:

\"Case processing is delayed.\"

Wrong conclusion:

Need faster employees.

RCA:

Why delayed?

↓

Reviewers spend time searching information.

Why?

↓

Data exists in multiple systems.

Why?

↓

No integration.

Root Cause:

Disconnected systems.

RCA Techniques

Common methods:

  1. 5 Whys

  2. Fishbone Diagram

  3. Fault Tree Analysis

5 Whys Example

Problem:

AI project adoption is low.

Why 1:

Users don\'t trust AI output.

Why 2:

AI explanations are unclear.

Why 3:

No confidence score provided.

Root Cause:

Lack of explainability.

Solution:

Add AI transparency features.

4. Fishbone Diagram (Ishikawa)

Used to categorize possible causes.

Categories:

People

Training issues

Process

Poor workflow

Technology

System limitations

Data

Poor quality

Environment

External factors

Example:

Problem:

High case review errors.

Possible causes:

People:

Insufficient training

Process:

Unclear SOP

Technology:

Poor validation

Data:

Incomplete records

5. Impact Analysis

Definition:

Impact Analysis evaluates how a change affects systems, processes, users, cost, and risks.

Whenever someone requests a change:

BA asks:

\"What will this affect?\"

Example Change:

Impact:

User Impact

Reviewers can work in multiple languages.

Process Impact

Translation workflow required.

Technical Impact

New AI language models.

Cost Impact

Additional infrastructure.

Risk Impact

Translation accuracy.

Lesson 28: Business Case & Product Value Analysis

Proving Why a Solution Should Be Built

A BA does not only define what to build. A senior BA helps answer: \"Why should we invest in this solution?\"

In enterprise projects, every idea competes for:

  • Budget

  • Resources

  • Development time

  • Management attention

A business case helps stakeholders decide:

\"Is this problem important enough to solve, and is this solution worth investing in?\"

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What is a business case

  • Business case vs BRD

  • Problem statement creation

  • Opportunity assessment

  • Value proposition

  • Cost-benefit analysis

  • ROI calculation

  • MVP justification

  • Healthcare AI business case example

1. What is a Business Case?

Definition:

A business case is a document that explains the reason for an initiative, expected benefits, costs, risks, and justification for investment.

Simple:

It answers:

  • Why do this project?

  • What value will it create?

  • How much will it cost?

  • Is it worth doing?

2. Business Case vs BRD

Very important BA interview question.

Business Case BRD

Why invest? What business needs

Justification Requirements

Financial value Business objectives

Before approval After approval

Example:

Business Case:

\"We should build AI Pharmacovigilance Platform because it can reduce processing costs by 40%.\"

BRD:

\"The business requires automated case extraction and review workflow.\"

3. Business Case Structure

A professional BA business case contains:

1. Executive Summary

Short overview.

Example:

\"The company proposes an AI-assisted pharmacovigilance platform to reduce manual case processing effort and improve regulatory compliance.\"

2. Problem Statement

Clearly define current pain.

Bad:

\"Process is inefficient.\"

Good:

\"Safety reviewers spend 60% of their time manually extracting information from adverse event reports, causing delays in regulatory submission.\"

3. Current Situation (AS-IS)

Example:

Current process:

Receive Report

↓

Manual Reading

↓

Data Entry

↓

Review

↓

Submission

Problems:

  • Slow processing

  • Human errors

  • Duplicate work

4. Opportunity Assessment

Opportunity means:

\"What improvement is possible?\"

Example:

AI can:

  • Extract information automatically

  • Summarize reports

  • Prioritize risks

5. Proposed Solution

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Copilot:

Capabilities:

  • Document processing

  • AI summary generation

  • Risk prediction

  • Reviewer assistance

6. Business Objectives

Objectives should be measurable.

Example:

Before:

Case review:

5 days

Target:

2 days

Objective:

Reduce processing time by 60%.

7. Value Proposition

Definition:

Value proposition explains why the solution is valuable and what benefit it provides.

Template:

\"For [user], our solution provides [benefit] by [capability].\"

Example:

\"For pharmacovigilance reviewers, AI Copilot reduces manual analysis effort by automatically extracting critical safety information.\"

8. Cost-Benefit Analysis

A project has:

Money/resources required.

Examples:

  • AI development

  • Cloud infrastructure

  • Training

  • Maintenance

Value gained.

Examples:

  • Faster processing

  • Better compliance

  • Fewer errors

1. What is UML?

UML stands for:

Unified Modeling Language

Definition:

UML is a standardized visual modeling language used to describe the structure, behavior, and interaction of software systems.

Simple:

UML helps answer:

  • Who uses the system?

  • What can users do?

  • How do systems communicate?

  • What data objects exist?

  • How does a system change state?

2. Why Does a BA Need UML?

A BA uses UML to:

✅ Clarify requirements\ ✅ Visualize system behavior\ ✅ Reduce ambiguity\ ✅ Communicate with developers\ ✅ Support solution design\ ✅ Improve documentation quality

Example:

Requirement:

\"System should allow AI case review.\"

UML helps define:

  • Who reviews?

  • What steps occur?

  • What systems interact?

  • What happens after approval?

Lesson 37: Wireframing for BA / Product Roles Masterclass

Translating Requirements into Visual Product Structure

A requirement explains what the system should do. A wireframe explains how the user will interact with that functionality.

A modern BA is not a UI designer, but a strong BA must understand wireframes because they help connect:

Business Requirement → User Need → Screen Design → Development

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What is wireframing

  • Why BAs create/use wireframes

  • Wireframe types

  • Low fidelity vs high fidelity

  • Wireframe components

  • Screen requirement documentation

  • User interaction mapping

  • Collaboration with UX designers

  • Healthcare AI dashboard wireframe example

1. What is a Wireframe?

Definition:

A wireframe is a visual blueprint of a digital product interface that shows the structure, layout, content placement, and user interactions before final design and development.

Simple:

A wireframe is the skeleton of an application screen.

It does not focus on:

  • Colors

  • Fonts

  • Branding

It focuses on:

  • What appears where

  • What users can do

  • How users navigate

Example

Requirement:

\"Reviewer should see AI risk assessment.\"

Without wireframe:

Developer may create anything.

With wireframe:

--------------------------------

Case Review Dashboard

Patient Information

Drug Information

AI Risk Score

[High Risk 85%]

Evidence

[Approve] [Request Review]

--------------------------------

2. Why Does a BA Need Wireframing?

A BA uses wireframes to:

✅ Clarify requirements\ ✅ Reduce misunderstanding\ ✅ Validate user expectations\ ✅ Support stakeholder discussions\ ✅ Collaborate with UX designers\ ✅ Help developers understand screens

3. Wireframe vs Prototype vs Mockup

Important interview topic.

Item Purpose Detail Level

Wireframe Structure/layout Low

Mockup Visual design Medium/High

Prototype Interactive experience High

Example:

Wireframe

Where button exists.

Mockup

Prototype

How button behaves when clicked.

1. What is Prototyping?

Definition:

A prototype is an interactive model of a product that demonstrates how users will interact with the system before actual development begins.

Simple:

Wireframe = Structure

Prototype = Experience

A BA uses prototypes to:

✅ Validate requirements\ ✅ Get stakeholder feedback early\ ✅ Reduce development rework\ ✅ Identify missing requirements\ ✅ Explain user journeys clearly\ ✅ Improve collaboration with UX and developers

Example:

Requirement:

Stakeholder sees prototype and says:

This requirement would have been missed without prototype validation.

1. Why UX Matters for a Business Analyst

Traditional BA thinking:

\"The system should perform this function.\"

Modern Product BA thinking:

\"The system should help users achieve their goal easily, efficiently, and confidently.\"

Example:

Business Requirement:

\"Create an AI risk scoring feature.\"

Traditional requirement:

System shall calculate risk score.

UX-focused BA requirement:

Safety reviewers should be able to understand case risk within seconds using an explainable AI risk score with supporting evidence.

2. What Are UX Requirements?

Definition:

UX requirements describe how the product should behave from the user\'s perspective to provide an effective, efficient, and satisfying experience.

They define:

  • Ease of use

  • User interaction

  • Navigation

  • Accessibility

  • User satisfaction

  • Error prevention

3. Functional Requirement vs UX Requirement

Very important BA concept.

Functional Requirement UX Requirement

What system does How user experiences it

Feature behavior User interaction quality

Business functionality Usability

Example:

Functional Requirement:

\"The system shall allow users to upload safety reports.\"

UX Requirement:

\"Users should be able to upload a report within three steps with clear progress indicators.\"

4. Types of UX Requirements

A BA should understand these categories:

1. Usability Requirements

Focus:

How easy is the system to use?

Examples:

  • User should complete case review within 5 minutes.

  • Frequently used actions should be accessible from dashboard.

2. Accessibility Requirements

Focus:

Can all users use the product?

Examples:

  • Support keyboard navigation.

  • Provide readable text contrast.

  • Support screen readers.

3. Navigation Requirements

Focus:

How users move through the system.

Example:

A reviewer should reach case details within two clicks.

4. Interaction Requirements

Focus:

How users interact.

Examples:

  • Confirmation before deleting data.

  • Show loading status during AI processing.

5. Visual Requirements

Focus:

Information presentation.

Examples:

  • Highlight critical risks.

  • Use consistent icons.

6. Performance Experience Requirements

Focus:

User perception.

Example:

\"The system shall display loading status if AI processing takes more than 3 seconds.\"

5. UX Principles Every BA Should Know

Principle 1: User-Centered Design

Design around user goals.

Bad:

\"We added 20 features.\"

Good:

\"We reduced reviewer effort.\"

Principle 2: Reduce Cognitive Load

Users should not think unnecessarily.

Example:

Before:

Reviewer reads 20-page report.

After:

AI provides:

  • Summary

  • Important findings

  • Risk indicators

Principle 3: Consistency

Similar actions should look similar.

Example:

Approve button should appear consistently.

Principle 4: Feedback

System should tell users what is happening.

Bad:

Click button → nothing happens.

Good:

\"AI analysis in progress...\"

Principle 5: Error Prevention

Prevent mistakes before they happen.

Example:

Before submitting:

\"Are you sure all required fields are completed?\"

6. BA Collaboration With UX Designer

A BA and UX designer work together.

BA Provides:

Business Context

Example:

Reduce safety review time.

User Requirements

Who needs it.

Example:

Business Rules

Example:

Example:

UX Designer Provides:

  • Layout

  • Visual style

  • Interaction patterns

User Experience Decisions

  • Navigation

  • Screen hierarchy

  • User testing

9. UX Acceptance Criteria

Traditional:

System shall display risk score.

Better:

Given a processed case, when the reviewer opens case details, then the AI risk score should be displayed prominently with confidence level and explanation.

Then case details should open within one action.

Error Handling

Given AI processing fails

When user opens the case

Then system should show failure reason and manual review option.

Feedback

Given user uploads a report

When processing starts

Then system should display processing status.

1. What is Requirement Elicitation?

Definition:

Requirement elicitation is the process of discovering, collecting, understanding, and documenting the needs, expectations, and constraints of stakeholders.

Simple:

Requirement elicitation means:

Finding out what people actually need before building the solution.

Example:

Stakeholder says:

\"We need an AI dashboard.\"

A junior BA writes:

\"Create dashboard.\"

A senior BA asks:

  • Who will use it?

  • What problem does it solve?

  • What decisions will they make?

  • What information do they need?

  • What success looks like?

2. Why is Requirement Elicitation Important?

Poor requirements cause:

❌ Wrong product\ ❌ Rework\ ❌ Increased cost\ ❌ Delayed delivery\ ❌ User dissatisfaction

Good elicitation creates:

✅ Clear scope\ ✅ Better user stories\ ✅ Better BRD/FRD\ ✅ Better acceptance criteria\ ✅ Higher product success

3. Requirement Elicitation vs Requirement Gathering

Important BA concept.

Many people use these terms interchangeably.

Requirement Gathering

Means:

Collecting already known information.

Example:

Stakeholder provides existing process documents.

Requirement Elicitation

Means:

Discovering hidden needs.

Example:

Through interviews, BA discovers:

\"Reviewers struggle because they cannot see historical cases.\"

A senior BA focuses more on elicitation.

A professional BA follows:

Pharmacovigilance Manager

  • How are cases currently reviewed?

  • What are major delays?

  • What decisions require expert judgment?

  • What reports are required?

Watching users perform real tasks.

Why important?

Users may not explain everything.

  • Email

  • Multiple systems

Requirement:

to understand requirements.

1. What is a BRD?

Definition

A Business Requirement Document (BRD) describes the business problem, objectives, expected business outcomes, scope, and high-level requirements of a project.

Simple:

BRD answers:

\"Why are we building this solution?\"

A BRD focuses on:

  • Business goals

  • Problems

  • Expected outcomes

  • Stakeholder needs

  • Scope

It does not focus on technical implementation.

3. BRD vs FRD vs SRS

Very important interview topic.

Document Main Question Audience

BRD Why do we need this? Business stakeholders

FRD What should the system do? BA + Developers

SRS How should the system behave in detail? Technical teams

Example:

Business Problem:

\"Safety reviewers spend too much time reviewing adverse event cases.\"

BRD:

\"We need AI automation to reduce review time by 50%.\"

FRD:

\"The system shall generate AI summaries from uploaded reports.\"

SRS:

\"The system shall process PDF documents, extract entities, and generate summary output within defined performance limits.\"

4. Why is BRD Important?

A good BRD provides:

✅ Clear business direction\ ✅ Stakeholder alignment\ ✅ Project scope definition\ ✅ Business justification\ ✅ Success measurement

Without BRD:

Different teams may have different expectations.

1. What is FRD?

Definition

A Functional Requirement Document (FRD) describes what the system must do, the functions it must provide, and how users interact with those functions.

Simple:

BRD asks:

\"Why are we building this?\"

FRD asks:

\"What should the system do?\"

Example:

BRD:

\"Reduce pharmacovigilance case review time.\"

FRD:

\"The system shall automatically generate a summary of uploaded adverse event reports.\"

BRD FRD

Business perspective System perspective

Explains goals Explains functionality

High-level Detailed

Written for business stakeholders Used by developers & testers

\"Improve adverse event processing.\"

Functional Requirements:

FR-001:

System shall generate risk classification.

11. FRD Writing Best Practices

1. Use \"The system shall\"

Professional standard.

Example:

\"The system shall display case status.\"

2. Avoid vague words

Avoid:

  • Fast

  • Easy

  • User-friendly

Instead:

Define measurable criteria.

Bad:

\"The system shall load quickly.\"

Good:

\"The system shall display dashboard within 3 seconds.\"

3. One requirement = One behavior

Bad:

\"The system shall upload documents and analyze and approve cases.\"

Too many functions.

Better:

FR-001 Upload document.

FR-002 Analyze document.

FR-003 Approve case.

Mistake 2:

Mistake 3:

Mistake 4:

1. What is a User Story?

Definition

A user story is a short description of a product requirement written from the perspective of the user, explaining who needs something, what they need, and why they need it.

Standard format:

As a \<user role>

I want \<goal/action>

So that \<business value>

Example:

As a safety reviewer,\ I want AI-generated case summaries,\ so that I can review adverse event reports faster.

2. Why Do We Use User Stories?

Traditional documents:

BRD → FRD → SRS

are useful for enterprise projects.

Agile teams need smaller, actionable requirements.

User stories help:

✅ Developers understand user needs\ ✅ Product owners prioritize work\ ✅ QA create tests\ ✅ Teams deliver incremental value

3. User Story vs Requirement

Important BA concept.

A requirement:

6. INVEST Principle

A good user story follows INVEST.

I -- Independent

Should be developed separately.

Bad:

\"Login and dashboard and reporting.\"

Too large.

Better:

Story 1:

Login functionality.

Story 2:

Dashboard access.

Story 3:

Report generation.

N -- Negotiable

Details can be discussed.

A story is not a fixed technical design.

V -- Valuable

Must provide user/business value.

Bad:

\"As a user, I want a database.\"

No user value.

Good:

\"As a reviewer, I want previous case history so that I can make better decisions.\"

E -- Estimable

Team should estimate effort.

S -- Small

Should fit into a sprint.

T -- Testable

Must have clear validation.

  • Why?

  • What information?

As a safety manager, I want a case monitoring dashboard so that I can track pending high-risk cases.

1. What are Acceptance Criteria?

Definition

Acceptance Criteria are a set of conditions that define when a user story or requirement is considered complete and acceptable by the business.

Simple:

Acceptance Criteria answer:

\"How will we know this feature is working correctly?\"

Example:

User Story:

As a safety reviewer, I want AI-generated summaries so that I can review cases faster.

Without Acceptance Criteria:

Developer may create any type of summary.

With Acceptance Criteria:

The team knows exactly what is expected.

2. Why are Acceptance Criteria Important?

Acceptance criteria help:

✅ Remove ambiguity\ ✅ Align BA, Product Owner, Developer, QA\ ✅ Create test cases\ ✅ Define completion\ ✅ Reduce disputes

Example:

Requirement:

\"System should send notifications.\"

Questions:

  • When?

  • To whom?

  • What type?

  • What happens if delivery fails?

Acceptance criteria clarify these.

5. Types of Acceptance Criteria

There are three major types.

Type 1: Scenario-Based Acceptance Criteria

Most common.

Uses:

Given -- When -- Then

(Gherkin format)

Structure:

Given

Initial condition

When

User action

Then

Expected result

Example:

User Story:

As a safety reviewer, I want to upload safety reports.

Acceptance Criteria:

Given the user is logged in

When the user uploads a valid PDF report

Then the system should store the document successfully

And display confirmation message.

Type 2: Rule-Based Acceptance Criteria

Used for business rules.

Example:

Requirement:

High-risk cases require approval.

Acceptance Criteria:

Given risk score is above 80%

When reviewer submits case

Then medical approval should be required.

Type 3: Checklist-Based Acceptance Criteria

Used for simple features.

Example:

Login Feature:

Acceptance:

☑ User enters username\ ☑ User enters password\ ☑ Invalid login shows error\ ☑ Successful login opens dashboard

6. Functional Acceptance Criteria

Defines system behavior.

Example:

User Story:

AI should generate risk score.

Acceptance Criteria:

Given a case has been analyzed

When reviewer opens case details

Then risk score should be displayed.

7. Non-Functional Acceptance Criteria

Defines quality expectations.

Examples:

  • Performance

  • Security

  • Availability

  • Usability

Example:

Performance:

Given dashboard has loaded

When user opens case list

Then data should display within 3 seconds.

Security:

Given user does not have permission

When accessing restricted case

Then system should deny access.

8. Positive and Negative Acceptance Criteria

A professional BA always covers both.

Positive Scenario

Expected behavior.

Example:

Valid document upload.

Given PDF file is valid

When user uploads

Then upload succeeds.

Negative Scenario

Error handling.

Example:

Invalid document.

Given file format is unsupported

When user uploads

Then system displays error message.

1. What are Non-Functional Requirements (NFR)?

Definition

Non-Functional Requirements define the quality attributes, performance expectations, security standards, and operational characteristics of a system.

Simple:

Functional Requirement:

What the system does.

Non-Functional Requirement:

How well the system should do it.

Example:

Functional Requirement:

\"The system shall generate AI risk scores.\"

Non-Functional Requirement:

\"The system shall generate risk scores within 30 seconds with 99% availability.\"

2. Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements

Functional Requirement Non-Functional Requirement

System behavior System quality

Features Performance & constraints

User actions User experience

What How well

Example:

Functional:

User can upload adverse event reports.

Non-Functional:

System should support 10,000 simultaneous uploads.

3. Why Are NFRs Important?

Without NFRs:

A system may work but fail in real-world usage.

Example:

AI system generates correct risk scores.

But:

  • Takes 10 minutes

  • Crashes frequently

  • Has weak security

The product fails.

NFRs ensure:

✅ Reliability\ ✅ Security\ ✅ Scalability\ ✅ Better user experience\ ✅ Regulatory compliance

4. Major Categories of Non-Functional Requirements

Industry BAs commonly use these categories:

  1. Performance

  2. Security

  3. Availability

  4. Reliability

  5. Scalability

  6. Usability

  7. Maintainability

  8. Compatibility

  9. Compliance

  10. Auditability

5. Performance Requirements

Definition:

Defines how fast and efficiently the system responds.

Examples:

Response Time

\"The dashboard shall load within 3 seconds.\"

Processing Time

\"AI document analysis shall complete within 60 seconds.\"

Throughput

\"The system shall process 5,000 reports per hour.\"

Healthcare AI Example:

Bad:

\"AI should be fast.\"

Good:

\"The AI engine shall generate case summaries within 30 seconds for documents up to 20 MB.\"

6. Security Requirements

Very important in healthcare.

Security covers:

  • Authentication

  • Authorization

  • Data protection

  • Encryption

  • Access control

Examples:

Authentication

\"Users shall authenticate using multi-factor authentication.\"

Authorization

\"Only medical reviewers can approve high-risk cases.\"

Encryption

\"Patient data shall be encrypted during storage and transmission.\"

Healthcare Example:

A safety reviewer should not access another company\'s patient data.

Requirement:

\"System shall enforce organization-level data isolation.\"

7. Availability Requirements

Definition:

How often the system should be operational.

Example:

\"The platform shall maintain 99.5% availability.\"

Calculation:

99.5% availability means approximately:

\~3.65 hours downtime per month.

Healthcare Example:

Regulatory reporting systems require high availability.

8. Reliability Requirements

Definition:

Ability of the system to operate consistently without failure.

Examples:

\"The system shall recover failed AI processing automatically.\"

\"The system shall not lose uploaded case information during failures.\"

Reliability Metrics:

  • Error rate

  • Recovery time

  • Failure frequency

9. Scalability Requirements

Definition:

Ability to handle increasing workload.

Example:

Today:

10,000 reports/month

Future:

100,000 reports/month

System should support growth.

Requirement:

\"The system shall support increasing case volume without performance degradation.\"

10. Usability Requirements

Focus:

User experience.

Examples:

\"The reviewer shall complete case approval within five steps.\"

\"The system shall provide clear error messages.\"

\"The dashboard shall support users with limited technical knowledge.\"

11. Maintainability Requirements

Focus:

Ease of modification and support.

Examples:

  • Code should be modular.

  • System should support future AI model updates.

  • Changes should not impact existing functionality.

12. Compatibility Requirements

Defines supported environments.

Examples:

\"The application shall support Chrome, Edge, and Firefox browsers.\"

\"The mobile application shall support Android and iOS.\"

13. Compliance Requirements

Critical for healthcare products.

Examples:

  • Data privacy

  • Regulatory reporting

  • Audit requirements

Very important in regulated industries.

System should record:

1. What is Backlog Refinement?

Definition

Backlog Refinement (also called Backlog Grooming) is the Agile activity where the Scrum team reviews, analyzes, clarifies, prioritizes, and prepares upcoming backlog items before they enter a sprint.

Simple:

Backlog refinement means:

Making sure the team is ready before development starts.

Without refinement:

Developer:

\"What exactly should I build?\"

QA:

\"How do I test this?\"

Product Owner:

\"I thought it meant something else.\"

With refinement:

Everyone understands:

  • What to build

  • Why to build

  • How to validate

2. Why is Backlog Refinement Important?

A good refinement process ensures:

✅ Clear requirements\ ✅ Smaller stories\ ✅ Better estimates\ ✅ Fewer sprint blockers\ ✅ Better collaboration\ ✅ Faster delivery

3. Who Participates in Backlog Refinement?

Typical participants:

Role Contribution

QA Testability

Scrum Master Facilitation

4. BA Role in Backlog Refinement

\"What to build\"

but:

\"Why it matters.\"

Example:

Story:

BA explains:

\"Reviewers currently spend hours identifying critical cases. Risk score helps prioritize.\"

BA Responsibility 2:

Clarify User Stories

BA checks:

  • Is user clear?

  • Is goal clear?

  • Is value clear?

Bad Story:

As a user, I want reports.

Questions:

Which user?

What reports?

Why?

Improved:

As a safety manager, I want compliance reports so that I can monitor regulatory submissions.

BA Responsibility 3:

Define Acceptance Criteria

BA ensures:

Developer knows expected behavior.

Example:

Story:

AI summary generation.

Acceptance Criteria:

Given a report is uploaded

When AI analysis completes

Then summary should display key safety information.

BA Responsibility 4:

Identify Missing Requirements

BA asks:

  • What happens if data is missing?

  • What happens if AI fails?

  • Who can access this feature?

  • What are business rules?

Definition of Ready is the checklist that determines whether a backlog item is prepared for development.

Ready.

1. What is UAT?

Definition

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) is the process where business users validate that the developed solution meets their business needs and is ready for real-world use.

Simple:

Testing team asks:

\"Does the system work correctly?\"

Business users ask:

\"Does this system solve my problem?\"

But business discovers:

Doctors lack continuous patient information.

Problem 2:

Patients delay seeking help when symptoms worsen.

Problem 3:

Healthcare providers spend more time managing critical cases.

5. Business Objective

The organization wants to:

  1. Monitor patients continuously.

  2. Detect health risks early.

  3. Reduce avoidable hospital visits.

  4. Improve patient engagement.

6. Stakeholder Analysis

Stakeholder Need

Patient Easy health monitoring

Doctor Patient insights

Nurse Follow-up management

Hospital Better care efficiency

IT Team Secure system

Compliance Team Regulatory adherence

Product Manager Product success

7. User Journey Mapping

Very important BA skill.

Patient Journey

Patient Enrollment

↓

Connect Device

↓

Health Data Collection

↓

AI Analysis

↓

Receive Alerts

↓

Doctor Consultation

Doctor Journey

Login Dashboard

↓

View Patient Data

↓

Review AI Alerts

↓

Contact Patient

↓

Update Care Plan

8. Functional Requirements

Now BA converts needs into system requirements.

FR-001

Patient Registration

The system shall allow patients to create accounts.

Acceptance Criteria:

Given:

Patient enters valid information.

When:

Registration is submitted.

Then:

Account should be created.

FR-002

Health Data Collection

The system shall collect:

  • Heart rate

  • Blood pressure

  • Blood glucose

  • Activity data

FR-003

AI Risk Prediction

The system shall analyze patient data and generate risk alerts.

FR-004

Doctor Dashboard

The system shall allow doctors to view patient health trends.

FR-005

Alert Management

The system shall notify healthcare providers when abnormal values are detected.

9. Non-Functional Requirements

Digital health products require strong NFRs.

Security

\"The system shall protect patient health information through encryption and access control.\"

Performance

\"The dashboard shall load patient information within 3 seconds.\"

Availability

\"The platform shall maintain 99.9% availability.\"

Scalability

\"The system shall support 1 million patient records.\"

Auditability

\"The system shall maintain complete activity history.\"

10. Healthcare UX Requirements

Healthcare UX is different from normal apps.

BA must consider:

  • Elderly users

  • Low technical knowledge

  • Emergency situations

  • Accessibility

Example:

Bad Requirement:

\"Create dashboard.\"

Better:

\"Create a patient dashboard that displays critical health information using simple visual indicators.\"

11. Patient App Requirements

Features:

Health Dashboard

Shows:

  • Current readings

  • Trends

  • Alerts

Medication Reminder

Allows:

  • Medication schedule

  • Notifications

  • Confirmation

Doctor Communication

Allows:

  • Secure messaging

  • Appointment requests

12. Doctor Dashboard Requirements

Doctor needs:

Patient Overview

Information:

  • Current condition

  • Risk level

  • Historical trends

AI Insights

Example:

\"Patient blood pressure trend increased by 20% in last 7 days.\"

Action Management

Doctor can:

  • Contact patient

  • Update care plan

  • Schedule follow-up

13. API & Integration Requirements

Digital health systems rarely work alone.

They integrate with:

  • Wearable devices

  • Hospital systems

  • Laboratory systems

  • Electronic Health Records

BA Requirement Example:

\"The system shall integrate with hospital EHR systems to retrieve patient clinical information.\"

14. Data Requirements

Healthcare data includes:

Patient Data

  • Demographics

  • Medical history

Clinical Data

  • Diagnosis

  • Medication

  • Lab results

Monitoring Data

  • Vital signs

  • Activity data

BA must define:

  • Data source

  • Data owner

  • Data access rules

15. AI Requirements

AI features need special BA analysis.

AI Prediction

Requirement:

\"The system shall generate patient risk scores based on historical health data.\"

Explainability

Requirement:

\"The system shall provide reasons behind generated alerts.\"

Human Oversight

Requirement:

\"AI-generated recommendations shall require healthcare professional review.\"

16. Agile Product Backlog Example

Epic:

Remote Patient Monitoring

Feature 1:

Patient Health Tracking

User Story:

\"As a patient, I want to view my health metrics so that I can monitor my condition.\"

Feature 2:

AI Health Alerts

User Story:

\"As a doctor, I want AI alerts so that I can identify high-risk patients early.\"

Feature 3:

Doctor Dashboard

User Story:

\"As a physician, I want patient trends so that I can make informed decisions.\"

17. UAT Example

Scenario:

AI Alert Generation

Steps:

  1. Patient data crosses threshold.

  2. AI analyzes information.

  3. Alert generated.

Expected:

Doctor receives notification.

18. Digital Health BA Deliverables

Portfolio artifacts:

Strategy

✅ Product Vision\ ✅ Business Case

Analysis

✅ Stakeholder Map\ ✅ User Journey\ ✅ Process Flow

Requirements

✅ BRD\ ✅ FRD\ ✅ User Stories\ ✅ Acceptance Criteria\ ✅ NFR Document

Delivery

19. Interview Answer Example

Question:

\"How do you gather requirements for a healthcare product?\"

Answer:

\"I start by understanding the healthcare workflow, identifying stakeholders such as patients, clinicians, and compliance teams. I analyze current processes, identify pain points, define business requirements, convert them into functional and non-functional requirements, and validate them through user stories and acceptance criteria.\"
