Create requirements for:

Product:

AI Remote Patient Monitoring Platform

Prepare:

  2. Business Problem

  3. Stakeholders

  4. Patient Journey

Lesson Summary

Today you learned:

✅ Digital health product analysis\ ✅ Patient journey mapping\ ✅ Healthcare UX requirements\ ✅ Functional requirements\ ✅ Non-functional requirements\ ✅ AI product requirements\ ✅ API/integration requirements\ ✅ Digital health BA portfolio structure

Final Project

AI Pharmacovigilance Intelligence Platform

Complete BA Portfolio Case Study

1. Project Overview

Project Name:

AI Pharmacovigilance Intelligence Platform

Industry:

Pharmaceutical / Life Sciences

Project Type:

AI-enabled Drug Safety Management System

BA Role:

Business Analyst / Product Analyst

2. Business Background

A pharmaceutical company receives thousands of adverse event reports every month.

Current process:

  • Manual report review

  • Manual data extraction

  • Manual risk assessment

  • Manual prioritization

This creates:

  • Processing delays

  • High operational cost

  • Reviewer workload

  • Compliance risks

3. Business Problem Statement

Current Situation

Safety teams manually analyze adverse event reports from multiple sources.

Problem

The existing process cannot efficiently handle increasing case volume.

Business Impact

  • Longer review cycles

  • Delayed safety decisions

  • Increased operational effort

Business Need

Build an AI-assisted pharmacovigilance platform that improves case processing efficiency while maintaining human oversight.

4. Stakeholder Analysis

Stakeholder Matrix

Stakeholder Role Interest

VP Pharmacovigilance Sponsor Business outcome

Safety Manager Product Owner Workflow efficiency

Safety Reviewer End User Faster review

Medical Reviewer Clinical Validator Accuracy

Compliance Team Regulator Audit readiness

IT Team Delivery System implementation

Data Science Team AI Model AI capability

5. Business Objectives

Objective 1

Reduce manual case review time by 50%.

Objective 2

Improve identification of high-risk cases.

Objective 3

Maintain regulatory compliance.

Objective 4

Provide complete audit transparency.

6. Scope Definition

In Scope

✅ Case intake management\ ✅ AI document extraction\ ✅ AI case summary\ ✅ Risk classification\ ✅ Reviewer dashboard\ ✅ Audit trail\ ✅ Regulatory reporting support

Out of Scope

❌ Drug discovery\ ❌ Clinical diagnosis\ ❌ Treatment recommendation

7. AS-IS Process Analysis

Current workflow:

Report Received

↓

↓

Safety Review

↓

Medical Assessment

↓

Regulatory Reporting

Problems Identified

Process Step Issue

Data Entry Manual effort

Review Time consuming

Risk Assessment Inconsistent

Reporting Delayed

8. TO-BE Process Design

Future workflow:

↓

AI Data Extraction

↓

Automatic Case Creation

↓

AI Summary Generation

↓

AI Risk Classification

↓

Human Validation

↓

Regulatory Submission

9. BPMN Workflow Concept

Actors:

  • Reporter

  • AI Engine

  • Safety Reviewer

  • Medical Reviewer

  • Compliance Team

Process:

↓

↓

Validate Minimum Criteria

↓

AI Extract Information

↓

Generate Summary

↓

Risk Assessment

↓

Reviewer Approval

10. Business Requirements (BRD)

BR-001

The organization requires an automated system to improve adverse event processing efficiency.

BR-002

BR-003

The system must maintain regulatory compliance.

BR-004

The system should provide AI-assisted decision support.

11. Functional Requirements (FRD)

FR-001: Case Creation

The system shall allow users to create adverse event cases.

Acceptance:

When submitted,

Then a case record should be created.

FR-002: AI Information Extraction

The system shall extract:

  • Medical events

FR-003: AI Summary Generation

The system shall generate case summaries.

FR-004: Risk Classification

The system shall classify cases based on risk level.

FR-005: Audit Trail

The system shall record:

  • Timestamp

12. Non-Functional Requirements

Performance

Security

Availability

Scalability

System should support increasing case volume.

Explainability

13. User Stories

Epic:

AI-Assisted Safety Review

Lesson 1: Business Case & Feasibility Analysis (Masterclass)

1. Why This Topic Matters for a Business Analyst

Many beginners think:

\"BA receives requirements and writes documents.\"

That is a junior BA mindset.

Industry BA works earlier:

Business Problem → Opportunity → Business Case → Feasibility → Requirements → Solution

Example:

A pharmaceutical company says:

\"We want an AI system to detect adverse drug reactions automatically.\"

A junior BA asks:

\"What fields should the form contain?\"

A senior BA asks:

\"Why do we need this system? What business problem exists? What value will AI create? Is it feasible?\"

2. What is a Business Case?

A Business Case is a document that explains:

\"Why should the organization invest money, time, and resources into this initiative?\"

It answers:

  • Why are we doing this?

  • What problem are we solving?

  • What benefits will we get?

  • How much will it cost?

  • What risks exist?

  • Should we proceed or not?

Simple Formula

Business Case

=

Problem

+

Opportunity

+

Solution Options

+

Cost

+

Benefits

+

Risk

+

Recommendation

3. Business Case vs Requirement Document

Many BA beginners confuse these.

Business Case Requirement Document

Explains WHY Explains WHAT

Created before project approval Created after approval

Business focused Solution focused

Used by executives Used by project teams

Contains ROI Contains features/functions

Example:

Business Case

Problem:

Pharmacovigilance team manually reviews 50,000 safety reports monthly.

Impact:

  • 30 days processing time

  • High operational cost

  • Risk of delayed reporting

Proposal:

AI-powered adverse event detection platform

Expected benefit:

  • Reduce review time by 70%

  • Improve compliance

Requirement Document

Functional requirement:

System shall classify adverse event reports into seriousness categories.

4. Components of a Business Case

A professional BA business case usually contains:

Section 1: Executive Summary

One-page overview.

Example:

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Intelligence Platform

Objective:

Reduce manual adverse event review using AI.

Expected Outcome:

Decrease processing time from 30 days to 10 days.

Section 2: Business Problem Statement

A good BA defines the problem clearly.

Bad:

\"We need AI.\"

Good:

\"The pharmacovigilance team currently spends 60% of its time manually reviewing incoming safety reports, causing delays in signal detection.\"

Problem Statement Template

Currently:

Who is affected?

What problem exists?

How often does it occur?

What is the business impact?

Why solve now?

Section 3: Current State Analysis (AS-IS)

BA documents current process.

Example:

Current ADR processing:

Doctor Report

|

↓

Safety Associate Review

|

↓

Manual Coding

|

↓

Medical Review

|

↓

Regulatory Submission

Problems:

  • Manual entry errors

  • Slow processing

  • Duplicate work

Section 4: Future State (TO-BE)

After improvement:

ADR Report

|

↓

AI NLP Extraction

|

↓

Auto Classification

|

↓

Human Validation

|

↓

Regulatory Submission

Section 5: Solution Options Analysis

BA does not directly jump to one solution.

Example:

Problem:

Slow adverse event processing.

Possible options:

Option Description

Option 1 Hire more analysts

Option 2 Improve existing software

Option 3 Build AI system

Then compare.

Section 6: Feasibility Analysis

This is a major BA responsibility.

There are five feasibility types.

Remember:

TELOS Framework

T - Technical

E - Economic

L - Legal

O - Operational

S - Schedule

1. Technical Feasibility

Question:

Can we build this technology?

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance System:

Check:

  • Data availability

  • AI model capability

  • Cloud infrastructure

  • Integration capability

2. Economic Feasibility

Question:

Does benefit justify cost?

Example:

Cost:

AI Development

\$300,000

Annual Maintenance

\$50,000

Benefits:

Reduced manual effort

\$250,000/year

Reduced compliance risk

\$150,000/year

ROI calculation:

ROI =

(Benefit - Cost)

-------------

Cost

3. Legal Feasibility

Especially important in healthcare.

Questions:

  • GDPR compliance?

  • HIPAA?

  • Patient privacy?

  • Data retention rules?

  • Regulatory requirements?

4. Operational Feasibility

Question:

Will users actually adopt it?

Example:

Safety associates may resist AI.

BA checks:

  • Training needs

  • Process changes

  • User acceptance

5. Schedule Feasibility

Question:

Can we deliver within required timeline?

Example:

Regulatory deadline:

6 months

Development estimate:

12 months

Project not feasible.

7. Cost-Benefit Analysis

BA compares:

Costs

Direct Cost

  • Development

  • Software licenses

  • Cloud cost

  • Training

Indirect Cost

  • Process change

  • Migration

  • Maintenance

Benefits

Tangible Benefits

Can be measured.

Example:

  • Save employee hours

  • Reduce operational cost

Intangible Benefits

Harder to measure.

Example:

  • Better customer trust

  • Improved compliance reputation

8. SWOT Analysis in Business Case

BA often uses SWOT.

Strengths

Internal advantages

Example:

Existing healthcare data

Weaknesses

Internal limitations

Example:

Poor data quality

Opportunities

External benefits

Example:

AI adoption

Threats

External risks

Example:

Regulatory changes

9. Business Case Approval Flow

Real organization:

Business Analyst

|

↓

Product Manager

|

↓

Business Sponsor

|

↓

Finance Review

|

↓

Steering Committee

|

↓

Project Approval

10. BA Deliverables Created During Business Case Phase

A BA may create:

Artifact Purpose

Problem Statement Define issue

Business Case Document Investment justification

SWOT Analysis Strategic analysis

Cost Benefit Analysis Financial justification

Feasibility Study Check viability

Stakeholder Analysis Identify decision makers

AS-IS Process Map Current workflow

TO-BE Process Map Future workflow

Industry Example: AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Business Problem

Drug safety teams receive millions of reports.

Manual review causes:

  • Slow signal detection

  • Compliance risk

Proposed Solution

AI system:

  • Extract adverse events

  • Detect safety signals

  • Prioritize cases

Feasibility

Technical:

✅ NLP models available

Economic:

✅ Saves analyst hours

Legal:

⚠ Requires patient data protection

Operational:

✅ Human-in-loop approach

Schedule:

✅ MVP possible in 6 months

BA Recommendation

Proceed with MVP.

Senior BA Interview Questions

Q1. Difference between Business Case and BRD?

Answer:

Business Case explains why the project should happen.

BRD explains what business requirements are needed after approval.

Q2. How do you decide whether a project should proceed?

Answer:

\"I perform feasibility analysis covering technical, economic, operational, legal, and schedule feasibility.\"

Q3. What happens if benefits are unclear?

Answer:

\"I work with stakeholders to define measurable business outcomes and KPIs before recommending investment.\"

Lesson 1 Assignment (Industry Practice)

Create a Business Case for:

\"AI-Based Pharmacovigilance Signal Detection Platform\"

Prepare:

  1. Problem Statement

  2. Current AS-IS Process

  3. Proposed TO-BE Process

  4. Solution Options (minimum 3)

  5. TELOS Feasibility Analysis

  6. Expected Benefits

  7. BA Recommendation

Lesson 2: Requirement Prioritization Masterclass

1. Why Requirement Prioritization Matters for a BA

In real projects, stakeholders rarely give 5--10 requirements.

They give hundreds.

Example:

A pharmaceutical company wants an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

Stakeholders request:

  • AI adverse event extraction

  • Mobile app

  • Dashboard

  • Voice reporting

  • Multiple language support

  • Blockchain audit trail

  • Chatbot

  • Automated regulatory submission

  • Patient portal

  • Predictive safety signals

But:

  • Budget is limited

  • Timeline is limited

  • Team capacity is limited

The BA must answer:

\"Which requirements should we build first?\"

This is Requirement Prioritization.

2. What is Requirement Prioritization?

Requirement prioritization is the process of:

Evaluating requirements based on business value, urgency, risk, cost, and feasibility to decide implementation order.

Simple Formula

Priority

=

Business Value

+

Urgency

+

Risk Reduction

-

Cost

-

Complexity

3. Who Prioritizes Requirements?

A BA does not prioritize alone.

Usually:

Business Sponsor

|

|

Product Owner

|

|

Business Analyst

|

|

Development Team

|

|

Users

Different stakeholders bring different perspectives.

4. Factors Used for Prioritization

A BA evaluates:

1. Business Value

Question:

How much value does this provide?

Example:

Automatic adverse event classification:

High value.

2. User Impact

Question:

How many users benefit?

Example:

Dashboard used by 500 safety analysts.

High impact.

3. Regulatory Importance

Important in healthcare.

Example:

FDA reporting compliance.

High priority.

4. Risk Reduction

Question:

Does this reduce business risk?

Example:

AI duplicate case detection.

Reduces compliance risk.

5. Cost

Question:

How expensive is implementation?

6. Complexity

Question:

How difficult is it?

5. Common Requirement Prioritization Techniques

A professional BA should know multiple techniques.

Technique 1: MoSCoW Prioritization

Most commonly used in Agile.

MoSCoW means:

M - Must Have

S - Should Have

C - Could Have

W - Won\'t Have Now

A) Must Have

Critical requirements.

Without this, product fails.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance MVP:

✅ Case ingestion\ ✅ Adverse event extraction\ ✅ User authentication\ ✅ Audit logging

B) Should Have

Important but not critical.

Example:

  • Advanced analytics dashboard

  • Export reports

C) Could Have

Nice to have.

Example:

  • Mobile app

  • Voice commands

D) Won\'t Have Now

Deferred.

Example:

  • Blockchain integration

MoSCoW Example

Requirement Priority

Login Must

ADR extraction Must

Dashboard Should

Mobile App Could

Blockchain Won\'t

Technique 2: Value vs Effort Matrix

Very popular with Product Managers.

Two dimensions:

Value

How much business benefit?

Effort

How much work required?

Matrix:

HIGH VALUE

|

Quick Wins | Strategic Projects

|

-----------------|-----------------

|

Low Priority | Avoid / Later

|

LOW VALUE

LOW EFFORT -------- HIGH EFFORT

Example:

Feature Value Effort Decision

ADR extraction High Medium Build

Voice bot Medium High Later

Login High Low Immediate

Blockchain Low High Avoid

Technique 3: Weighted Scoring Model

Used in enterprise organizations.

BA assigns scores.

Example criteria:

Criteria Weight

Business Value 40%

User Impact 25%

Risk Reduction 20%

Complexity 15%

Example:

Requirement:

AI Signal Detection

Scores:

Factor Score

Business Value 9

User Impact 8

Risk Reduction 10

Complexity 6

Calculation:

Priority Score =

(Value × Weight)

+

(Impact × Weight)

+

(Risk × Weight)

-

(Complexity × Weight)

Highest score gets priority.

Technique 4: RICE Framework

Used heavily in Product Management.

RICE:

R = Reach

I = Impact

C = Confidence

E = Effort

Formula:

RICE Score

=

Reach × Impact × Confidence

--------------------------

Effort

Example:

Feature:

AI duplicate case detection

Reach:

1000 users

Impact:

3

Confidence:

80%

Effort:

5 months

Score:

1000 × 3 × 0.8

--------------

5

=480

Technique 5: Kano Model

Focuses on customer satisfaction.

Three major categories:

1. Basic Needs

Expected features.

Missing → unhappy.

Example:

Secure login.

2. Performance Needs

More is better.

Example:

Faster report generation.

3. Delighters

Unexpected value.

Example:

AI recommendation engine.

Diagram:

Customer Satisfaction

\^

|

Delighter

|

Performance

|

Basic ---------------->

Functionality

Technique 6: WSJF (Weighted Shortest Job First)

Used in SAFe Agile.

Formula:

WSJF =

Cost of Delay

-------------

Job Size

Where:

Cost of Delay:

Business Value

+

Time Criticality

+

Risk Reduction

Example:

Feature A:

Business Value = 8

Time Criticality = 7

Risk Reduction = 9

Job Size = 4

Cost of Delay:

8+7+9=24

WSJF:

24/4 = 6

Higher WSJF = higher priority.

6. Prioritization in AI Products

AI products require additional criteria.

Traditional:

  • Business value

  • Cost

  • Time

AI adds:

Data Availability

Example:

AI prediction model needs enough historical data.

Model Accuracy

Example:

90% accuracy required.

Explainability

Especially healthcare.

Example:

Doctor must understand why AI flagged a case.

Regulatory Risk

Example:

AI cannot make final medical decisions without human review.

7. Requirement Prioritization Workshop (BA Skill)

A BA facilitates:

Step 1:

Collect requirements

↓

Step 2:

Define evaluation criteria

↓

Step 3:

Score requirements

↓

Step 4:

Discuss conflicts

↓

Step 5:

Finalize priority

↓

Step 6:

Document decision

8. Prioritization Documentation

BA creates:

Prioritization Matrix

Example:

ID Requirement Value Effort Priority

R1 AI extraction 10 5 P1

R2 Mobile app 5 8 P3

R3 Audit log 9 2 P1

9. Common BA Interview Questions

Q1. How do you prioritize conflicting requirements?

Answer:

\"I bring stakeholders together, define objective criteria like business value, urgency, risk, and effort, then use prioritization techniques such as MoSCoW or weighted scoring.\"

Q2. Difference between Must Have and Should Have?

Answer:

Must Have:

Without it, solution cannot succeed.

Should Have:

Important but can be delayed.

Q3. Which prioritization technique do you use?

Senior answer:

\"The technique depends on project context. For Agile teams I commonly use MoSCoW, WSJF, and Value-Effort analysis. For product decisions I use RICE and Kano.\"

10. BA Portfolio Exercise

Create prioritization for:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Requirements:

  1. AI adverse event extraction

  2. Mobile reporting app

  3. Regulatory submission automation

  4. User login

  5. Voice reporting

  6. Safety dashboard

  7. Blockchain audit trail

  8. AI chatbot assistant

Prepare:

  • MoSCoW classification

  • Value vs Effort matrix

  • Weighted scoring table

Key Takeaway

A junior BA asks:

\"What requirements do stakeholders want?\"

A senior BA asks:

\"Which requirements create maximum business value with minimum risk and effort?\"

Lesson 4: Business Rules & Decision Modeling Masterclass

1. Why Business Rules Matter for a BA

A modern system does not only store data or perform actions.

It makes decisions.

Examples:

A banking system decides:

  • Approve or reject loan?

  • Calculate interest rate?

  • Detect fraud?

A healthcare system decides:

  • Is an adverse event serious?

  • Does a case require expedited reporting?

  • Should a safety signal be escalated?

These decisions are controlled by Business Rules.

2. What is a Business Rule?

A business rule is a statement that defines:

\"How an organization makes decisions, operates, or enforces policies.\"

Simple Examples

Banking

IF customer credit score > 750

THEN loan eligibility = High

Insurance

IF claim amount > ₹5 lakh

THEN manager approval required

Pharmacovigilance

IF adverse event = Serious

AND patient outcome = Death

THEN expedited regulatory reporting required

3. Business Rule vs Requirement

Many BAs confuse these.

Business Rule Requirement

Defines decision logic Defines system capability

Business policy System behavior

\"What should happen?\" \"What should system do?\"

Example:

Business Rule

Serious adverse events must be reported within 15 days.

Requirement

System shall automatically identify serious adverse events and generate regulatory reports.

4. Characteristics of Good Business Rules

A good business rule should be:

1. Clear

Bad:

High-risk cases should be reviewed quickly.

Good:

Cases classified as critical must be reviewed within 24 hours.

2. Atomic

One rule = one decision.

Bad:

If patient is old and drug is risky and symptoms are severe,

send report and notify doctor and update database.

Too many rules combined.

3. Testable

A QA team should validate it.

4. Traceable

Connected to:

  • Policy

  • Regulation

  • Requirement

  • Test case

5. Sources of Business Rules

BA discovers rules from:

1. Regulations

Example:

FDA reporting timelines.

2. Company Policies

Example:

Internal safety review process.

3. Subject Matter Experts

Example:

Medical experts.

4. Existing Systems

Example:

Legacy application logic.

5. Contracts

Example:

Insurance agreements.

Lesson 5: Use Case Modeling Masterclass

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what a Use Case is

  • Differentiate Use Cases from User Stories

  • Identify Actors and System Boundaries

  • Draw UML Use Case Diagrams

  • Write a professional Use Case Specification

  • Model Alternate Flows and Exception Flows

  • Convert Use Cases into Test Cases

  • Apply Use Case Modeling to AI and Healthcare products

  • Answer Use Case interview questions confidently

1. Why Use Case Modeling Matters

Imagine you\'re building an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

A stakeholder says:

\"The system should detect adverse events.\"

This is too broad.

As a BA, you need to answer:

  • Who uses the system?

  • What exactly do they do?

  • What happens if data is missing?

  • What happens if AI confidence is low?

  • What if the user cancels midway?

A Use Case answers these questions.

2. What is a Use Case?

A Use Case describes:

How a user (actor) interacts with a system to achieve a specific business goal.

It focuses on behavior, not implementation.

Simple Definition

Actor + Goal + System Interaction = Use Case

Example:

Actor: Safety Analyst

Goal: Review AI-classified adverse event

Use Case: Review Adverse Event

3. What is an Actor?

An Actor is anyone or anything that interacts with the system.

Actors are external to the system.

Examples:

Human Actors

  • Safety Analyst

  • Medical Reviewer

  • Regulatory Officer

  • Administrator

  • Product Manager

System Actors

  • Regulatory Database

  • Email Server

  • AI Model

  • Authentication Service

  • Hospital Information System

4. System Boundary

Everything inside the boundary belongs to the application.

+--------------------------------------+

| AI Pharmacovigilance Platform |

| |

| (Review Case) |

| (Generate Report) |

| (Manage Users) |

| (Detect Duplicate Cases) |

+--------------------------------------+

Safety Analyst -------->

This clearly separates:

  • External users

  • Internal system functions

5. Components of a Use Case Diagram

A UML Use Case Diagram contains:

Component Meaning

Actor User or external system

Use Case Function performed

System Boundary Application scope

Association Interaction

Include Mandatory reusable process

Extend Optional behavior

Generalization Inheritance

6. Basic Use Case Diagram

Example:

Safety Analyst

|

|

+------------------------------+

| AI PV Platform |

| |

| (Login) |

| (Upload Case) |

| (AI Classification) |

| (Review Classification) |

| (Submit Report) |

+------------------------------+

7. Relationships in Use Case Diagrams

A. Association

Shows interaction.

Example:

Safety Analyst -------- (Upload Case)

B. Include Relationship

Used when one process always calls another.

Example:

Submit Report

|

\<\<include>>

|

Generate Report

Meaning:

Generating report is always required.

C. Extend Relationship

Optional behavior.

Example:

Review Case

|

\<\<extend>>

|

Escalate Serious Case

Escalation only happens if conditions are met.

D. Generalization

Inheritance between actors.

Example:

User

/ \

/ \

Safety Analyst Administrator

Both inherit common capabilities.

8. Use Case Specification Document

The diagram gives the overview.

The specification provides the detailed behavior.

Typical template:

Field Description

Use Case ID UC-001

Name Upload Adverse Event

Goal Upload a new safety case

Primary Actor Safety Analyst

Secondary Actors AI Engine

Preconditions User logged in

Trigger User selects Upload

Main Flow Normal process

Alternate Flow Different valid path

Exception Flow Error handling

Postconditions Case stored successfully

9. Example Use Case Specification

UC-001 -- Upload Adverse Event

Goal

Upload a new adverse event report.

Primary Actor

Safety Analyst

Preconditions

  • User logged in

  • User has upload permission

Trigger

User clicks Upload Report

Main Flow

  1. User selects report.

  2. System validates file.

  3. System uploads report.

  4. AI extracts information.

  5. System stores case.

  6. Confirmation displayed.

Alternate Flow

If duplicate case detected:

  • System alerts user.

  • User reviews duplicate.

  • User decides whether to continue.

Exception Flow

If upload fails:

  • Error message displayed.

  • Upload cancelled.

  • Activity logged.

Postconditions

  • Report stored successfully.

  • Audit trail created.

  • AI processing initiated.

10. Main Flow vs Alternate Flow vs Exception Flow

Flow Meaning

Main Flow Normal successful process

Alternate Flow Valid alternative path

Exception Flow Error or failure scenario

Example:

Main:

Upload succeeds.

Alternate:

Duplicate report found.

Exception:

Server unavailable.

This is one of the most common interview questions.

Use Case User Story

Detailed interaction Short Agile requirement

Focus on process Focus on user value

Includes alternate flows Usually no alternate flows

UML supported Agile backlog item

Large scope Small scope

Example:

User Story

Use Case

Explains:

  • Login

  • Upload

  • Validation

  • Duplicate check

  • AI processing

  • Confirmation

  • Errors

  • Exceptions

Process Flow Use Case

Shows business process Shows user interaction

Organization view System view

BPMN often used UML used

↓

↓

Regulatory Submission

↓

System validates

↓

AI processes

↓

User reviews

↓

A QA engineer uses the Use Case to write tests.

Use Case

Review AI Classification

Actor:

Medical Reviewer

Goal:

Approve AI-generated classification.

Main Flow

  1. Reviewer opens case.

  2. AI prediction displayed.

  3. Confidence score shown.

  4. Reviewer accepts or edits.

  5. Decision saved.

  6. Audit trail updated.

↓

❌ Writing technical implementation instead of user interaction.

❌ Missing alternate flows.

❌ Forgetting preconditions.

❌ Ignoring exception handling.

❌ Creating overly large use cases.

❌ Confusing user stories with use cases.

10. SQL Essentials for Business Analysts

SQL is one of the most valuable technical skills for a BA.

You don\'t need advanced database administration, but you should confidently retrieve and summarize data.

Common SQL Operations

Retrieve Data

SELECT *

FROM adverse_events;

Select Specific Columns

SELECT case_id, seriousness

FROM adverse_events;

Filter Data

SELECT *

FROM adverse_events

WHERE seriousness = \'Serious\';

Sort Data

SELECT *

FROM adverse_events

ORDER BY report_date DESC;

Count Records

SELECT COUNT(*)

FROM adverse_events;

Group Data

SELECT country,

COUNT(*)

FROM adverse_events

GROUP BY country;

Average

SELECT AVG(processing_time)

FROM safety_cases;

Join Tables

SELECT c.case_id,

d.drug_name

FROM cases c

JOIN drugs d

ON c.drug_id = d.drug_id;

Every BA should be comfortable reading and writing queries like these.

Lesson 9: BA Metrics & KPI Framework (Masterclass)

Goal: Learn how a Business Analyst defines, measures, tracks, and improves business performance using meaningful metrics and KPIs. One of the biggest differences between a junior and senior BA is the ability to prove business value with measurable outcomes.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand Metrics, KPIs, KRIs, and OKRs

  • Differentiate leading and lagging indicators

  • Build a KPI framework

  • Measure business, project, product, and BA performance

  • Design executive dashboards

  • Define AI and healthcare KPIs

  • Measure ROI after implementation

  • Answer KPI-related interview questions

1. Why Metrics Matter

Imagine two Business Analysts complete the same project.

BA 1 says:

\"The system has been delivered successfully.\"

BA 2 says:

\"The system reduced manual processing time by 62%, increased user productivity by 38%, achieved 97% user adoption within three months, and reduced compliance errors by 81%.\"

Which BA demonstrates more business value?

The second one.

Modern organizations want measurable outcomes, not just completed documentation.

2. What is a Metric?

A Metric is any measurable value.

Examples:

  • Number of users

  • Processing time

  • Revenue

  • Number of defects

  • Number of safety cases

  • API response time

Metrics describe performance but don\'t necessarily indicate strategic success.

3. What is a KPI?

A Key Performance Indicator (KPI) is a metric that measures progress toward an important business objective.

Example:

Metric:

Average review time = 18 minutes

KPI:

Reduce average review time to under 15 minutes by the end of Q4.

Every KPI is a metric, but not every metric is a KPI.

4. KPI vs Metric vs KRI vs OKR

Term Purpose

Metric Measures something

KPI Measures success against a business objective

KRI (Key Risk Indicator) Warns about increasing risk

OKR (Objectives & Key Goal-setting framework Results)

Example:

Objective:

Improve pharmacovigilance efficiency.

Key Results:

  • Reduce manual review time by 40%

  • Increase AI accuracy to 95%

  • Reduce duplicate reports by 50%

KPIs are then tracked to determine whether these key results are being achieved.

5. Characteristics of Good KPIs (SMART)

KPIs should be:

  • Specific

  • Measurable

  • Achievable

  • Relevant

  • Time-bound

Poor KPI:

Improve AI performance.

Better KPI:

Increase AI classification accuracy from 90% to 95% within six months.

6. Types of Business Metrics

A. Business Metrics

Measure business outcomes.

Examples:

  • Revenue

  • Profit

  • Cost savings

  • Customer retention

  • Regulatory compliance

B. Operational Metrics

Measure day-to-day operations.

Examples:

  • Processing time

  • Queue length

  • Cases handled per analyst

  • SLA compliance

C. Product Metrics

Measure product performance.

Examples:

  • Active users

  • Feature adoption

  • Session duration

  • User retention

D. Project Metrics

Measure project execution.

Examples:

  • Schedule variance

  • Budget variance

  • Defect rate

  • Sprint velocity

7. Leading vs Lagging Indicators

A favorite interview topic.

Leading Indicator Lagging Indicator

Predicts future performance Measures completed outcomes

Proactive Reactive

Examples:

Leading:

  • Training completion

  • User adoption trend

  • AI confidence score

  • Requirement stability

Lagging:

  • Revenue increase

  • Compliance penalties

  • Customer satisfaction score

  • ROI

A mature KPI framework includes both.

8. KPI Framework Design

A BA should design KPIs by starting with the business goal.

Business Goal

↓

Success Criteria

↓

KPIs

↓

Target Values

↓

Dashboard

↓

Review

↓

Improvement

Never start with available data. Start with the business objective.

9. Balanced Scorecard

Many organizations group KPIs into four perspectives.

Perspective Example KPI

Financial Cost reduction

Customer Customer satisfaction

Internal Process Processing time

Learning & Growth Employee training completion

This ensures success is measured from multiple angles.

10. BA Performance Metrics

How can a Business Analyst measure their own effectiveness?

Examples:

KPI Target

Requirements approved without major rework >95%

Requirement change requests after sign-off \<10%

UAT first-pass success >90%

Stakeholder satisfaction >4.5/5

Requirement defect leakage \<2%

Documentation review cycle time \<5 business days

These focus on outcomes, not simply document volume.

11. Product KPI Example

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Possible KPIs:

KPI Target

AI Classification Accuracy >95%

Average Review Time \<15 minutes

Duplicate Detection Rate >98%

User Adoption >85%

Report Processing Time \<3 minutes

Regulatory Submission Success 100%

12. AI Product Metrics

AI systems require additional measurements.

Examples:

Metric Purpose

Precision Quality of positive predictions

Recall Ability to detect actual positives

F1 Score Balance of precision and recall

Model Drift Detect performance degradation

Confidence Score AI certainty

Human Override Rate Frequency of manual corrections

These metrics help determine whether the AI continues to perform safely after deployment.

13. Executive Dashboard

Executives need concise information.

A dashboard should answer:

  • Are we meeting business goals?

  • What changed?

  • Where are the risks?

  • What action is needed?

Example:

Executive Dashboard

AI Accuracy 96%

Manual Review Time 12 min

User Adoption 91%

Pending Cases 153

Compliance 100%

API Availability 99.95%

14. Measuring ROI

Many BA projects end at deployment.

Senior BAs continue measuring value.

ROI Formula:

ROI =

(Benefits - Costs)

-----------------

Costs

Example:

Benefits:

₹50,00,000/year

Costs:

₹20,00,000

ROI:

150%

The BA validates whether the expected business case has actually been achieved.

15. KPI Review Cycle

KPIs should not be created and forgotten.

Review cycle:

Define KPI

↓

Collect Data

↓

Analyze Results

↓

Present Dashboard

↓

Identify Improvements

↓

Update KPIs

Business priorities change, so KPIs should evolve as well.

16. Common KPI Mistakes

Avoid:

❌ Tracking too many KPIs

❌ Measuring activities instead of outcomes

❌ Defining vague KPIs

❌ No target values

❌ No review schedule

❌ KPIs not aligned with business goals

A dashboard with 80 metrics usually helps no one.

17. BA Interview Questions

Q1. What is the difference between a KPI and a metric?

Answer:

\"A metric measures performance, while a KPI measures progress toward a strategic business objective.\"

Q2. Why are leading indicators important?

Answer:

\"They provide early signals that allow organizations to take corrective action before business outcomes are affected.\"

Q3. How do you define KPIs?

Answer:

\"I start with the business objective, identify success criteria, define measurable KPIs with SMART targets, determine data sources, and establish a review process.\"

Q4. What metrics would you track for an AI product?

Answer:

\"I would track business outcomes such as adoption and processing time, operational metrics like API availability, and AI-specific metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, confidence score, model drift, and human override rate.\"

Q5. Why should a BA measure ROI after implementation?

Answer:

\"To verify whether the project delivered the expected business benefits outlined in the business case and to identify opportunities for continuous improvement.\"

Lesson 11: BA Workshop Facilitation Masterclass

Goal: Learn how a Business Analyst plans, facilitates, and leads workshops that uncover requirements, resolve conflicts, build stakeholder alignment, and accelerate project decisions. This is one of the defining skills of a senior Business Analyst.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand workshop facilitation

  • Plan and conduct BA workshops

  • Manage different stakeholder personalities

  • Resolve requirement conflicts

  • Use facilitation techniques

  • Document workshop outcomes

  • Handle difficult situations

  • Facilitate AI and healthcare discovery workshops

  • Answer workshop-related interview questions

1. Why Workshop Facilitation is Important

Imagine this situation:

A hospital wants to build an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

Participants include:

  • Medical Director

  • Safety Manager

  • Regulatory Affairs

  • Product Owner

  • Developers

  • QA Team

  • AI Engineers

  • UX Designer

Everyone has different expectations.

Without proper facilitation:

  • Meetings become discussions without decisions.

  • Requirements conflict.

  • Scope grows uncontrollably.

  • Stakeholders leave frustrated.

A skilled BA keeps the workshop focused and productive.

2. What is a BA Workshop?

A BA Workshop is:

A structured meeting where stakeholders collaborate to discover, analyze, prioritize, validate, or approve business requirements and solutions.

Unlike a status meeting, a workshop has a clear objective and expected outputs.

3. Why Use Workshops?

Compared to separate interviews, workshops:

✅ Collect multiple viewpoints simultaneously

✅ Resolve conflicts quickly

✅ Build shared understanding

✅ Speed up decision-making

✅ Increase stakeholder ownership

4. Common Types of BA Workshops

Workshop Purpose

Discovery Workshop Understand the business problem

Requirement Workshop Gather requirements

Process Mapping Workshop Document AS-IS and TO-BE processes

Prioritization Workshop Rank requirements

Solution Workshop Explore solution options

Risk Workshop Identify project risks

UAT Workshop Validate business readiness

Retrospective Capture lessons learned

5. BA Workshop Lifecycle

A successful workshop follows a structured approach.

Plan

↓

Prepare

↓

Facilitate

↓

Document

↓

Follow Up

Skipping preparation often leads to poor outcomes.

6. Planning the Workshop

Before scheduling, define:

Objective

Example:

\"Identify functional requirements for AI adverse event classification.\"

Participants

Invite only people who can contribute or make decisions.

Example:

  • Product Owner

  • Medical Reviewer

  • Safety Analyst

  • Regulatory Expert

  • Technical Architect

Avoid inviting unnecessary attendees.

Agenda

Example:

09:00 -- Introductions

09:15 -- Current Process

10:00 -- Pain Points

11:00 -- Future Process

12:00 -- Requirement Prioritization

12:45 -- Decisions & Actions

A time-boxed agenda helps keep discussions focused.

7. Preparation

The BA prepares:

  • Meeting agenda

  • Objectives

  • Existing documentation

  • Process diagrams

  • Data samples

  • Wireframes

  • Questions

  • Collaboration tools

The better the preparation, the better the workshop.

8. Facilitation Skills

A facilitator guides discussion without dominating it.

Key skills include:

  • Active listening

  • Asking open-ended questions

  • Summarizing discussions

  • Encouraging participation

  • Managing time

  • Remaining neutral

  • Resolving conflicts

The facilitator\'s job is to help the group reach understanding and decisions.

9. Asking Effective Questions

Avoid:

\"Do you like this feature?\"

Better:

\"How do you currently process serious adverse events?\"

Even better:

\"Walk me through the steps from receiving a safety report to regulatory submission.\"

Open-ended questions reveal richer information.

10. Stakeholder Management During Workshops

Different personalities require different approaches.

Stakeholder Type BA Approach

Quiet participant Invite their opinion directly

Dominant speaker Acknowledge and redirect discussion

Subject Matter Expert Validate detailed business rules

Executive Focus on outcomes and decisions

Technical Lead Clarify feasibility and constraints

Skeptical stakeholder Explore concerns with evidence

The goal is balanced participation.

11. Managing Conflicts

Conflict is normal.

Example:

Regulatory Team:

\"We need every AI recommendation manually reviewed.\"

Product Team:

\"Manual review slows everything down.\"

The BA should:

  • Clarify the underlying business need.

  • Identify regulatory constraints.

  • Explore alternatives.

  • Evaluate risks.

  • Facilitate agreement.

Focus on solving the problem, not \"winning\" the argument.

12. Common Facilitation Techniques

Brainstorming

Generate ideas without immediate evaluation.

Affinity Mapping

Group similar ideas into themes.

Example:

Ideas:

  • Faster processing

  • Better dashboards

  • AI suggestions

  • Mobile access

Themes:

  • Automation

  • Reporting

  • User Experience

MoSCoW Prioritization

Rank requirements:

  • Must

  • Should

  • Could

  • Won\'t

Dot Voting

Each participant receives votes to prioritize ideas.

Useful when many options exist.

Five Whys

Identify root causes.

Problem:

Late regulatory submissions.

Why?

Manual review delays.

Why?

Too many duplicate reports.

Continue asking \"Why?\" until the underlying cause is identified.

13. Workshop Documentation

After the session, the BA documents:

  • Decisions made

  • Agreed requirements

  • Open issues

  • Risks

  • Action items

  • Owners

  • Deadlines

Documentation should be shared promptly while discussions are still fresh.

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Decisions

  • AI classifies all incoming reports.

  • Human review required for confidence below 90%.

  • Serious cases prioritized automatically.

Open Questions

  • Final confidence threshold?

  • Regulatory approval process?

Action Owner Due Date

Validate reporting rules Regulatory Lead Friday

Confirm API specification Architect Monday

15. Virtual Workshop Best Practices

Many workshops are now remote.

Recommendations:

  • Share materials beforehand.

  • Keep sessions interactive.

  • Use visual diagrams.

  • Encourage camera/microphone participation where appropriate.

  • Schedule breaks for longer sessions.

  • Record decisions immediately.

Challenge BA Response

Scope keeps expanding Park new topics for later review

Discussion goes off-topic Redirect to agenda

Decisions not made Escalate to decision-makers if needed

One person dominates Invite input from quieter participants

18. Measuring Workshop Success

A successful workshop should produce:

  • Clear requirements

  • Documented decisions

  • Prioritized backlog

  • Assigned action items

  • Stakeholder alignment

  • Reduced ambiguity

These outcomes matter more than simply holding the meeting.

19. BA Interview Questions

Q1. What is the purpose of a BA workshop?

Answer:

\"A BA workshop brings stakeholders together to collaboratively discover, analyze, validate, and prioritize requirements while building alignment and accelerating decision-making.\"

Q2. How do you handle conflicting stakeholder opinions?

Answer:

\"I clarify the underlying business objectives, gather supporting evidence, evaluate impacts, facilitate discussion, and guide stakeholders toward a mutually acceptable solution.\"

Q3. What preparation is required before a workshop?

Answer:

\"I define objectives, identify participants, prepare an agenda, review existing documentation, prepare discussion materials, and establish expected outcomes.\"

Q4. How do you encourage participation from quiet stakeholders?

Answer:

\"I ask open-ended questions directly, create a respectful environment, and ensure everyone has an opportunity to contribute before decisions are finalized.\"

Q5. What should be documented after a workshop?

Answer:

\"I document decisions, requirements, action items, open issues, risks, owners, and deadlines, then distribute the meeting summary to all participants.\"

Lesson 1: SQL Fundamentals for Business Analysts

Goal: Learn SQL from a Business Analyst perspective so you can analyze data, validate requirements, communicate with developers/data teams, and make data-driven decisions.

1. Why SQL is Important for a Modern BA

Traditional BA:

\"Can you provide the customer data report?\"

Technical BA:

\"I need all active customers who purchased Product A in the last 90 days, grouped by region, with average transaction value.\"

The second BA understands:

  • What data is needed

  • Where it exists

  • How to validate it

  • How to extract insights

2. What is SQL?

SQL stands for:

Structured Query Language

It is used to communicate with databases.

Simple analogy:

Database = Library

Tables = Bookshelves

Rows = Books

Columns = Book details

SQL = Language used to find information from the library.

3. Database Basics

A database stores structured information.

Example:

Healthcare Application Database:

Hospital Database

├── Patients

├── Doctors

├── Appointments

├── Prescriptions

├── Lab Results

├── Billing

└── Medical Records

Each entity becomes a table.

4. Understanding Tables

Example:

Patient Table

patient_id name age gender city

101 Rahul 45 M Ahmedabad

102 Priya 32 F Mumbai

103 Amit 55 M Delhi

A table contains:

Rows

Individual records.

Example:

101 Rahul 45 M Ahmedabad

Columns

Attributes of the record.

Example:

patient_id

name

age

city

5. Primary Key

A primary key uniquely identifies each record.

Example:

Patient table:

patient_id name

101 Rahul

102 Priya

Here:

patient_id

is the primary key.

Rules:

  • Unique

  • Cannot be empty

  • Identifies one record

6. Foreign Key

A foreign key connects tables.

Example:

Patients table:

patient_id name

101 Rahul

Appointments table:

appointment_id patient_id date

5001 101 10-Aug-2026

Here:

Appointments.patient_id

connects to:

Patients.patient_id

Relationship:

Patients

|

|

↓

Appointments

7. Relational Database Concept

Real systems contain many connected tables.

Example:

Pharmacovigilance System:

Patient

|

|

Drug Exposure

|

|

Adverse Event

|

|

Safety Report

|

|

Regulatory Submission

A BA should understand these relationships.

8. SQL Command Categories

SQL commands are grouped into categories.

DQL (Data Query Language)

Used to retrieve data.

Main command:

SELECT

DML (Data Manipulation Language)

Used to modify data.

Commands:

INSERT

UPDATE

DELETE

DDL (Data Definition Language)

Used to define database structure.

Commands:

CREATE

ALTER

DROP

As a BA, you mostly use:

SELECT

for analysis.

9. SELECT Statement

The most important SQL command.

Purpose:

Retrieve data.

Syntax:

SELECT column_name

FROM table_name;

Example:

Patient names:

SELECT name

FROM patients;

Output:

name

Rahul

Priya

Amit

10. Selecting Multiple Columns

Requirement:

\"Show patient name and age.\"

SQL:

SELECT

name,

age

FROM patients;

Output:

name age

Rahul 45

Priya 32

11. Selecting All Columns

Use:

SELECT *

FROM patients;

Meaning:

Give me everything.

Example output:

id name age city

101 Rahul 45 Ahmedabad

12. WHERE Clause

Used to filter data.

Business requirement:

\"Find all patients above age 50.\"

SQL:

SELECT *

FROM patients

WHERE age > 50;

Result:

name age

Amit 55

13. Multiple Conditions

Requirement:

Find male patients above age 40.

SQL:

SELECT *

FROM patients

WHERE gender=\'M\'

AND age > 40;

14. Operators in SQL

Comparison Operators

Operator Meaning

= Equal

> Greater than

\< Less than

>= Greater or equal

\<= Less or equal

\<> Not equal

Logical Operators

AND

Both conditions must be true.

Example:

WHERE age > 40

AND city=\'Delhi\'

OR

Either condition can be true.

Example:

WHERE city=\'Delhi\'

OR city=\'Mumbai\'

NOT

Reverse condition.

Example:

WHERE NOT gender=\'M\'

15. ORDER BY

Sort results.

Requirement:

\"Show patients from oldest to youngest.\"

SQL:

SELECT *

FROM patients

ORDER BY age DESC;

DESC:

Descending

ASC:

Ascending

16. LIMIT

Restrict number of records.

Example:

Show first 10 patients:

SELECT *

FROM patients

LIMIT 10;

Useful for large datasets.

17. Real BA Example

Requirement:

\"Find all serious adverse events reported in India.\"

Database:

Table:

adverse_events

Columns:

event_id

country

seriousness

drug_name

date

SQL:

SELECT *

FROM adverse_events

WHERE country=\'India\'

AND seriousness=\'Serious\';

18. SQL and Requirement Validation

Business Requirement:

\"System should show all pending safety cases.\"

BA checks:

Where is status stored?

Example:

Table:

safety_cases

Column:

case_status

Query:

SELECT *

FROM safety_cases

WHERE case_status=\'Pending\';

Now the BA validates whether the system output matches business expectations.

19. Common SQL Mistakes Beginners Make

❌ Selecting unnecessary columns

Bad:

SELECT *

FROM huge_table;

Better:

SELECT case_id,status

FROM safety_cases;

❌ Forgetting filters

Bad:

SELECT *

FROM patients;

May return millions of records.

❌ Ignoring relationships

A BA must understand:

Which table contains what information?

20. BA SQL Interview Questions

Q1. Why should a Business Analyst know SQL?

Answer:

\"SQL helps a BA validate requirements, analyze business data, verify system behavior, and communicate effectively with technical teams.\"

Q2. Difference between Primary Key and Foreign Key?

Answer:

\"A primary key uniquely identifies a record within a table. A foreign key creates relationships between tables.\"

Q3. What is SELECT used for?

Answer:

\"SELECT retrieves data from one or more database tables.\"

Q4. Difference between WHERE and HAVING?

(Advanced topic, covered later)

WHERE filters rows before grouping.

HAVING filters grouped results.

21. Practical Assignment

Scenario:

You are BA for an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

Database table:

adverse_events

Column Description

event_id Unique event

patient_id Patient identifier

drug_name Drug involved

country Reporting country

severity Event severity

status Review status

report_date Date reported

Write SQL queries for:

Task 1

Get all adverse events.

Task 2

Find all serious events.

Task 3

Find pending cases from India.

Task 4

Show only:

  • event_id

  • drug_name

  • severity

Task 5

Show latest reports first.

Lesson 1 Summary

Today you learned:

✅ What SQL is\ ✅ Database concepts\ ✅ Tables, rows, columns\ ✅ Primary keys\ ✅ Foreign keys\ ✅ SELECT queries\ ✅ Filtering data\ ✅ Sorting data\ ✅ How BAs use SQL in real projects

Lesson 2: Advanced SQL for Business Analysts

Goal: Move from basic data retrieval to business analysis using SQL. A senior BA should be able to analyze trends, validate KPIs, identify patterns, and answer business questions directly from data.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • Aggregate functions

  • COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX

  • GROUP BY analysis

  • HAVING filtering

  • CASE statements

  • JOINs between tables

  • Subqueries

  • Window functions

  • Real healthcare analytics examples

  • BA SQL interview scenarios

1. Why Advanced SQL Matters for BA

A business stakeholder rarely asks:

\"Show me all records.\"

They ask:

\"How many serious adverse events occurred this month?\"

\"Which drug has the highest safety signals?\"

\"Which region has the highest reporting volume?\"

\"Is AI reducing review time?\"

These require analysis, not simple retrieval.

2. Aggregate Functions

Aggregate functions perform calculations on multiple rows.

Common functions:

Function Purpose

COUNT() Count records

SUM() Add values

AVG() Calculate average

MIN() Minimum value

MAX() Maximum value

3. COUNT()

Business Question:

How many adverse event reports exist?

Table:

adverse_events

SQL:

SELECT COUNT(*)

FROM adverse_events;

Output:

count

25000

Meaning:

There are 25,000 reports.

Count Specific Records

Question:

How many serious cases exist?

SELECT COUNT(*)

FROM adverse_events

WHERE severity=\'Serious\';

4. SUM()

Used for totals.

Example:

Table:

claims

claim_id amount

1 5000

2 7000

Query:

SELECT SUM(amount)

FROM claims;

Output:

12000

Healthcare Example:

Total reimbursement paid:

SELECT SUM(payment_amount)

FROM insurance_claims;

5. AVG()

Calculate average.

Example:

Average patient age:

SELECT AVG(age)

FROM patients;

Output:

42.5

Business Question:

What is the average AI review confidence score?

Table:

ai_predictions

SELECT AVG(confidence_score)

FROM ai_predictions;

6. MIN() and MAX()

Find lowest and highest values.

Example:

Oldest patient:

SELECT MAX(age)

FROM patients;

Highest AI confidence:

SELECT MAX(confidence_score)

FROM predictions;

7. GROUP BY

One of the most important SQL concepts for analysts.

Purpose:

Group similar records together.

Example:

Question:

How many adverse events came from each country?

Data:

country

India

India

USA

UK

SQL:

SELECT

country,

COUNT(*) AS total_cases

FROM adverse_events

GROUP BY country;

Result:

country total_cases

India 12000

USA 8000

UK 5000

8. GROUP BY Multiple Columns

Question:

Number of serious events by country and drug.

SQL:

SELECT

country,

drug_name,

COUNT(*) AS cases

FROM adverse_events

WHERE severity=\'Serious\'

GROUP BY

country,

drug_name;

9. HAVING Clause

HAVING filters grouped results.

Difference:

WHERE

Filters rows before grouping.

HAVING

Filters after grouping.

Example:

Question:

Show countries having more than 1000 adverse events.

SQL:

SELECT

country,

COUNT(*) AS total

FROM adverse_events

GROUP BY country

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000;

Result:

Only high-volume countries appear.

10. WHERE vs HAVING Example

Question:

Find drugs with more than 500 serious cases.

Correct:

SELECT

drug_name,

COUNT(*) AS cases

FROM adverse_events

WHERE severity=\'Serious\'

GROUP BY drug_name

HAVING COUNT(*) > 500;

Flow:

Filter serious cases

↓

Group by drug

↓

Count cases

↓

Keep groups >500

11. CASE Statement

CASE allows decision logic inside SQL.

Think of it as:

IF / ELSE.

Example:

Classify patient age.

SELECT

name,

age,

CASE

WHEN age \< 18 THEN \'Child\'

WHEN age >=18 AND age \<60 THEN \'Adult\'

ELSE \'Senior\'

END AS age_group

FROM patients;

Output:

name age_group

Rahul Adult

Amit Senior

12. Business Rule Example

Requirement:

High-risk adverse events:

Rules:

  • Serious = Yes

  • Severity Score > 8

SQL:

SELECT

event_id,

CASE

WHEN seriousness=\'Yes\'

AND severity_score>8

THEN \'High Risk\'

ELSE \'Normal\'

END AS risk_level

FROM adverse_events;

A BA can convert business rules into data logic.

13. SQL JOINs

Real systems store data in multiple tables.

Example:

Patients:

patient_id name

101 Rahul

Adverse Events:

event_id patient_id drug

5001 101 Drug A

Need:

Patient name + event details.

We need JOIN.

14. INNER JOIN

Returns matching records.

Example:

SELECT

patients.name,

adverse_events.drug_name

FROM patients

INNER JOIN adverse_events

ON patients.patient_id =

adverse_events.patient_id;

Result:

name drug

Rahul Drug A

15. LEFT JOIN

Returns all records from left table, even without matches.

Example:

Show all patients, including those without adverse events.

SELECT

patients.name,

adverse_events.event_id

FROM patients

LEFT JOIN adverse_events

ON patients.patient_id=

adverse_events.patient_id;

16. JOIN Business Example

Requirement:

\"Show all doctors and the number of patients assigned.\"

Tables:

Doctors

Patients

SQL:

SELECT

doctor_name,

COUNT(patient_id)

FROM doctors

LEFT JOIN patients

ON doctors.doctor_id=

patients.doctor_id

GROUP BY doctor_name;

17. Subqueries

A query inside another query.

Example:

Find patients older than average age.

Step 1:

Average age:

SELECT AVG(age)

FROM patients;

Complete query:

SELECT *

FROM patients

WHERE age >

(

SELECT AVG(age)

FROM patients

);

18. Window Functions

Used for advanced analytics.

Unlike GROUP BY, window functions keep individual rows.

Example:

Rank drugs by number of safety cases.

SELECT

drug_name,

cases,

RANK()

OVER(

ORDER BY cases DESC

) AS ranking

FROM drug_summary;

Result:

drug cases rank

Drug A 5000 1

Drug B 3000 2

19. Real AI Pharmacovigilance Example

Business Question:

Which drugs generated the most serious adverse events in the last quarter?

SQL:

SELECT

drug_name,

COUNT(*) AS serious_cases

FROM adverse_events

WHERE severity=\'Serious\'

AND report_date >= \'2026-04-01\'

GROUP BY drug_name

ORDER BY serious_cases DESC;

Business Output:

Drug A → 2500 cases

Drug B → 1800 cases

Drug C → 900 cases

20. SQL for KPI Validation

KPI:

\"Reduce average safety review time below 24 hours.\"

Table:

case_reviews

Columns:

  • case_id

  • review_time_hours

Query:

SELECT

AVG(review_time_hours)

FROM case_reviews;

Output:

18 hours

Conclusion:

KPI achieved.

21. SQL BA Workflow

A Business Analyst typically follows:

Business Question

↓

Identify Data Source

↓

Understand Tables

↓

Write Query

↓

Validate Results

↓

Generate Insight

↓

Recommend Action

22. Common BA SQL Interview Questions

Q1. Difference between WHERE and HAVING?

Answer:

\"WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation. HAVING filters aggregated results after GROUP BY.\"

Q2. Difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?

Answer:

\"INNER JOIN returns only matching records. LEFT JOIN returns all records from the first table and matching records from the second table.\"

Q3. Why does a BA need SQL?

Answer:

\"SQL enables a BA to validate requirements, analyze business data, verify system behavior, and support data-driven decisions.\"

Q4. What is GROUP BY used for?

Answer:

\"GROUP BY combines records with similar values so aggregate calculations can be performed, such as counts, averages, and totals.\"

23. Practical Assignment

Database:

adverse_events

Columns:

event_id

drug_name

country

severity

status

review_time_hours

report_date

Answer using SQL:

Task 1

Count total adverse events.

Task 2

Find number of cases by country.

Task 3

Find top 5 drugs by serious cases.

Task 4

Calculate average review time.

Task 5

Classify cases:

  • Review time \<24 hours → Fast

  • Review time >=24 hours → Delayed

Using CASE.

Task 6

Create ranking of drugs by safety cases.

Lesson 2 Summary

Today you learned:

✅ Aggregate analysis\ ✅ COUNT/SUM/AVG\ ✅ GROUP BY\ ✅ HAVING\ ✅ CASE statements\ ✅ JOINs\ ✅ Subqueries\ ✅ Window functions\ ✅ KPI validation using SQL

Lesson 3: Database Concepts & Architecture for Business Analysts

Goal: Understand how enterprise applications store, manage, and process data so that you can communicate effectively with developers, architects, data engineers, and product teams.

A BA does not need to become a database administrator, but a modern BA must understand data architecture.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What databases are and why they exist

  • Different database types

  • Relational vs NoSQL databases

  • OLTP vs OLAP systems

  • Data warehouse concepts

  • Data lake concepts

  • Enterprise healthcare data architecture

  • AI data pipelines

  • How BAs document database requirements

1. Why Database Knowledge Matters for BA

A business requirement often sounds simple:

\"The system should show patient\'s complete medical history.\"

But technically, this may require data from:

Patient Registration System

|

|

Electronic Health Record

|

|

Laboratory System

|

|

Pharmacy System

|

|

Insurance System

A BA must understand:

  • Where data comes from

  • How systems communicate

  • How data is stored

  • How data is transformed

2. What is a Database?

A database is an organized collection of information stored electronically.

Example:

Hospital Database:

Hospital DB

├── Patient Information

├── Doctor Information

├── Appointment Records

├── Lab Reports

├── Prescription Data

└── Billing Information

The database allows applications to:

  • Store data

  • Retrieve data

  • Update data

  • Analyze information

3. Database Management System (DBMS)

A DBMS is software that manages databases.

Examples:

  • Oracle Corporation Database

  • Microsoft SQL Server

  • PostgreSQL Global Development Group PostgreSQL

  • MySQL

A DBMS provides:

  • Security

  • Data storage

  • Query processing

  • Backup

  • Recovery

  • Access control

4. Database Architecture Basics

A typical enterprise application follows:

User

|

|

Frontend Application

|

|

Backend API

|

|

Database

Example:

Pharmacovigilance Application:

Safety Analyst

|

↓

Web Dashboard

|

↓

Application Server

|

↓

Safety Database

5. Types of Databases

Major categories:

  1. Relational Databases

  2. NoSQL Databases

  3. Data Warehouses

  4. Data Lakes

  5. Graph Databases

6. Relational Database (RDBMS)

Most traditional enterprise systems use relational databases.

Data is stored in tables.

Example:

Patient Table:

Patient_ID Name Age

101 Rahul 45

Appointment Table:

Appointment_ID Patient_ID Date

5001 101 10-Aug

Relationships connect tables.

Common relational databases:

  • PostgreSQL

  • MySQL

  • Oracle

  • SQL Server

7. Advantages of Relational Databases

Structured Data

Information follows a fixed format.

Example:

Patient:

Name

Age

Gender

DOB

Data Integrity

Rules prevent incorrect data.

Example:

A patient ID cannot duplicate.

Powerful Queries

SQL allows complex analysis.

8. Limitations of Relational Databases

Traditional relational databases struggle with:

  • Huge unstructured data

  • Images

  • Videos

  • Documents

  • Rapidly changing structures

Example:

Medical documents:

  • PDFs

  • Doctor notes

  • Images

  • Scan reports

These may require other storage approaches.

9. NoSQL Databases

NoSQL means:

\"Not only SQL\"

Designed for flexible and large-scale data.

Types:

Document Database

Stores JSON-like documents.

Example:

Patient record:

{

\"name\":\"Rahul\",

\"age\":45,

\"conditions\":[

\"Diabetes\",

\"Hypertension\"

]

}

Key-Value Database

Stores:

Key → Value

Example:

User123 → Login Preferences

Column Database

Optimized for analytics.

Graph Database

Stores relationships.

Example:

Drug relationship:

Drug A

|

causes

|

Adverse Event

|

reported by

|

Patient

10. Relational vs NoSQL

Feature Relational NoSQL

Structure Fixed tables Flexible

Schema Strict Dynamic

Relationships Strong Flexible

Best For Business systems Large-scale apps

Query SQL Various methods

11. OLTP Systems

OLTP = Online Transaction Processing

Purpose:

Handle daily business operations.

Examples:

  • Hospital registration

  • Banking transactions

  • Pharmacy billing

Characteristics:

  • Many small transactions

  • Fast updates

  • Current data

Example:

Patient books appointment:

INSERT appointment record

12. OLAP Systems

OLAP = Online Analytical Processing

Purpose:

Analyze historical data.

Examples:

  • Business dashboards

  • Reports

  • Trend analysis

Characteristics:

  • Large datasets

  • Aggregations

  • Historical analysis

Example:

\"How many adverse events occurred per year?\"

13. OLTP vs OLAP

OLTP OLAP

Daily operations Analytics

Current data Historical data

Many updates Mostly read

Normalized tables Optimized reporting

14. Data Warehouse

A data warehouse stores data from multiple systems for analysis.

Example:

Hospital Data Warehouse:

Hospital System

|

Laboratory System

|

Pharmacy System

|

Insurance System

|

↓

Data Warehouse

|

↓

Power BI Dashboard

Used for:

  • Reports

  • KPIs

  • Business intelligence

  • Decision making

15. Data Lake

A data lake stores raw data in different formats.

Examples:

  • Text files

  • Images

  • Videos

  • Logs

  • Sensor data

Healthcare example:

Medical Images

Doctor Notes

Research Papers

Genomic Data

Patient Records

16. Data Warehouse vs Data Lake

Data Warehouse Data Lake

Processed data Raw data

Structured Structured + unstructured

Reporting AI/ML analytics

Business users Data scientists

17. Modern Healthcare Data Architecture

Example:

Users

|

↓

Healthcare Apps

|

↓

APIs Layer

|

┌──────────┼──────────┐

↓ ↓ ↓

Patient DB Lab DB Pharmacy DB

|

↓

Data Warehouse

|

↓

AI Analytics Platform

18. AI Data Pipeline

AI systems require additional steps.

Data Sources

|

↓

Data Collection

|

↓

Data Cleaning

|

↓

Data Labeling

|

↓

Feature Engineering

|

↓

Machine Learning Model

|

↓

Prediction

|

↓

Monitoring

19. BA Role in Database Projects

A BA contributes by defining:

Data Requirements

Example:

\"The system must capture patient age, gender, drug exposure, and adverse event details.\"

Data Rules

Example:

\"Date of birth cannot be future date.\"

Data Relationships

Example:

\"Each safety case must link to one or more adverse event records.\"

Data Validation

Example:

\"Drug name must match approved drug master list.\"

20. Database Documentation for BA

Important documents:

Data Dictionary

Defines:

Field Meaning Type

patient_id Unique patient identifier Integer

drug_name Medicine name Text

ER Diagram

Shows:

Patient

|

|

Adverse Event

|

|

Drug

Data Mapping Document

Example:

Source System:

Hospital CRM

↓

Target System:

AI Safety Platform

Mapping:

CRM.patient_name

|

↓

Safety.patient_full_name

21. AI Pharmacovigilance Example

Requirement:

\"AI should identify high-risk adverse events.\"

Required data:

Patient Data

  • Age

  • Gender

  • Medical history

Drug Data

  • Drug name

  • Dosage

  • Indication

Event Data

  • Symptoms

  • Severity

  • Timeline

Outcome Data

  • Recovery

  • Hospitalization

  • Death

The BA ensures all required data exists.

22. Interview Questions

Q1. Difference between OLTP and OLAP?

Answer:

\"OLTP supports daily transactions, while OLAP supports analytical reporting and decision-making using historical data.\"

Q2. Why do companies use data warehouses?

Answer:

\"Data warehouses combine data from multiple systems and provide a centralized source for reporting and analytics.\"

Q3. What is the role of BA in database design?

Answer:

\"A BA defines business data requirements, relationships, validation rules, and ensures the database supports business processes.\"

Q4. Difference between SQL and NoSQL?

Answer:

\"SQL databases use structured tables with predefined schemas, while NoSQL databases provide flexible structures suitable for large-scale and changing data.\"

23. Practical Assignment

You are designing an:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Create:

1. Identify Data Sources

Example:

  • Drug Database

  • Patient System

  • Safety Reports

  • Regulatory Database

2. Define Core Tables

Example:

Patient

Drug

Adverse_Event

Safety_Case

AI_Prediction

Review_Action

3. Define Relationships

Example:

Patient

|

Safety Case

|

Adverse Event

|

Drug

Lesson 3 Summary

You learned:

Lesson 4: ER Diagrams & Data Modeling for Business Analysts

Goal: Learn how Business Analysts translate business requirements into structured data models and communicate effectively with database designers, architects, and developers.

A BA does not usually design the physical database, but a strong BA understands how business information is structured, related, and stored.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What data modeling means

  • What an ER Diagram is

  • Entities, attributes, and relationships

  • Primary keys and foreign keys

  • Cardinality (1:1, 1:M, M:M)

  • Normalization basics

  • How to create healthcare data models

  • How AI systems use data models

  • How BAs document data requirements

1. What is Data Modeling?

Data modeling is the process of defining:

  • What data the system stores

  • How data elements relate

  • What rules apply to data

It converts business requirements into a structured representation.

Example:

Business Requirement:

\"A patient can have multiple appointments with doctors.\"

Data Model:

Patient

|

|

Appointments

|

|

Doctor

2. Why Data Modeling Matters for BA

Without understanding data:

A BA may write:

\"System should store patient details.\"

But developers need more information:

Which details?

  • Name?

  • Age?

  • Address?

  • Medical history?

  • Insurance?

How are they related?

A good BA clarifies these questions.

3. What is an ER Diagram?

ERD = Entity Relationship Diagram

It visually represents:

  • Entities

  • Attributes

  • Relationships

Example:

+-------------+

| PATIENT |

+-------------+

| patient_id |

| name |

| age |

+-------------+

|

|

|

+----------------+

| APPOINTMENT |

+----------------+

| appointment_id |

| date |

| doctor_id |

+----------------+

4. Components of ER Diagram

An ER Diagram has three main components:

1. Entity

An object about which we store information.

Examples:

Healthcare:

  • Patient

  • Doctor

  • Drug

  • Prescription

  • Adverse Event

2. Attribute

Properties of an entity.

Example:

Entity:

Patient

Attributes:

patient_id

name

DOB

gender

phone

address

3. Relationship

Shows how entities connect.

Example:

Patient

HAS

Appointment

Attribute Description

name Patient name

DOB Date of birth

Entity:

Attributes:

Attribute Description

doctor_id Unique ID

name Doctor name

specialization Department

6. Primary Key in Data Modeling

Primary Key:

A unique identifier for each record.

Example:

Patient:

patient_id

Data:

patient_id name

101 Rahul

102 Priya

No two patients can have the same ID.

7. Foreign Key in Data Modeling

Foreign Key creates relationships.

Example:

Patient Table:

patient_id name

101 Rahul

Appointment Table:

appointment_id patient_id

5001 101

The appointment knows which patient it belongs to.

8. Relationships in ERD

There are three major relationship types.

Relationship 1: One-to-One (1:1)

One record connects to one record.

Example:

Patient ↔ Medical Insurance Profile

Patient

|

|

Insurance Profile

One patient has one insurance profile.

Relationship 2: One-to-Many (1:M)

Most common relationship.

Example:

One patient can have many appointments.

Patient

|

|

|

Appointments

Database:

Patient:

Patient_ID

101

Appointments:

Appointment_ID | Patient_ID

5001 101

5002 101

5003 101

Relationship 3: Many-to-Many (M:M)

Many records connect to many records.

Example:

Doctors and Patients.

A doctor treats many patients.

A patient can visit many doctors.

Doctor

|

|

Doctor_Patient

|

|

Patient

Usually solved using a bridge table.

Example:

Doctor_Patient:

doctor_id patient_id

1 101

2 101

1 102

9. Cardinality

Cardinality defines relationship quantity.

Symbols:

1 One

M Many

Examples:

Patient 1 -------- M Appointment

Means:

One patient can have many appointments.

Normalization means organizing data to reduce duplication.

Goal: Learn how a Business Analyst defines, documents, and controls data movement between systems. This skill is critical for enterprise applications, healthcare systems, integrations, migrations, and AI projects.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What data mapping is

Modern applications rarely work alone.

2. What is Data Mapping?

Data Mapping is the process of defining:

How data from a source system is converted and transferred into a target system.

Simple example:

Source System Target System

Patient_Name ─────→ Full_Name

DOB ─────→ Date_of_Birth

Mobile_No ─────→ Contact_Number

A BA uses data mapping for:

System Integration

Data Migration

Old application → New application

API Integration

Reporting

Operational database → Dashboard

AI Projects

Example:

Raw medical records → AI training dataset

A professional mapping document usually contains:

Field Purpose

Target System Destination

Mandatory/Optional Requirement

Lesson 6: Data Quality Analysis & Data Governance for Business Analysts

Goal: Learn how Business Analysts ensure that data used by business systems, analytics platforms, and AI models is accurate, complete, reliable, secure, and compliant.

A modern BA does not only ask:

\"What data do we need?\"

A senior BA asks:

\"Can we trust this data?\"

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What data quality means

  • Data quality dimensions

  • Data profiling

  • Data cleansing

  • Data validation rules

  • Master Data Management (MDM)

  • Data governance framework

  • Data ownership

  • Healthcare data governance

  • AI data quality requirements

1. Why Data Quality Matters

A system can be technically correct but still produce wrong results if the data is poor.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Input:

Drug Name: Paracitamol

Severity: ?

Patient Age: 250

Problems:

  • Drug name spelling error

  • Missing severity

  • Invalid age

AI output may become unreliable.

2. The Data Quality Principle

Garbage In → Garbage Out

Meaning:

Poor quality data produces poor quality results.

Example:

Poor Patient Data

|

↓

AI Model

|

↓

Incorrect Risk Prediction

3. What is Data Quality?

Data quality means:

The degree to which data is accurate, complete, consistent, valid, timely, and suitable for business use.

4. Six Major Data Quality Dimensions

A BA should understand these deeply.

Dimension 1: Accuracy

Question:

Is the data correct?

Example:

Patient DOB:

Actual:

15-08-1985

Database:

15-08-1995

Problem:

Data is inaccurate.

Dimension 2: Completeness

Question:

Is required information missing?

Example:

Adverse Event:

Field Value

Drug Name Aspirin

Severity NULL

Severity missing.

Data incomplete.

Dimension 3: Consistency

Question:

Is data the same across systems?

Example:

Hospital System:

Patient Gender = Male

Insurance System:

Gender = M

Both are acceptable.

But:

Gender = Female

creates inconsistency.

Dimension 4: Validity

Question:

Does data follow business rules?

Example:

Age:

Valid:

45

Invalid:

-5

Rule:

Age must be between 0-120

Dimension 5: Uniqueness

Question:

Are duplicate records present?

Example:

Patient database:

Patient ID 101

Rahul Sharma

Patient ID 101

Rahul Sharma

Duplicate.

Dimension 6: Timeliness

Question:

Is data available when needed?

Example:

Drug safety reporting requires recent information.

Delayed data:

Report received after 30 days

may affect regulatory timelines.

5. Data Quality Framework

A BA evaluates:

Data Quality

|

------------------------------------------------

| | | | |

Accuracy Completeness Consistency Validity Timeliness

Data profiling means:

Examining data to understand its quality and characteristics.

Data governance means:

Managing data ownership, quality, security, and usage across an organization.

Lesson 7: API Testing for Business Analysts (Postman)

Goal: Understand APIs from a Business Analyst perspective and learn how to validate integrations, review API requirements, test responses, and communicate effectively with development teams.

Modern systems rarely work independently.

A BA must understand:

1. Why APIs Matter for Business Analysts

A business user sees:

\"Customer data should appear in our application.\"

A technical team needs:

  • Which system provides the data?

  • How will data travel?

  • What format will be used?

  • What happens if the connection fails?

API knowledge helps a BA answer these questions.

2. What is an API?

API = Application Programming Interface

Simple definition:

An API allows two software systems to communicate with each other.

Analogy:

Restaurant example:

Customer

|

↓

Waiter (API)

|

↓

Kitchen (System)

Customer does not directly enter the kitchen.

The waiter transfers the request and returns the response.

  • Government

  • Healthcare legacy systems

Allows clients to request exactly needed data.

Example:

Instead of:

\"Give me complete patient record\"

Request:

\"Give me only patient name and medications.\"

Goal: Understand modern enterprise application architecture so a BA can define requirements, analyze system behavior, and communicate with architects and development teams.

Modern products like healthcare platforms, banking systems, and AI applications are rarely built as one large application. They are built using multiple independent services.

1. What is Software Architecture?

Software architecture describes:

How different parts of a software system are organized and communicate with each other.

Example:

A hospital application contains:

  • Appointment booking

  • Pharmacy

3. Problems With Monolithic Architecture

Problem 1: Difficult Scaling

Example:

But entire application must scale.

Problem 2: Slow Development

A small change requires rebuilding the whole application.

Problem 3: Technology Limitations

Entire system uses one technology stack.

Example:

All Java or all .NET.

Microservices breaks a large application into smaller independent services.

Example:

Instead of:

Hospital Application

We create:

Billing Service

Each service performs one business capability.

Other services may continue.

Lesson 11: System Integration Patterns for Business Analysts

Goal: Learn common integration patterns used in enterprise systems and understand how a BA decides which integration approach fits a business requirement.

A senior BA should not only ask:

\"Do we need an integration?\"

A senior BA asks:

\"What type of integration pattern best solves this business problem?\"

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What integration patterns are

  • Request-Response pattern

  • Publish-Subscribe pattern

  • Message Queue pattern

  • Event Streaming pattern

  • File-Based integration

  • Batch processing

  • Real-time vs asynchronous integration

  • Integration decision matrix

  • Healthcare enterprise examples

1. What is an Integration Pattern?

An integration pattern is:

A reusable approach for connecting systems and exchanging information.

Different business needs require different patterns.

Example:

A hospital wants:

  1. Immediate patient alert → Real-time integration

  2. Daily reporting → Batch integration

  3. Large historical data migration → File-based integration

2. Why BAs Need Integration Patterns

Without understanding patterns, requirements may be incomplete.

Example:

Business says:

\"Send patient data to AI system.\"

BA must clarify:

  • Immediately or daily?

  • One record or millions?

  • What happens if transmission fails?

  • Should systems wait for response?

These answers decide the architecture.

Advantages

  • Easy to understand

  • Good for real-time actions

  • Easy error handling

Limitations

System A waits or fails.

When BA Should Choose This

Use when:

  • User needs immediate response

  • Data volume is small

  • Action depends on result

Examples:

✅ Login\ ✅ Patient search\ ✅ Payment verification

Lesson 12: Application Architecture Fundamentals

Goal: Learn how enterprise software applications are structured so you can confidently discuss architecture with Solution Architects, Developers, Technical Leads, and Product Managers.

Important: A Business Analyst is not expected to design software architecture, but you must understand it well enough to gather requirements, analyze impacts, identify risks, and communicate effectively with technical teams.
