Lesson 13 -- Agile Sprint Execution Simulation

Working as a BA During Real Development Sprints

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ What a BA does during a sprint\ ✅ How requirements move from backlog to production\ ✅ BA activities in Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Refinement, Review, and Retrospective\ ✅ How to support developers and testers\ ✅ How to handle requirement changes during development\ ✅ How to simulate a real Agile project environment

1. Role of BA in Agile Sprint

Many beginners think:

\"BA finishes requirements before development starts.\"

In real Agile projects:

A BA continuously works with:

  • Product Owner

  • Developers

  • QA Engineers

  • UX Designers

  • Stakeholders

throughout the sprint.

BA Agile Lifecycle

Backlog Refinement

↓

Sprint Planning

↓

Development Support

↓

Testing Support

↓

Sprint Review

↓

Feedback Analysis

↓

Backlog Updates

2. Sprint Simulation

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Sprint Duration:

2 Weeks

Sprint Goal:

Enable PV Associates to upload safety reports and view AI extraction results.

Sprint Backlog

ID User Story Priority Story Points

US-001 Login Must 3

US-002 Upload Safety Report Must 5

US-003 AI Data Extraction Must 8

US-004 Case Dashboard Should 5

3. BA Activity Before Sprint

Backlog Refinement

The BA helps ensure stories are ready.

BA checks:

✅ Is requirement clear?

✅ Is user identified?

✅ Are acceptance criteria written?

✅ Are business rules defined?

✅ Are dependencies known?

Example:

Developer asks:

\"What happens if the uploaded document is corrupted?\"

BA clarifies:

Requirement update:

\"The system shall display an error message when document validation fails.\"

4. Sprint Planning

The team selects stories.

Example:

Sprint Goal:

\"Allow users to submit safety reports.\"

Selected Stories:

US-001 Login

US-002 Upload Report

US-003 AI Extraction

BA Responsibility:

Explain:

  • Business value

  • User expectation

  • Acceptance criteria

5. During Development

The BA supports the team daily.

Scenario 1: Developer Question

Developer:

\"Should AI extraction happen automatically after upload?\"

BA:

Business clarification:

\"Yes. Once the file is successfully uploaded, processing should start automatically.\"

Scenario 2: Missing Requirement

Developer:

\"Should users edit AI extracted data?\"

BA investigates.

Medical team says:

\"Yes, reviewers must correct AI mistakes.\"

New requirement:

\"The system shall allow authorized users to modify extracted information.\"

6. Daily Scrum Support

Daily Scrum is mainly for developers.

But BA may attend.

BA observes:

  • Requirement blockers

  • Questions

  • Dependency issues

Example:

Developer:

\"We cannot complete AI extraction because sample documents are unavailable.\"

BA Action:

Coordinate with PV team and provide test documents.

7. QA Testing Support

A BA helps QA understand expected behavior.

8. Handling Requirement Changes

Agile accepts change.

But BA manages impact.

Scenario:

\"Add automatic translation of reports.\"

BA performs:

Impact Analysis

Questions:

  • Does it affect scope?

  • Does it affect timeline?

  • Does it affect architecture?

  • Does it require new stories?

Result:

New Story:

As a PV Associate,

I want reports translated automatically,

So that I can process global cases faster.

9. Sprint Review

The team demonstrates completed work.

Participants:

  • Product Owner

  • Stakeholders

  • Users

BA Role:

Validate:

Does the solution meet business needs?

Example Feedback:

Medical Reviewer:

\"I need to see the original document alongside AI extraction.\"

BA captures:

New backlog item:

\"Display source document with extracted information.\"

10. Sprint Retrospective

Team discusses:

What went well?

What can improve?

BA Contribution:

Example:

Problem:

Requirements were unclear.

Improvement:

Add more detailed acceptance criteria.

Lesson 14 -- UAT Planning & Execution

Validating the Solution Before Business Go-Live

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ What UAT means in real projects\ ✅ Difference between QA Testing and UAT\ ✅ BA role in UAT planning and execution\ ✅ How to create UAT scenarios and test cases\ ✅ How to manage defects and business feedback\ ✅ How to prepare UAT sign-off documents

1. What is UAT?

UAT = User Acceptance Testing

UAT verifies:

\"Does the solution actually solve the business user\'s problem?\"

It is the final validation before production release.

Simple Example

Development Team checks:

\"Does the button work?\"

Business User checks:

\"Can I complete my daily work using this system?\"

2. QA Testing vs UAT

Important BA interview question.

QA Testing UAT

Performed by QA team Performed by business users

Checks system correctness Checks business suitability

Focuses on defects Focuses on business acceptance

Technical perspective User perspective

Example:

QA Test

\"Does the upload button accept PDF files?\"

UAT Test

\"Can PV scientists successfully upload safety reports and process cases?\"

3. BA Role in UAT

A BA is the bridge between:

Business Users ↔ Development Team

BA responsibilities:

Prepare UAT Plan

↓

Identify Business Scenarios

↓

Create UAT Cases

↓

Coordinate Users

↓

Track Defects

↓

Validate Fixes

↓

Obtain Sign-Off

Lesson 15 -- Project Closure & BA Handover

Completing the Full Project Lifecycle as a Business Analyst

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ What happens after development and UAT completion\ ✅ BA responsibilities during project closure\ ✅ How to prepare project handover documents\ ✅ How to conduct knowledge transfer\ ✅ How to capture lessons learned\ ✅ How to create a complete BA project portfolio package

1. Why Project Closure Matters for a BA?

Many beginners think:

\"BA work ends when requirements are delivered.\"

In reality, BA involvement continues until:

  • Business accepts the solution

  • Users are ready

  • Documentation is complete

  • Operations can support the system

Complete BA Project Lifecycle

↓

Discovery

↓

Requirements

↓

Process Analysis

↓

Design

↓

Development

↓

Testing

↓

UAT

↓

↓

Continuous Improvement

2. Project Closure Activities

2. Complete Documentation

3. Conduct Knowledge Transfer

4. Confirm Business Acceptance

5. Capture Lessons Learned

6. Archive Project Artifacts

Knowledge Transfer ensures business teams understand the solution.

Participants:

  • PV users

Lesson 1 -- Building a Professional Business Analyst Portfolio

Turning Learning Into Proof of Capability

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ Why a BA portfolio is important\ ✅ What recruiters expect from a BA portfolio\ ✅ How to structure portfolio projects\ ✅ How to present BA deliverables professionally\ ✅ How to convert our AI Pharmacovigilance project into a job-ready case study

1. Why Does a BA Need a Portfolio?

A common problem for aspiring BAs:

\"I understand BA concepts, but I don\'t have experience.\"

A portfolio solves this problem.

Instead of saying:

\"I know BRD, BPMN, User Stories, UAT.\"

You show:

\"Here is a complete project where I analyzed a business problem, created requirements, designed processes, and validated the solution.\"

2. What Recruiters Look For in a BA Portfolio

A hiring manager wants evidence of:

Business Understanding

Can you understand business problems?

Example:

\"Pharmacovigilance teams spend excessive time processing safety cases.\"

Analysis Skills

Can you analyze current processes?

Example:

AS-IS BPMN + Gap Analysis

Requirement Skills

Can you define what needs to be built?

Example:

BRD + FRD + User Stories

Collaboration Skills

Can you work with stakeholders?

Example:

Workshop notes + stakeholder analysis

Delivery Understanding

Do you understand the full lifecycle?

Example:

Sprint → Testing → UAT → Release

3. Portfolio Project Structure

A professional BA portfolio should look like a real project repository.

Example:

BA Portfolio

│

├── Project 1

│ AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

│

├── Project 2

│ AI Healthcare Appointment Assistant

│

↓

5. Portfolio Project #1

AI Pharmacovigilance Automation Platform

This becomes your flagship project.

Why?

Because it combines:

  • Healthcare domain knowledge

  • AI understanding

  • BA skills

  • Product thinking

Project Overview

Business Problem

Pharmaceutical companies receive thousands of adverse event reports.

Current challenges:

  • Manual document review

  • Slow case processing

  • High operational workload

  • Limited visibility

Proposed Solution

AI-assisted pharmacovigilance platform that:

  • Extracts safety information

  • Creates case summaries

  • Supports medical review

  • Tracks case workflow

BA Role in Project

You present yourself as:

Business Analyst responsible for discovery, requirement analysis, process improvement, Agile delivery support, and validation.

Do not upload random documents.

Example:

3. Solution

\"I defined requirements for an AI-assisted workflow platform.\"

4. Delivery

\"I translated requirements into user stories and supported Agile development.\"

5. Outcome

\"The solution aimed to reduce processing time and improve case visibility.\"

Lesson 2 -- Creating BA Case Study Documentation

Writing a Recruiter-Friendly Project Story

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ How recruiters evaluate BA project experience\ ✅ How to convert documents into a compelling case study\ ✅ How to write a project summary like an experienced BA\ ✅ How to explain your contribution clearly\ ✅ How to present BA deliverables as business outcomes

1. What is a BA Case Study?

A BA case study is a structured story explaining:

\"What problem existed, how you analyzed it, what solution was designed, and what value was delivered.\"

A Portfolio Is NOT:

❌ A folder full of documents

Example:

BRD.pdf

FRD.pdf

BPMN.png

User Stories.xlsx

Recruiters do not understand the value.

A Portfolio IS:

A business story:

Problem

↓

Analysis

↓

Requirements

↓

Solution

↓

Delivery

↓

Outcome

2. The STAR Framework for BA Case Studies

A very useful interview structure.

S --- Situation

What was happening?

T --- Task

What was your responsibility?

A --- Action

What did you do?

R --- Result

What business value was achieved?

Example:

Situation

A pharmaceutical company was processing safety cases manually, resulting in long processing cycles.

Task

As a BA, analyze the workflow and define requirements for an AI-assisted solution.

Action

  • Conducted stakeholder interviews

  • Created AS-IS process models

  • Performed gap analysis

  • Created BRD and FRD

  • Defined user stories and acceptance criteria

Result

Designed a future-state workflow aimed at reducing manual effort and improving case visibility.

3. Case Study Template

Every portfolio project should follow this structure.

Project Title

4. Common BA Interview Questions

Question 1:

How do you gather requirements?

Strong Answer:

\"I first understand the business problem, identify stakeholders, conduct workshops or interviews, analyze current processes, document requirements, validate them with stakeholders, and maintain traceability.\"

Question 2:

How do you handle conflicting requirements?

Answer:

\"I understand the reason behind each request, analyze business impact, discuss priorities with stakeholders, document decisions, and align requirements with business objectives.\"

Question 3:

How do you prioritize requirements?

Answer:

\"I use techniques like MoSCoW prioritization, business value analysis, risk assessment, effort estimation, and stakeholder input.\"

Question 4:

What happens if requirements change during development?

Answer:

\"I perform impact analysis, understand affected areas, update documentation, communicate changes, and ensure the team understands the revised requirement.\"

Healthcare organizations face increasing challenges:

PART 1 -- BUSINESS REQUIREMENTS DOCUMENT (BRD)

2. BRD Overview

Project Name

AI Healthcare Appointment Assistant Platform

Document Purpose

The purpose of this document is to define the business objectives, scope, stakeholders, and high-level requirements for implementing an AI-powered healthcare appointment management solution.

3. Executive Summary

Current Situation

Healthcare organizations experience challenges in appointment management due to:

  • Manual scheduling processes

  • High dependency on reception teams

  • Difficulty finding appropriate specialists

  • Missed appointments

  • Limited patient engagement

Proposed Solution

An AI-powered appointment assistant that enables patients to:

  • Search doctors

  • Receive intelligent recommendations

  • Book appointments

  • Get reminders

  • Manage consultations

4. Business Problem

Problem Statement

Patients often face difficulty accessing healthcare services efficiently because appointment scheduling depends heavily on manual processes, resulting in delays, poor experience, and increased administrative workload.

5. Business Objectives

Objective Expected Outcome

Enable self-service booking Improve patient convenience

Automate doctor discovery Faster doctor selection

Reduce manual scheduling Lower administrative effort

Improve reminders Reduce missed appointments

6. Project Scope

In Scope

✅ Patient registration

✅ Doctor search

✅ AI recommendations

✅ Appointment booking

✅ Appointment reminders

✅ Appointment dashboard

Out of Scope

❌ Medical diagnosis

❌ Treatment recommendations

❌ Prescription generation

❌ Insurance claim processing

7. Stakeholders

Stakeholder Responsibility

Hospital Management Business approval

Patients Primary users

Doctors Appointment providers

Reception Team Operational users

IT Team System implementation

Compliance Team Healthcare governance

8. Business Requirements

BR-001: Digital Appointment Booking

Requirement:

The organization needs a digital platform that allows patients to schedule appointments without manual intervention.

BR-002: Intelligent Doctor Discovery

Requirement:

The system should help patients identify suitable doctors based on their needs.

BR-003: Automated Communication

Requirement:

The system should provide automated appointment confirmations and reminders.

BR-004: Operational Visibility

Requirement:

Hospital management should have visibility into appointment activities.

9. Success Criteria

Metric Expected Improvement

Booking process Faster patient scheduling

Reception workload Reduced manual activities

Patient engagement Improved experience

Appointment attendance Reduced missed appointments

3. Executive Summary

Background

Clinical trials require coordination between multiple teams including sponsors, research sites, investigators, and monitoring teams.

Proposed Solution

An AI-enabled Clinical Trial Management Platform that provides:

  • Patient recruitment tracking

Clinical trial organizations lack a centralized intelligent system to monitor trial progress, identify risks early, and improve operational decision-making.

Management cannot quickly understand trial health.

Challenge 2: Patient Recruitment Delay

Recruitment progress is manually monitored.

Impact:

Trials may exceed timelines.

Challenge 3: Site Performance Monitoring

Current Situation:

CRA teams identify problems after delays occur.

Impact:

Reactive problem solving.

Challenge 4: Reporting Complexity

Current Situation:

Reports require manual consolidation.

Impact:

Slow decision making.

Reduce trial delays.

7. Root Cause Analysis (RCA)

Problem:

Document Review Takes Too Long

5 Why Analysis

Why 1:

Why is review slow?

Because employees manually read documents.

Why 2:

Why manually read?

Because information extraction is not automated.

Why 3:

Why no automation?

Because documents are unstructured.

Why 4:

Why are documents difficult?

Because they contain text, tables, images, and different formats.

Why 5:

Why no intelligent system?

Because existing systems only store documents, they do not understand content.

Root Cause:

Lack of AI-powered document understanding capability.

90%

9. Responsible AI Requirements

Principle 1: Explainability

Principle 2: Human Oversight

Requirement:

Principle 3: Bias Management

Requirement:

Example:

AI should not perform differently because of document source variations.

Principle 4: Privacy Protection

Requirement:

Patient and confidential information must be protected.

Hospital Management System (HMS)

Lesson 1 -- Project Introduction, Business Problem & Industry Context

Enterprise Healthcare Operations Case Study

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ What a Hospital Management System is\ ✅ Why hospitals need digital transformation\ ✅ How a BA approaches a hospital software project\ ✅ Business problems behind HMS implementation\ ✅ Key stakeholders and business objectives

1. Project Introduction

Project Name:

Hospital Management System (HMS)

Industry:

Healthcare / Hospital Operations

Project Type:

Enterprise Healthcare Management Platform

Business Scenario

A multi-specialty hospital group operates:

  • 3 hospitals

  • 500+ beds

  • 200+ doctors

  • 1000+ healthcare staff

  • Thousands of daily patients

Current operations are managed through:

  • Paper records

  • Excel sheets

  • Multiple disconnected systems

  • Manual approvals

The hospital wants to implement a centralized HMS platform.

2. What is a Hospital Management System?

A Hospital Management System is a software platform that manages:

Patient Journey

↓

Registration

↓

Appointment

↓

Consultation

↓

Diagnosis

↓

Treatment

↓

Billing

↓

Discharge

↓

Follow-up

It connects:

Clinical Operations

Doctors, nurses, labs

Administrative Operations

Reception, billing, insurance

Management Operations

Hospital leadership, analytics

3. Why Hospitals Need HMS?

Problem 1: Patient Data Fragmentation

Current Situation:

Patient visits hospital.

Reception has data.

Doctor has separate notes.

Lab has separate reports.

Billing has separate records.

Problem:

No single patient view.

Business Impact:

❌ Slow treatment decisions

❌ Duplicate data entry

❌ Poor patient experience

Solution:

Centralized Electronic Patient Record (EPR)

4. Problem 2: Appointment Management Issues

Current Process:

Patient calls reception.

Reception checks doctor availability manually.

Appointment recorded in diary.

Problems:

❌ Long waiting time

❌ Double booking

❌ Poor doctor utilization

HMS Solution:

Online appointment scheduling:

Patient

↓

Select Doctor

↓

Check Availability

↓

Book Slot

↓

Confirmation

5. Problem 3: Manual Billing Process

Current:

Doctor consultation completed.

↓

Billing staff manually creates invoice.

↓

Insurance team verifies documents.

Problems:

❌ Billing errors

❌ Claim delays

❌ Revenue leakage

HMS Solution:

Automated billing workflow:

Treatment Data

↓

Billing Engine

↓

Insurance Verification

↓

Invoice Generation

↓

Payment

6. Problem 4: Lack of Hospital Visibility

Management cannot easily answer:

  • How many patients today?

  • Which department is overloaded?

  • Revenue status?

  • Bed availability?

  • Doctor performance?

HMS Solution:

Management Dashboard:

Example:

Today\'s Patients:

850

Available Beds:

42

Revenue:

₹25 Lakhs

Emergency Cases:

35

7. Business Problem Statement (BA Artifact)

A BA documents the problem clearly.

Business Problem:

The hospital currently operates through fragmented manual processes resulting in inefficient patient management, delayed information access, billing errors, and poor operational visibility. A centralized Hospital Management System is required to improve healthcare delivery efficiency, data accuracy, and patient experience.

8. Project Objectives

Primary Objectives:

Objective 1

Create a centralized patient information system.

Objective 2

Digitize hospital workflows.

Objective 3

Improve operational efficiency.

Objective 4

Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS)

Pharma Clinical Research Enterprise Case Study 🚀

Lesson 1 -- Project Introduction, Business Problem & Clinical Trial Industry Context

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ What a Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS) is\ ✅ How pharmaceutical companies manage clinical trials\ ✅ Business problems in manual clinical trial operations\ ✅ Role of a Business Analyst in CTMS implementation\ ✅ High-level stakeholders and objectives

1. Project Introduction

Project Name:

Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS)

Industry:

Pharmaceutical / Biotechnology / Clinical Research

Project Type:

Enterprise Research Operations Platform

Business Scenario

A global pharmaceutical company conducts clinical trials for new medicines.

Current operations:

  • Multiple clinical trial studies running globally

  • Hundreds of investigators

  • Multiple research sites

  • Thousands of patients

  • Regulatory documentation requirements

Current management:

  • Excel trackers

  • Emails

  • Separate databases

  • Manual reporting

Problem:

The company cannot efficiently track:

  • Trial progress

  • Patient recruitment

  • Site performance

  • Investigator activities

  • Regulatory milestones

  • Monitoring visits

Solution:

Implement a centralized:

Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS)

2. What is Clinical Trial Management System?

A CTMS is an enterprise software platform that helps pharmaceutical companies manage the complete lifecycle of clinical trials.

Clinical Trial Lifecycle

Drug Discovery

↓

Preclinical Research

↓

Clinical Trial Planning

↓

Regulatory Approval

↓

Patient Recruitment

↓

Clinical Execution

↓

Data Collection

↓

Analysis

↓

Regulatory Submission

↓

Drug Approval

3. Where CTMS Fits?

CTMS mainly manages:

Trial Operations

  • Study planning

  • Sites

  • Investigators

  • Patients

  • Monitoring

  • Reporting

It does NOT replace:

Clinical Data Management System (CDMS)

which manages detailed clinical data.

Safety Database

which manages adverse events.

CTMS coordinates operations.

4. Why Pharma Companies Need CTMS?

Problem 1: Trial Tracking Issues

Current Situation:

Clinical teams maintain Excel trackers.

Example:

Study A

Site 1:

Patients recruited: 25

Site 2:

Patients recruited: 10

Site 3:

Delayed

Problems:

❌ No real-time visibility

❌ Data inconsistency

❌ Manual reporting

CTMS Solution:

Central trial dashboard.

Problem 2: Site Management Challenges

Clinical trials depend on research sites.

Example:

Hospital A

Hospital B

Research Center C

Current Problems:

❌ Difficult to compare site performance

❌ Delayed communication

❌ Missing documents

CTMS Solution:

Site performance tracking.

Problem 3: Patient Recruitment Delay

Clinical trials require enough participants.

Current:

Recruitment tracked manually.

Problems:

❌ Cannot predict delays

❌ Slow enrollment

CTMS Solution:

Recruitment dashboard:

Example:

Target Enrollment:

500 patients

Current:

350 patients

Progress:

70%

Problem 4: Monitoring Visit Management

Clinical monitors visit research sites.

Current Problems:

  • Visit schedules in spreadsheets

  • Missing reports

  • Delayed follow-up

CTMS Solution:

Automated monitoring workflow.

5. CTMS Business Problem Statement (BA Artifact)

A BA documents:

Business Problem:

The pharmaceutical organization currently manages clinical trial operations through fragmented manual processes, resulting in poor visibility into study progress, inefficient site management, delayed reporting, and increased operational risk. A centralized CTMS platform is required to improve clinical trial execution, compliance, and decision-making.

6. Project Objectives

Objective 1:

Improve Clinical Trial Visibility

Expected Result:

Real-time study dashboards.

Objective 2:

Optimize Site Management

Expected Result:

Better tracking of investigator and site performance.

Objective 3:

Improve Patient Recruitment Tracking

Expected Result:

Faster enrollment monitoring.

Objective 4:

Improve Regulatory Compliance

Expected Result:

Complete audit trails and documentation.

Objective 5:

Reduce Manual Operations

Expected Result:

Automated workflows and reporting.

7. CTMS Scope Overview

IN SCOPE

Study Management

  • Protocol information

  • Trial milestones

  • Study timelines

Site Management

  • Site selection

  • Site activation

  • Site performance

Investigator Management

  • Investigator profiles

  • Qualifications

  • Assignments

Patient Recruitment Tracking

  • Enrollment targets

  • Recruitment status

Monitoring Management

  • Monitoring visits

  • Visit reports

  • Follow-ups

Document Management

  • Trial documents

  • Approvals

  • Version control

Reporting & Analytics

  • Trial dashboards

  • Performance reports

OUT OF SCOPE (Initial Version)

❌ Clinical diagnosis

❌ Patient medical treatment decisions

❌ Laboratory data analysis

❌ Drug safety case processing

(These belong to other systems)

8. Key CTMS Stakeholders (High Level)

Stakeholder Role

Clinical Trial Sponsor Business Owner

Clinical Project Manager Trial Operations Owner

Clinical Research Associate (CRA) Site Monitoring

Investigator Clinical Site Lead

Study Coordinator Site Operations

Regulatory Affairs Team Compliance

Data Management Team Clinical Data

Quality Assurance Team Audit & Compliance

Patients Trial Participants

IT Team System Support

  • How are trials planned today?

  • Who approves milestones?

  • How are delays tracked?

Site Management

  • How are sites selected?

  • How is site performance measured?

Compliance

  • What documents require approval?

  • What audit records are required?

Reporting

  • Which KPIs does management need?

\"A CTMS is an enterprise platform used by pharmaceutical companies to manage clinical trial operations. It helps manage studies, research sites, investigators, recruitment tracking, monitoring activities, and compliance reporting. As a BA, I analyze clinical workflows, gather requirements from stakeholders, document processes, create user stories, and support Agile delivery.\"

Clinical trials involve many organizations:

  • Pharmaceutical sponsor

  • CRO (Contract Research Organization)

  • Hospitals

  • Investigators

  • Regulatory teams

  • Patients

A BA must understand:

\"Who makes decisions, who performs activities, and who needs information?\"

5. Clinical Trial AS-IS Process

Now we analyze the current manual workflow.

Pharma company starts a new clinical trial.

Lesson 3 -- TO-BE Process Design, Digital Clinical Trial Workflow & BPMN Automation

Transforming Manual Clinical Operations Into a Digital Platform

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ How a BA redesigns clinical trial processes\ ✅ Difference between AS-IS and TO-BE CTMS workflows\ ✅ How CTMS automates clinical operations\ ✅ How to identify functional requirements from processes\ ✅ How BPMN supports enterprise healthcare transformation

1. AS-IS vs TO-BE Thinking

A BA starts with:

\"How does the business work today?\"

Then designs:

\"How should the business work after the solution?\"

Current State (AS-IS)

Study Planning

↓

Excel Tracking

↓

Email Communication

↓

Manual Reports

↓

Delayed Decisions

Problems:

❌ No single source of truth

❌ Difficult trial monitoring

❌ Delayed risk identification

❌ High administrative workload

Future State (TO-BE)

Create Study in CTMS

↓

Manage Sites Digitally

↓

Track Recruitment Real-Time

↓

Schedule Monitoring Visits

↓

Automated Reports

↓

Risk-Based Decisions

2. TO-BE Clinical Trial Lifecycle Workflow

Lesson 4 -- BRD, Scope, Business Requirements & Clinical Trial KPIs

Converting Clinical Trial Problems Into Business Requirements

Learning Objective

After this lesson, you will understand:

✅ How to create a CTMS Business Requirement Document (BRD)\ ✅ How to define clinical trial business objectives\ ✅ How to define CTMS scope\ ✅ How to write business requirements\ ✅ How to identify clinical operations KPIs

1. Requirement Engineering in CTMS

A BA converts:

Clinical Trial Problem

↓

Business Objective

↓

↓

↓

User Story

2. CTMS Business Requirement Document (BRD)

Project Name:

Clinical Trial Management System (CTMS)

Industry:

Pharmaceutical Clinical Research

Project Vision:

Build a centralized clinical trial operations platform that enables pharmaceutical organizations to efficiently manage studies, sites, investigators, recruitment, monitoring activities, and compliance reporting.

3. Business Problem Statement

The pharmaceutical organization currently manages clinical trial operations through fragmented systems, spreadsheets, and manual communication.

This creates:

  • Limited trial visibility

  • Delayed enrollment tracking

  • Inefficient site management

  • Manual reporting effort

  • Compliance risks

  • Difficulty identifying operational issues early

4. Business Objectives

Objective 1

Improve Trial Visibility

Current Issue:

Management receives delayed trial updates.

Solution:

Real-time CTMS dashboards.

Expected Benefit:

Faster decision-making.

Objective 2

Improve Site Performance Management

Current Issue:

Site progress tracked manually.

Solution:

Centralized site performance monitoring.

Expected Benefit:

Identify delayed sites early.

Objective 3

Improve Patient Recruitment Monitoring

Current Issue:

Enrollment status updated late.

Solution:

Real-time recruitment tracking.

Expected Benefit:

Reduce trial delays.

Objective 4

Improve Regulatory Compliance

Current Issue:

Documents and approvals are difficult to track.

Solution:

Controlled document workflows.

Expected Benefit:

Inspection readiness.

Objective 5

Reduce Administrative Work

Current Issue:

Teams spend time preparing reports.

Solution:

Automated reporting.

Expected Benefit:

Higher operational efficiency.

5. CTMS Scope Definition

A BA defines:

\"What will be delivered?\"

IN SCOPE

Module 1: Study Management

Features:

✅ Study creation

✅ Protocol information

✅ Trial milestones

✅ Study status tracking

Module 2: Site Management

Features:

✅ Site profiles

✅ Site selection

✅ Site activation

✅ Site performance tracking

Module 3: Investigator Management

Features:

✅ Investigator profiles

✅ Qualification tracking

✅ Training status

Module 4: Patient Recruitment Tracking

Features:

✅ Enrollment targets

✅ Recruitment progress

✅ Recruitment reports

Module 5: Monitoring Management

Features:

✅ CRA visit scheduling

✅ Monitoring reports

✅ Action tracking

Module 6: Document Management

Features:

✅ Document upload

✅ Review workflow

✅ Version control

✅ Audit history

Module 7: Reporting & Analytics

Features:

✅ Trial dashboards

✅ Site reports

✅ Recruitment analytics

OUT OF SCOPE (Initial Release)

Not included:

❌ Clinical data analysis

❌ Patient diagnosis

❌ Drug safety case processing

❌ Statistical analysis

❌ Laboratory result management

6. CTMS Business Requirements

BR-CTMS-001

Centralized Study Management

Requirement:

The system shall provide a centralized platform to create, manage, and track clinical trial studies throughout their lifecycle.

Business Value:

Improve study visibility.

BR-CTMS-002

Site Performance Tracking

Requirement:

The system shall enable clinical teams to monitor research site activation, performance, and operational status.

Business Value:

Reduce site-related delays.

BR-CTMS-003

Recruitment Monitoring

Requirement:

The system shall provide real-time visibility into patient enrollment progress against study targets.

Business Value:

Improve recruitment management.

BR-CTMS-004

Monitoring Visit Management

Requirement:

The system shall allow CRAs to plan, execute, and track monitoring visits.

Business Value:

Improve trial oversight.

BR-CTMS-005

Compliance Documentation

Requirement:

The system shall maintain controlled clinical trial documents with version history and audit records.

Business Value:

Support regulatory compliance.

7. Clinical Trial KPIs

A BA defines success measurements.

KPI 1: Patient Enrollment Rate

Formula:

Patients Enrolled / Target Patients × 100

Example:

Target:

1000 patients

Actual:

800 patients

Enrollment Rate:

80%

Business Question:

\"Are we recruiting fast enough?\"

KPI 2: Site Activation Time

Formula:

Date Site Activated - Date Site Selected

Measures:

How quickly sites become operational.

KPI 3: Trial Timeline Adherence

Formula:

Completed Milestones / Planned Milestones × 100

Measures:

Study progress.

KPI 4: Monitoring Visit Completion Rate

Formula:

Completed Visits / Planned Visits × 100

KPI 5: Protocol Deviation Rate

Formula:

Protocol Deviations / Total Trial Activities

KPI 6: Document Approval Cycle Time

Measures:

Time taken from document submission to approval.

Stakeholder Goal CTMS Capability

Sponsor Trial visibility Dashboard

Clinical Manager Track milestones Study Management

Module 2 -- Agile Frameworks

Lesson 14: Introduction to Agile Frameworks

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What an Agile framework is.

  • Why Agile frameworks are needed.

  • The relationship between Agile values and frameworks.

  • The major Agile frameworks you will study.

  • How to choose an appropriate framework for a project.

  • How Agile frameworks apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What is an Agile framework?

An Agile framework is a structured approach that helps teams apply Agile values and principles in their day-to-day work.

While Agile provides the mindset and philosophy, frameworks provide the practical structure for implementing that mindset.

Simple definition: An Agile framework is a set of practices, roles, workflows, and guidelines that help teams deliver value iteratively and adapt to change.

Relationship between Agile and frameworks

Agile

Values and principles

↓

Agile frameworks

Scrum, Kanban, XP, Lean, SAFe, etc.

↓

Team practices

Sprints, boards, reviews, retrospectives, flow management

Agile is the philosophy; frameworks are the methods used to apply that philosophy.

Why Agile frameworks are needed

Agile values and principles provide direction, but teams also need practical guidance on:

  • How to organize work.

  • How to plan and prioritize tasks.

  • How to collaborate with stakeholders.

  • How to track progress.

  • How to improve continuously.

Example:

  • The Agile principle says: "Deliver working software frequently."

  • A framework such as Scrum explains how to do this through Sprints.

  • A framework such as Kanban explains how to do this through continuous flow.

Major Agile frameworks

Framework Primary focus

Scrum Structured iterative development with defined roles and events.

Kanban Visual workflow management and continuous flow.

Lean Eliminating waste and maximizing customer value.

Extreme Technical excellence and engineering practices. Programming

Crystal People-centric approach tailored to team size and project criticality.

DSDM Agile project delivery with business involvement and fixed time/cost.

SAFe Scaling Agile practices across large organizations.

LeSS Scaling Scrum across multiple teams.

Nexus Coordinating multiple Scrum teams working on one product.

Spotify model Autonomous squads and organizational alignment.

Simple analogy

Agile as the philosophy

Agile is like the philosophy of healthy living:

  • Stay active.

  • Eat nutritious food.

  • Adapt habits based on health needs.

  • Continuously improve your lifestyle.

Frameworks as specific methods

  • Scrum is like a structured workout program with scheduled sessions.

  • Kanban is like a daily activity tracker that helps you maintain a steady flow.

  • Lean is like removing unhealthy habits to improve efficiency.

  • XP is like focusing on high-quality training techniques.

All support the same goal, but each provides a different way to achieve it.

Overview of frameworks

Scrum

  • Uses fixed-length Sprints.

  • Defines roles such as Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers.

  • Includes events such as Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective.

  • Best for teams that need structure and regular feedback cycles.

Kanban

  • Visualizes work on a Kanban board.

  • Uses WIP limits to control work in progress.

  • Focuses on continuous flow rather than fixed iterations.

  • Best for support, maintenance, and continuous delivery work.

Lean

  • Focuses on eliminating waste.

  • Improves workflow efficiency.

  • Maximizes customer value.

  • Best for organizations seeking process optimization.

Extreme Programming (XP)

  • Emphasizes technical excellence.

  • Uses practices such as pair programming, test-driven development (TDD), and continuous integration.

  • Best for projects requiring high code quality and rapid feedback.

Scaled frameworks

  • SAFe helps large organizations coordinate many Agile teams.

  • LeSS applies Scrum principles to multiple teams.

  • Nexus focuses on integrating work from several Scrum teams.

  • Spotify model emphasizes autonomous squads and alignment.

How to choose an Agile framework

Project situation Suitable framework

Team needs structured iterations and roles. Scrum

Work arrives continuously and priorities change Kanban frequently.

Organization wants to reduce waste and improve Lean efficiency.

Project requires strong engineering practices and Extreme Programming code quality. (XP)

Multiple teams must coordinate on one product. SAFe, LeSS, or Nexus

Healthcare example

Hospital Management System

  • Scrum can be used to develop modules such as patient registration, appointment scheduling, and prescription management in Sprints.

  • Kanban can be used for ongoing support tickets and bug fixes.

  • Lean can help reduce delays in patient workflow processes.

Pharmacovigilance example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform:

  • Scrum would be useful for developing major features such as ICSR management, AI data extraction, MedDRA coding, and reporting.

  • Kanban would be useful for managing continuous regulatory updates, bug fixes, and AI model improvements.

  • Lean would help optimize the case processing workflow and reduce manual effort.

AI product example

For an AI Medical Chatbot:

  • Scrum can manage planned feature development.

  • Kanban can manage continuous model improvements and user feedback requests.

  • XP can ensure high-quality code and automated testing.

Common misconceptions

  • "Agile and Scrum are the same." Scrum is one Agile framework, but Agile includes many frameworks.

  • "One framework is best for all projects." The best framework depends on team size, project complexity, workflow type, and organizational context.

  • "Frameworks replace Agile mindset." Frameworks are tools; they are effective only when supported by Agile values and principles.

Best practices

  • Understand the Agile mindset before selecting a framework.

  • Choose a framework based on project needs, team structure, and workflow characteristics.

  • Start with Scrum if the team needs clear structure and iterative delivery.

  • Use Kanban for continuous flow and support work.

  • Combine frameworks when appropriate, such as Scrumban.

  • Continuously inspect and adapt the framework implementation.

Interview questions

Q1. What is an Agile framework?

Answer: An Agile framework is a structured approach that provides practices, roles, workflows, and guidelines for applying Agile values and principles in product development and project management.

Q2. What is the difference between Agile and an Agile framework?

Answer: Agile is a mindset and set of values and principles, while an Agile framework is a practical method for implementing those values and principles.

Q3. Name some common Agile frameworks.

Answer: Common Agile frameworks include Scrum, Kanban, Lean, Extreme Programming (XP), Crystal, DSDM, SAFe, LeSS, Nexus, and the Spotify model.

Mini quiz

Try answering these without looking back:

  • What is the difference between Agile and an Agile framework?

  • Name four common Agile frameworks.

  • Which framework uses fixed-length Sprints?

  • Which framework focuses on visualizing workflow and limiting WIP?

  • Which framework emphasizes eliminating waste?

Practical assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

  • Identify which Agile framework would be most suitable for the main product development work.

  • Identify which framework would be most suitable for ongoing support and regulatory updates.

  • Explain why each framework is appropriate for those activities.

  • Describe how Scrum, Kanban, and Lean could be combined in this project.

Summary

Agile frameworks provide the practical structure needed to apply Agile values and principles in real projects. Different frameworks are suitable for different situations:

  • Scrum provides structured iterative development.

  • Kanban manages continuous workflow.

  • Lean improves efficiency by reducing waste.

  • XP enhances technical quality.

  • SAFe, LeSS, and Nexus help scale Agile across multiple teams.

For healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development, the choice of framework should depend on the nature of the work, team structure, regulatory requirements, and need for continuous feedback.

Key takeaways

  • Agile is the mindset; frameworks are the practical implementation methods.

  • Scrum is best for structured iterative development.

  • Kanban is best for continuous flow work.

  • Lean is best for process optimization and waste reduction.

  • XP is best for improving technical excellence.

  • Framework selection should be based on project context, team needs, and workflow characteristics.

Lesson 15: Scrum Framework -- Purpose, History, and When to Use It

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Scrum is.

  • The purpose of Scrum.

  • The history and origin of Scrum.

  • The key ideas behind Scrum.

  • When Scrum should be used.

  • When Scrum may not be the best choice.

  • How Scrum applies to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What is Scrum?

Scrum is an Agile framework used to develop, deliver, and sustain complex products through iterative and incremental work.

Instead of building the entire product at once, Scrum teams work in short cycles called Sprints, usually lasting 1 to 4 weeks.

Simple definition: Scrum is a lightweight Agile framework that helps teams deliver valuable product increments through collaboration, transparency, inspection, and adaptation.

Purpose of Scrum

Scrum was designed to help teams:

  • Deliver value quickly through small, usable increments.

  • Adapt to changing requirements without disrupting the entire project.

  • Improve collaboration between business and technical teams.

  • Increase transparency so everyone understands the work and progress.

  • Continuously improve the product and the team's process.

  • Reduce risk by getting feedback early and often.

Example

Imagine building an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

  • Traditional approach: Build all modules for 12 months, then release the full platform.

  • Scrum approach: Build Login and Dashboard in Sprint 1, get feedback, then continue with ICSR Management, AI Data Extraction, and MedDRA Coding in later Sprints.

The Scrum approach reduces the risk of building features that users may not need or use.

History of Scrum

Origin of the term

The term "Scrum" comes from the sport of rugby, where players work together closely to move the ball toward a goal.

In rugby, a scrum is a formation where team members collaborate tightly, adjust to changing conditions, and work as a unit.

Early inspiration

In 1986, Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka published an article in Harvard Business Review titled "The New New Product Development Game".

They observed that successful product development teams:

  • Worked collaboratively.

  • Moved quickly.

  • Adapted to changing conditions.

  • Developed products in overlapping phases rather than strict sequential stages.

This article inspired the Scrum framework.

Formal development of Scrum

Scrum was formally developed in the early 1990s by:

  • Jeff Sutherland.

  • Ken Schwaber.

They presented Scrum publicly in 1995 and later became co-authors of the Scrum Guide, which defines the official Scrum framework.

Scrum timeline

1986

Takeuchi and Nonaka describe the "Scrum" concept in product development.

1993

Jeff Sutherland begins applying Scrum ideas in software development.

1995

Sutherland and Schwaber present Scrum publicly.

2001

Agile Manifesto is published, and Scrum becomes one of the most popular Agile frameworks.

2010+

Scrum becomes widely adopted across software, healthcare, finance, and product development industries.

Key ideas behind Scrum

Empirical process control

Scrum is based on empirical process control, which means decisions are made based on observation, experience, and experimentation rather than assumptions.

Scrum relies on three pillars:

Pillar Meaning

Transparency Everyone can see the work, progress, and challenges.

Inspection The team regularly reviews the product and process.

Adaptation The team adjusts plans and practices based on feedback and findings.

Iterative and incremental development

  • Iterative means the team repeats cycles of planning, building, testing, and reviewing.

  • Incremental means each Sprint produces a usable addition to the product.

Sprint 1

Login and Dashboard

↓

Sprint 2

ICSR Management

↓

Sprint 3

AI Data Extraction

↓

Sprint 4

MedDRA Coding

Scrum values

Scrum is guided by five core values:

Value Meaning

Commitment The team commits to achieving the Sprint Goal.

Focus The team concentrates on the work selected for the Sprint.

Openness The team is transparent about progress and challenges.

Respect Team members value each other's contributions.

Courage The team is willing to face difficult problems and make improvements.

When Scrum should be used

Scrum is most suitable when:

  • The project is complex and evolving.

  • Requirements are likely to change.

  • Customer or stakeholder feedback is important.

  • The product can be delivered in small increments.

  • The team can work collaboratively in short iterations.

  • Continuous improvement is desired.

Examples of suitable projects

  • Software development projects.

  • AI and machine learning products.

  • Healthcare software systems.

  • Pharmacovigilance platforms.

  • Mobile and web applications.

  • Product innovation initiatives.

When Scrum may not be the best choice

Scrum may be less suitable when:

  • Requirements are fully fixed and unlikely to change.

  • The project involves physical construction or manufacturing.

  • Work is primarily continuous support or maintenance with unpredictable incoming tasks.

  • The organization cannot support cross-functional collaboration.

  • Stakeholders are not available for regular feedback.

In such cases, Waterfall, Kanban, or a hybrid approach may be more appropriate.

Healthcare example

Hospital Management System

  • Why Scrum works:

    • Doctors and nurses can test modules early.

    • Workflows can be refined based on feedback.

    • Features such as patient registration and appointment scheduling can be delivered incrementally.

  • Scrum approach:

    • Sprint 1: Patient registration module.

    • Sprint 2: Appointment scheduling module.

    • Sprint 3: Prescription management module.

    • Sprint Review: Healthcare staff provide feedback after each Sprint.

Pharmacovigilance example

AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform

Scrum is highly suitable for this project because:

  • Regulatory requirements may evolve.

  • AI extraction models need continuous improvement.

  • Pharmacovigilance professionals can provide regular feedback.

  • Features can be prioritized based on business value.

Sprint 2 ICSR Management module.

Sprint 3 AI Data Extraction feature.

Sprint 4 MedDRA Coding module.

AI product example

AI Medical Chatbot

  • Why Scrum works:

    • User feedback can improve chatbot responses.

    • AI models can be refined iteratively.

    • New features can be added incrementally.

  • Scrum approach:

    • Sprint 1: Basic chatbot interface.

    • Sprint 2: Symptom-checking feature.

    • Sprint 3: Appointment scheduling integration.

    • Sprint 4: AI response improvement based on user feedback.

Advantages of Scrum

  • Faster delivery of value through frequent increments.

  • Better adaptability to changing requirements.

  • Improved collaboration between business and technical teams.

  • Higher transparency through regular events and visible backlog.

  • Continuous improvement through retrospectives.

  • Reduced project risk through early feedback and inspection.

Limitations of Scrum

  • Requires active stakeholder involvement.

  • Requires cross-functional teams.

  • May feel too structured for some continuous-flow environments.

  • Can be difficult in organizations with rigid hierarchical structures.

  • Requires discipline in following Scrum roles and events.

Common misconceptions

  • "Scrum is the same as Agile." Scrum is one Agile framework, not Agile itself.

  • "Scrum guarantees success." Scrum improves transparency and adaptability, but success depends on team collaboration and proper implementation.

  • "Scrum means no planning." Scrum involves continuous planning through backlog refinement and Sprint Planning.

Best practices

  • Keep the Product Backlog prioritized and transparent.

  • Define a clear Sprint Goal for each Sprint.

  • Ensure the team is cross-functional.

  • Conduct regular Sprint Reviews with stakeholders.

  • Use Sprint Retrospectives to improve the team's process.

  • Deliver a usable product increment at the end of each Sprint.

Interview questions

Q1. What is Scrum?

Answer: Scrum is a lightweight Agile framework that helps teams develop, deliver, and sustain complex products through iterative and incremental work in fixed-length Sprints.

Q2. Who created Scrum?

Answer: Scrum was formally developed by Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber in the early 1990s.

Q3. What is the purpose of Scrum?

Answer: The purpose of Scrum is to help teams deliver valuable product increments quickly, adapt to changing requirements, improve collaboration, and continuously improve their process.

Q4. When should Scrum be used?

Answer: Scrum should be used for complex projects with evolving requirements, where incremental delivery, stakeholder feedback, and cross-functional collaboration are important.

Summary

Scrum is a lightweight Agile framework designed to help teams develop complex products through iterative and incremental delivery. It originated from the idea of close teamwork and adaptability, inspired by rugby and formalized by Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber.

Scrum is most effective when:

Lesson 16: Scrum Roles -- Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, and Stakeholders

Learning objectives

  • The responsibilities of the Developers.

  • The role of Stakeholders.

  • How these roles collaborate in real projects.

  • How Scrum roles apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

Overview of Scrum roles

The Scrum Team is a small, self-managing, and cross-functional team responsible for delivering a valuable product increment each Sprint.

According to the Scrum Guide, the Scrum Team consists of:

  • Product Owner -- Maximizes product value.

  • Scrum Master -- Facilitates Scrum and helps the team improve.

  • Developers -- Build the product increment.

Product Owner

Purpose

The Product Owner (PO) is responsible for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.

Key responsibilities

  • Define and communicate the Product Goal.

  • Create and manage the Product Backlog.

  • Prioritize backlog items based on business value.

  • Ensure backlog items are clear and understood.

  • Collaborate with stakeholders to gather requirements and feedback.

  • Make decisions about what should be built next.

Simple analogy

The Product Owner is like a restaurant owner who decides:

  • What dishes should be on the menu.

  • Which dishes are most important to prepare first.

  • What customers value most.

Healthcare example

In a Hospital Management System, the Product Owner may prioritize:

  • Patient registration.

  • Appointment scheduling.

  • Prescription management.

  • Billing integration.

Pharmacovigilance example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, the Product Owner may prioritize:

  • ICSR Management.

  • AI Data Extraction.

  • MedDRA Coding.

  • Duplicate Detection.

  • Signal Detection.

Common mistakes

  • Not prioritizing the backlog clearly.

  • Acting as a project manager instead of a value maximizer.

  • Ignoring stakeholder feedback.

  • Writing unclear backlog items.

Scrum Master

Purpose

The Scrum Master is responsible for establishing Scrum and helping everyone understand and apply Scrum theory and practice.

Key responsibilities

  • Facilitate Scrum events such as Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective.

  • Remove impediments that block the team's progress.

  • Coach the Scrum Team in Agile and Scrum practices.

  • Help the team become self-managing and cross-functional.

  • Promote continuous improvement.

  • Support collaboration between the Scrum Team and stakeholders.

Simple analogy

The Scrum Master is like a sports coach who:

  • Ensures the team follows the rules.

  • Removes obstacles affecting performance.

  • Helps team members improve their skills.

  • Encourages collaboration and discipline.

Healthcare example

In a Hospital Management System project, the Scrum Master may:

  • Facilitate discussions between developers and hospital staff.

  • Resolve blockers related to system integration.

  • Ensure Sprint ceremonies are effective.

Pharmacovigilance example

For the AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, the Scrum Master may:

  • Remove blockers related to AI model training.

  • Coordinate with regulatory experts.

  • Help the team improve Sprint delivery.

Common mistakes

  • Acting as a manager who assigns tasks.

  • Ignoring impediments.

  • Focusing only on meetings instead of team improvement.

  • Not coaching the team in Scrum values and practices.

Developers

Purpose

Developers are the members of the Scrum Team who are responsible for creating the product increment each Sprint.

Key responsibilities

  • Plan the work needed to achieve the Sprint Goal.

  • Build, test, and integrate product features.

  • Maintain the quality of the product increment.

  • Collaborate with each other and with the Product Owner.

  • Manage their own work and commitments.

  • Inspect progress daily and adapt the Sprint plan as needed.

Simple analogy

Developers are like the chefs in a restaurant who prepare the dishes selected by the restaurant owner.

Healthcare example

In a Hospital Management System, Developers may include:

  • Frontend developers.

  • Backend developers.

  • Database engineers.

  • QA testers.

  • Integration specialists.

Pharmacovigilance example

For the AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, Developers may include:

  • Software developers.

  • AI/ML engineers.

  • Data engineers.

  • QA testers.

  • Pharmacovigilance domain experts contributing to validation.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting for the Scrum Master to assign tasks.

  • Working in silos without collaboration.

  • Ignoring quality practices.

  • Not communicating progress or blockers.

Stakeholders

Purpose

Stakeholders are individuals or groups who have an interest in the product and can influence or be affected by its outcome.

Stakeholders are not part of the Scrum Team, but they play an important role by providing feedback, requirements, and business context.

Examples of stakeholders

  • Customers.

  • End users.

  • Business managers.

  • Regulatory authorities.

  • Healthcare professionals.

  • Investors or sponsors.

Role in Scrum

  • Support product vision and adoption.

Lesson 17: Scrum Artifacts -- Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Scrum artifacts are.

  • The purpose of the Product Backlog.

  • The purpose of the Sprint Backlog.

  • The purpose of the Increment.

  • How these artifacts relate to each other.

  • How Scrum artifacts apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What are Scrum artifacts?

Scrum artifacts are key information sources that represent work or value in a Scrum project. They provide transparency, so everyone can see:

  • What work is needed.

  • What work has been selected for the current Sprint.

  • What value has been delivered.

Simple definition: Scrum artifacts are tools that make work visible, track progress, and support inspection and adaptation.

The three Scrum artifacts

Artifact Purpose

Product Backlog Represents all desired work for the product.

Sprint Backlog Represents the work selected for the current Sprint.

Increment Represents the usable product delivered during the Sprint.

Relationship between the artifacts

Product Backlog

All desired work

↓

Sprint Backlog

Selected work for the Sprint

↓

Increment

Usable product delivered

Product Backlog

Purpose

The Product Backlog is an ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product. It is the single source of requirements for the Scrum Team.

Key characteristics

  • Ordered by priority and business value.

  • Dynamic and continuously updated.

  • Owned by the Product Owner.

  • Contains features, enhancements, bug fixes, technical work, and research items.

  • Refined regularly through Backlog Refinement.

Example Product Backlog

Priority Backlog item

1 Login and authentication

2 Dashboard

3 ICSR Management

4 AI Data Extraction

5 MedDRA Coding

Healthcare example

For a Hospital Management System, the Product Backlog may include:

  • Patient registration.

  • Appointment scheduling.

  • Prescription management.

  • Billing integration.

  • Laboratory report access.

Pharmacovigilance example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, the Product Backlog may include:

  • ICSR Management.

  • AI Data Extraction.

  • Duplicate Detection.

  • Signal Detection.

  • Compliance Dashboard.

Sprint Backlog

Purpose

The Sprint Backlog is the set of Product Backlog items selected for the current Sprint, along with a plan for delivering them.

Key characteristics

  • Created during Sprint Planning.

  • Owned and managed by the Developers.

  • Includes the Sprint Goal.

  • Includes selected Product Backlog items.

  • Includes tasks and plans for completing the work.

  • Can be updated during the Sprint as the team learns more.

Example Sprint Backlog

Sprint Goal Deliver a functional login and dashboard module.

Selected item Tasks

Login feature Design UI, develop API, test authentication.

Dashboard Create widgets, integrate data, test display.

Healthcare example

In a Sprint for a Hospital Management System, the Sprint Backlog may include:

  • Patient registration screen.

  • Patient database integration.

  • Validation rules for patient data.

  • Testing of registration workflow.

Pharmacovigilance example

For the AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, a Sprint Backlog may include:

  • Develop AI extraction API.

  • Integrate case upload functionality.

  • Create extraction results dashboard.

  • Test extraction accuracy.

Increment

Purpose

The Increment is the usable product result produced during a Sprint. It is the sum of all completed Product Backlog items during the Sprint, plus the value of previous increments.

Key characteristics

  • Usable and potentially releasable.

  • Meets the Definition of Done.

  • Provides value to users or stakeholders.

  • Builds upon previous increments.

  • Inspected during the Sprint Review.

Example Increment

Sprint Increment delivered

Sprint 1 Login and Dashboard module.

Sprint 2 ICSR Management module.

Sprint 3 AI Data Extraction feature.

Healthcare example

A usable patient registration module at the end of a Sprint is an Increment because hospital staff can use it for real patient registration.

Pharmacovigilance example

A functional AI data extraction feature that can process uploaded case reports is an Increment because it provides real value to pharmacovigilance professionals.

Definition of Done

An Increment is considered complete only when it meets the Definition of Done (DoD).

The DoD is a shared understanding of what "completed" means.

Example Definition of Done

  • Code is developed.

  • Code is reviewed.

  • Unit tests are passed.

  • Integration tests are passed.

  • Documentation is updated.

  • Feature is accepted by the Product Owner.

Comparison of Scrum artifacts

Artifact Owner Purpose

Product Product Represents all desired work for the product. Backlog Owner

Sprint Backlog Developers Represents the work selected for the current Sprint.

Increment Scrum Team Represents the usable product delivered during the Sprint.

Common mistakes

  • Product Backlog: Treating it as a fixed requirements document.

  • Sprint Backlog: Changing Sprint scope without proper discussion.

  • Increment: Delivering work that is not usable or not tested.

  • Definition of Done: Having different interpretations of what "done" means.

Best practices

  • Keep the Product Backlog prioritized and transparent.

  • Ensure Sprint Backlog items are small enough to complete within a Sprint.

  • Define a clear Sprint Goal.

  • Maintain a shared Definition of Done.

  • Deliver usable increments at the end of every Sprint.

  • Use Sprint Reviews to gather feedback on the Increment.

Interview questions

Q1. What is the Product Backlog?

Answer: The Product Backlog is an ordered list of all desired work for the product. It is managed by the Product Owner and continuously refined.

Q2. What is the Sprint Backlog?

Answer: The Sprint Backlog is the set of Product Backlog items selected for the current Sprint, along with the plan for delivering them. It is managed by the Developers.

Q3. What is an Increment?

Answer: An Increment is the usable product result produced during a Sprint. It must meet the Definition of Done and provide value to users or stakeholders.

Q4. What is the difference between Product Backlog and Sprint Backlog?

Answer: The Product Backlog contains all desired work for the product, while the Sprint Backlog contains only the work selected for the current Sprint.

Scrum artifacts provide transparency and help the Scrum Team manage work effectively:

  • Product Backlog = all desired work for the product.

  • Sprint Backlog = selected work for the current Sprint.

Together, these artifacts support inspection, adaptation, and continuous delivery of value, which are essential principles of Scrum.

  • Product Backlog is owned by the Product Owner and contains all desired work.

  • Sprint Backlog is managed by the Developers and contains work selected for the current Sprint.

Lesson 18: Scrum Events -- Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Scrum events are.

  • The purpose of the Sprint.

  • The purpose and process of Sprint Planning.

  • The purpose and format of the Daily Scrum.

  • The purpose of the Sprint Review.

  • The purpose of the Sprint Retrospective.

  • How these events work together in a Scrum cycle.

  • How Scrum events apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What are Scrum events?

Scrum events are time-boxed activities that create regular opportunities for the Scrum Team to inspect work, adapt plans, collaborate with stakeholders, and improve their process.

The main Scrum events are:

  • Sprint -- The container for all other events.

  • Sprint Planning -- Plan the work for the Sprint.

  • Daily Scrum -- Inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.

  • Sprint Review -- Inspect the Increment and gather stakeholder feedback.

  • Sprint Retrospective -- Inspect the process and identify improvements.

Scrum event cycle

Sprint Planning

↓

Sprint

Daily Scrum occurs every day during the Sprint

↓

Sprint Review

↓

Sprint Retrospective

↓

Next Sprint Planning

Sprint

Purpose

The Sprint is a fixed-length iteration during which the Scrum Team works to deliver a usable product Increment.

Key characteristics

  • Usually lasts 1 to 4 weeks.

  • Has a clear Sprint Goal.

  • Contains all other Scrum events.

  • Produces a potentially releasable Increment.

  • Maintains a consistent duration throughout the project.

Example

A 2-week Sprint for an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform might focus on:

  • Sprint Goal: Deliver a functional AI data extraction module.

  • Selected work: API development, UI integration, testing, and validation.

  • Increment: A usable AI extraction feature.

Sprint Planning

Purpose

Sprint Planning is the event where the Scrum Team decides:

  • What work will be done in the Sprint.

  • How the work will be accomplished.

  • What the Sprint Goal will be.

Key outputs

  • Sprint Goal.

  • Selected Product Backlog items.

  • Sprint Backlog.

  • Plan for delivering the selected work.

Participants

  • Product Owner -- Clarifies backlog items and priorities.

  • Developers -- Estimate capacity and plan the work.

  • Scrum Master -- Facilitates the event.

Typical questions

  • Why is this Sprint valuable? (Sprint Goal)

  • What can be completed this Sprint? (Selected backlog items)

  • How will the work get done? (Tasks and plan)

Healthcare example

For a Hospital Management System:

  • Sprint Goal: Enable patients to book appointments online.

  • Selected items: Appointment form, doctor availability check, confirmation notification.

  • Plan: Design UI, build backend API, integrate database, test workflow.

Daily Scrum

Purpose

The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute daily meeting for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan for the next 24 hours.

Key characteristics

  • Occurs every day during the Sprint.

  • Time-boxed to 15 minutes.

  • Focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal.

  • Led by the Developers.

  • Helps identify blockers early.

Common discussion points

  • What progress has been made toward the Sprint Goal?

  • What work is planned before the next Daily Scrum?

  • Are there any impediments blocking progress?

Pharmacovigilance example

In the AI Pharmacovigilance Platform project:

  • A developer reports progress on AI extraction API integration.

  • A QA tester reports that validation testing is in progress.

  • An impediment is identified: access to a required dataset is delayed.

  • The team adjusts the plan and requests support from the Scrum Master.

Sprint Review

Purpose

The Sprint Review is held at the end of the Sprint to:

  • Inspect the Increment.

  • Demonstrate completed work to stakeholders.

  • Gather feedback.

  • Discuss progress toward the Product Goal.

  • Update the Product Backlog if needed.

Participants

  • Scrum Team.

  • Stakeholders.

  • Product Owner presents progress and discusses future priorities.

Outputs

  • Feedback on the Increment.

  • Updated Product Backlog.

  • Refined priorities and future work.

Healthcare example

For a Hospital Management System:

  • The team demonstrates the online appointment booking feature.

  • Doctors and hospital administrators provide feedback on usability.

  • Stakeholders request an additional appointment reminder feature.

  • The Product Owner adds and prioritizes the new request in the Product Backlog.

Sprint Retrospective

Purpose

The Sprint Retrospective is held after the Sprint Review and before the next Sprint Planning. It focuses on improving the team's process.

Key discussion areas

  • What went well?

  • What did not go well?

  • What can be improved?

  • What actions will the team take in the next Sprint?

Participants

  • Product Owner.

  • Scrum Master.

  • Developers.

Outputs

  • Identified process improvements.

  • Action items for the next Sprint.

  • Improved collaboration and efficiency.

AI product example

For an AI Medical Chatbot project:

  • What went well: AI model integration was completed successfully.

  • What did not go well: Testing took longer than expected.

  • Improvement: Add automated test cases earlier in the Sprint.

  • Action item: Include QA planning in Sprint Planning.

Comparison of Scrum events

Event Purpose Typical time-box

Sprint Deliver a usable Increment. 1--4 weeks.

Sprint Planning Plan the Sprint work. Up to 8 hours for a 1-month Sprint.

Daily Scrum Inspect progress toward the 15 minutes. Sprint Goal.

Sprint Review Inspect the Increment and Up to 4 hours for a gather feedback. 1-month Sprint.

Sprint Improve the team's process. Up to 3 hours for a Retrospective 1-month Sprint.

How Scrum events support Agile principles

Agile principle Scrum event support

Deliver value frequently. Sprint and Increment.

Respond to change. Sprint Review and Product Backlog updates.

Collaborate daily. Daily Scrum.

Continuous improvement. Sprint Retrospective.

Customer feedback. Sprint Review.

Common mistakes

  • Sprint Planning: Selecting too much work for the Sprint.

  • Daily Scrum: Turning it into a status meeting for the Scrum Master.

  • Sprint Review: Treating it as a formal approval meeting instead of a collaborative feedback session.

  • Sprint Retrospective: Discussing problems without creating actionable improvements.

  • Sprint: Changing the Sprint Goal frequently.

Best practices

  • Define a clear Sprint Goal.

  • Keep Scrum events time-boxed and focused.

  • Encourage active participation from all team members.

  • Use Sprint Reviews to gather real stakeholder feedback.

  • Use Sprint Retrospectives to implement continuous improvements.

  • Maintain transparency through the Sprint Backlog and progress tracking.

Interview questions

Q1. What is the purpose of a Sprint?

Answer: A Sprint is a fixed-length iteration during which the Scrum Team works to deliver a usable product Increment that supports the Sprint Goal.

Q2. What happens during Sprint Planning?

Answer: During Sprint Planning, the Scrum Team decides what work will be done in the Sprint, how it will be accomplished, and what the Sprint Goal will be.

Q3. What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?

Answer: The Daily Scrum helps Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal, identify impediments, and adapt the plan for the next 24 hours.

Q4. What is the difference between Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective?

Answer: The Sprint Review focuses on inspecting the product Increment and gathering stakeholder feedback, while the Sprint Retrospective focuses on improving the team's process and collaboration.
