Lesson 19: Scrum Metrics -- Velocity, Burndown Chart, Burnup Chart, Story Points, and Planning Poker

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Scrum metrics are and why they are important.

  • What Story Points are and how they are used.

  • How Planning Poker works.

  • What Velocity means and how to calculate it.

  • How to read a Burndown Chart.

  • How to read a Burnup Chart.

  • How these metrics apply to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What are Scrum metrics?

Scrum metrics are measurements that help the Scrum Team understand progress, forecast future work, and improve their process.

Simple definition: Scrum metrics provide visibility into how much work has been completed, how much work remains, and how effectively the team is delivering value.

Why metrics are important

  • Help the team estimate and plan work.

  • Provide transparency to stakeholders.

  • Identify risks and bottlenecks early.

  • Support continuous improvement.

  • Help forecast future delivery dates.

Story Points

Purpose

Story Points are a relative measure of effort used to estimate Product Backlog items.

What Story Points consider

  • Complexity -- How difficult is the work?

  • Effort -- How much work is required?

  • Risk -- How uncertain or risky is the task?

Common Story Point scale

Story Points Meaning

1 Very small, simple task.

2 Small task.

3 Moderate task.

5 Complex task.

8 Very complex task.

13 Large task with high uncertainty.

Example

Backlog item Story Points

Login feature 3

Dashboard 5

ICSR Management 8

AI Data Extraction 13

MedDRA Coding 8

Healthcare example

For a Hospital Management System:

  • Patient registration screen = 3 points.

  • Appointment scheduling = 5 points.

  • Prescription management = 8 points.

Pharmacovigilance example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

  • ICSR Management = 8 points.

  • AI Data Extraction = 13 points.

  • Duplicate Detection = 8 points.

Planning Poker

Purpose

Planning Poker is a collaborative estimation technique used by Scrum Teams to assign Story Points to backlog items.

How it works

  • The Product Owner explains a backlog item.

  • Team members discuss the requirements.

  • Each member privately selects a Story Point estimate.

  • All estimates are revealed simultaneously.

  • If estimates differ, the team discusses the reasons.

  • The team repeats the process until a consensus is reached.

Benefits

  • Encourages team collaboration.

  • Reduces the influence of dominant personalities.

  • Surfaces hidden assumptions and risks.

  • Improves estimation accuracy.

AI product example

For an AI Medical Chatbot:

  • A developer estimates symptom-checking integration as 8 points.

  • A QA tester estimates it as 13 points due to testing complexity.

  • After discussion, the team agrees on 13 points.

Velocity

Purpose

Velocity measures the amount of work completed by the Scrum Team in a Sprint, usually measured in Story Points.

Formula

Velocity = Total Story Points completed in a Sprint

Example calculation

Sprint Story Points completed

Sprint 1 20

Sprint 2 25

Sprint 3 22

Sprint 4 23

Average velocity 22.5

How velocity is used

  • Sprint Planning -- Helps determine how much work the team can realistically commit to.

  • Release Planning -- Helps forecast how many Sprints are needed to complete remaining work.

  • Team improvement -- Helps the team understand delivery patterns over time.

Important note

Velocity should not be used to compare teams because Story Point estimation is relative and specific to each team.

Burndown Chart

Purpose

A Burndown Chart shows the remaining work in a Sprint over time.

How to read it

  • X-axis = Sprint days.

  • Y-axis = Remaining Story Points or tasks.

  • Ideal line = Planned rate of work completion.

  • Actual line = Real progress of the team.

Example Burndown Chart

Remaining work (Story Points)

40 ┤●

30 ┤ ●

20 ┤ ●

10 ┤ ●

0 ┤____●

Day 1 3 5 7 10

Interpretation: The line moving downward indicates that the team is completing work and reducing the remaining Sprint workload.

Interpretation

  • If the actual line is above the ideal line, the team may be behind schedule.

  • If the actual line is below the ideal line, the team may be ahead of schedule.

  • If the line is flat, little or no work is being completed.

Pharmacovigilance example

For the AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, a Burndown Chart can show:

  • Remaining Story Points for AI extraction tasks.

  • Progress of MedDRA coding feature development.

  • Whether the team is on track to meet the Sprint Goal.

Burnup Chart

Purpose

A Burnup Chart shows the work completed over time and compares it with the total scope.

How to read it

  • X-axis = Time or Sprint days.

  • Y-axis = Story Points.

  • Total scope line = Total work planned.

  • Completed work line = Work completed so far.

Example Burnup Chart

Story Points

40 ┤──────────── Total scope

30 ┤ ●

20 ┤ ●

10 ┤ ●

0 ┤____

Day 1 3 5 7 10

Interpretation: The upward line shows cumulative work completed. If the total scope line changes, it indicates scope changes during the project.

Burndown vs Burnup

Aspect Burndown Chart Burnup Chart

Shows Remaining work. Completed work and total scope.

Direction Line moves downward. Line moves upward.

Scope Less visible. More visible. changes

Best for Tracking Sprint Tracking project progress and scope progress. changes.

Healthcare example

For a Hospital Management System:

  • Story Points estimate features such as patient registration and billing.

  • Velocity helps forecast future module delivery.

  • Burndown Chart tracks progress during a Sprint.

  • Burnup Chart shows completed modules versus the total project scope.

AI product example

For an AI Medical Chatbot:

  • Story Points estimate AI model integration tasks.

  • Planning Poker helps the team agree on estimation.

  • Velocity helps forecast when chatbot features may be completed.

  • Burnup Chart helps track scope changes as new AI capabilities are added.

Common mistakes

  • Story Points: Treating them as exact hours.

  • Velocity: Using it as a performance target instead of a planning tool.

  • Burndown Chart: Ignoring the reasons behind deviations from the ideal line.

  • Planning Poker: Allowing one person to dominate the estimation discussion.

  • Metrics: Focusing on numbers instead of delivering customer value.

Best practices

  • Use Story Points for relative estimation, not time tracking.

  • Use Planning Poker to encourage collaborative estimation.

  • Use Velocity for Sprint and release forecasting.

  • Review Burndown Charts regularly during the Sprint.

  • Use Burnup Charts when scope changes are common.

  • Interpret metrics in context and focus on continuous improvement.

Interview questions

Q1. What are Story Points?

Answer: Story Points are a relative measure of effort used to estimate Product Backlog items based on complexity, effort, and risk.

Q2. What is Planning Poker?

Answer: Planning Poker is a collaborative estimation technique in which team members independently estimate backlog items using Story Points and discuss differences until consensus is reached.

Q3. What is Velocity?

Answer: Velocity is the amount of work completed by a Scrum Team in a Sprint, usually measured in Story Points.

Q4. What is the difference between Burndown and Burnup Charts?

Answer: A Burndown Chart shows remaining work decreasing over time, while a Burnup Chart shows completed work increasing over time and compares it with the total scope.

Mini quiz

Try answering these without looking back:

  • What do Story Points measure?

  • What is the purpose of Planning Poker?

  • How is Velocity calculated?

  • What does a Burndown Chart show?

  • What advantage does a Burnup Chart have over a Burndown Chart?

Practical assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

  • Assign Story Points to five backlog items.

  • Simulate a Planning Poker discussion for one complex feature.

  • Calculate Velocity for four hypothetical Sprints.

  • Draw a simple Burndown Chart for a 2-week Sprint.

  • Explain how a Burnup Chart would help if the project scope changes frequently.

Summary

Scrum metrics help teams estimate work, track progress, and improve delivery:

  • Story Points measure relative effort.

  • Planning Poker supports collaborative estimation.

  • Velocity measures completed work per Sprint.

  • Burndown Chart shows remaining work decreasing over time.

  • Burnup Chart shows completed work increasing over time and highlights scope changes.

These metrics provide transparency and forecasting ability, helping Scrum Teams deliver value more predictably.

Key takeaways

  • Story Points estimate relative effort, not exact time.

  • Planning Poker improves estimation through team discussion.

  • Velocity helps forecast future Sprint capacity.

  • Burndown Chart tracks remaining work during a Sprint.

  • Burnup Chart tracks completed work and total scope.

  • Metrics should be used for planning and improvement, not for comparing teams or judging individual performance.

Lesson 20: Kanban Framework -- Purpose, Principles, and Workflow Management

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Kanban is.

  • The purpose of Kanban.

  • The core principles of Kanban.

  • How a Kanban board works.

  • What Work In Progress (WIP) limits are.

  • How Kanban improves workflow efficiency.

  • When Kanban should be used.

  • How Kanban applies to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI product development.

What is Kanban?

Kanban is a workflow management method used to visualize work, limit work in progress, and improve the flow of tasks through a process.

The word "Kanban" comes from Japanese and means "visual signal" or "signboard".

Simple definition: Kanban is an Agile method that helps teams manage and improve their workflow by making work visible and limiting the amount of work being done at the same time.

Purpose of Kanban

Kanban was created to help teams:

  • Visualize the workflow.

  • Identify bottlenecks.

  • Reduce multitasking.

  • Improve flow efficiency.

  • Deliver work continuously.

  • Adapt to changing priorities.

Simple analogy

Imagine a pharmacy dispensing counter:

  • Prescriptions arrive continuously.

  • Each prescription moves through stages: Received → Verification → Dispensing → Completed.

  • If too many prescriptions are in Verification, it becomes a bottleneck.

  • Limiting the number of prescriptions in verification helps maintain smooth flow.

This is similar to how Kanban manages work in software and product development.

History of Kanban

Kanban originated in the Toyota Production System in the 1940s and 1950s.

  • Toyota used visual cards to signal when more materials were needed.

  • This helped reduce waste and improve production flow.

  • Later, Kanban principles were adapted for knowledge work and software development by David J. Anderson.

Core principles of Kanban

1. Visualize the workflow

Make all work visible so the team can understand:

  • What work is waiting.

  • What work is in progress.

  • What work is completed.

2. Limit Work In Progress (WIP)

WIP limits restrict the number of tasks allowed in a workflow stage at one time.

  • Prevents overloading the team.

  • Reduces context switching.

  • Highlights bottlenecks quickly.

3. Manage flow

Focus on moving work smoothly from start to completion.

  • Reduce delays.

  • Remove blockers.

  • Improve cycle time.

4. Make policies explicit

Clearly define:

  • How work enters the system.

  • What each workflow stage means.

  • When work is considered complete.

5. Implement feedback loops

Regularly review workflow performance and identify improvement opportunities.

6. Improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally

Kanban encourages teams to make small, continuous improvements rather than large disruptive changes.

Kanban board

A Kanban board is a visual tool that represents the workflow.

Simple Kanban board

Dashboard

Testing

Typical Kanban columns

Column Meaning

In Progress Work currently being worked on.

Testing Work being validated.

Done Completed work.

Work In Progress (WIP) limits

What is WIP?

Work In Progress (WIP) refers to tasks that have been started but not yet completed.

Why WIP limits are important

  • Prevent the team from starting too many tasks at once.

  • Encourage the team to finish existing work before starting new work.

  • Reveal bottlenecks when a column reaches its limit.

  • Improve focus and flow efficiency.

Example WIP limits

Column WIP limit

To Do No limit

In Progress 3 tasks

Testing 2 tasks

Done No limit

Bottleneck example

If the Testing column has a WIP limit of 2 and already contains two tasks:

  • Developers cannot move additional tasks into Testing.

  • The team focuses on completing testing work first.

  • This prevents unfinished work from piling up.

How Kanban improves workflow

  • Visual transparency -- Everyone can see the status of work.

  • Bottleneck identification -- Blocked stages become visible.

  • Reduced multitasking -- WIP limits encourage focus.

  • Faster delivery -- Work moves continuously through the system.

  • Continuous improvement -- Teams regularly analyze and improve flow.

Kanban vs Scrum

Aspect Kanban Scrum

Work cycle Continuous flow. Time-boxed Sprints.

Roles No mandatory roles. Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers.

Planning Continuous prioritization. Sprint Planning.

WIP limits Core practice. Not a core requirement.

Best for Support, maintenance, and Complex product development. continuous work.

When to use Kanban

Kanban is most suitable when:

  • Work arrives continuously.

  • Priorities change frequently.

  • The team handles support or maintenance tasks.

  • Work items vary in size and urgency.

  • The team wants to improve workflow efficiency.

Examples

  • IT support teams.

  • Bug-fixing teams.

  • Operations teams.

  • Regulatory update management.

  • Continuous AI model improvement.

Hospital IT support

Pharmacovigilance example

Kanban can manage ongoing work such as:

  • Regulatory rule updates.

  • Bug fixes in AI extraction.

  • MedDRA coding updates.

  • Signal detection improvements.

  • User support requests.

AI product example

Kanban is useful for managing:

  • User feedback requests.

  • AI model retraining tasks.

  • Bug fixes.

  • Performance monitoring.

  • New feature enhancements.

Advantages of Kanban

  • Simple to implement.

  • Highly visual.

  • Flexible for changing priorities.

  • Reduces bottlenecks.

  • Improves flow efficiency.

  • Supports continuous delivery.

Limitations of Kanban

  • May provide less structure than Scrum.

  • Can be difficult to forecast long-term delivery without additional metrics.

  • Requires discipline in respecting WIP limits.

  • May not provide enough cadence for teams needing regular review cycles.

Best practices

  • Keep the Kanban board simple and visible.

  • Set realistic WIP limits.

  • Regularly review the board for bottlenecks.

  • Measure cycle time and throughput.

  • Continuously refine workflow policies.

  • Use Kanban alongside Scrum when appropriate (Scrumban).

Interview questions

Q1. What is Kanban?

Answer: Kanban is a workflow management method that helps teams visualize work, limit work in progress, and improve the flow of tasks through a process.

Q2. What is the main purpose of a Kanban board?

Answer: The main purpose of a Kanban board is to visualize the workflow, show the status of work items, and help identify bottlenecks.

Q3. What are WIP limits?

Answer: WIP limits restrict the number of tasks allowed in a workflow stage at one time, helping teams reduce multitasking and improve flow efficiency.

Q4. When is Kanban most suitable?

Answer: Kanban is most suitable for continuous work environments such as support, maintenance, operations, and projects with frequently changing priorities.

Summary

Kanban is a visual workflow management method that helps teams improve the flow of work by:

  • Visualizing tasks on a Kanban board.

  • Limiting Work In Progress (WIP).

  • Managing workflow continuously.

  • Identifying and removing bottlenecks.

  • Encouraging continuous improvement.

Kanban is particularly useful for support, maintenance, operations, regulatory updates, and continuous AI product improvement.

Key takeaways

  • Kanban means "visual signal" or "signboard."

  • A Kanban board visualizes workflow stages.

  • WIP limits prevent too much work from being in progress at the same time.

  • Kanban focuses on continuous flow, while Scrum focuses on time-boxed Sprints.

  • Kanban is ideal for continuous work and changing priorities.

  • It can be effectively applied to healthcare support, pharmacovigilance updates, and AI product maintenance.

Lesson 21: Lean Framework -- Principles, Waste Elimination, and Value Optimization

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Lean is.

  • The history of Lean.

  • Why Lean was created.

  • The Lean mindset.

  • The 5 principles of Lean.

  • The 8 types of waste.

  • Value stream mapping.

  • Lean vs Agile vs Scrum vs Kanban.

  • How Lean applies to healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI products.

1. What is Lean?

Simple definition

Lean is a methodology focused on maximizing customer value while minimizing waste.

In simple words:

Build what customers need, remove unnecessary work, and continuously improve the process.

Simple analogy

Imagine a hospital emergency department.

A patient arrives.

The process:

Patient arrival\ ↓\ Registration\ ↓\ Waiting\ ↓\ Doctor consultation\ ↓\ Tests\ ↓\ Treatment

Now imagine:

  • Patient waits 2 hours for registration.

  • Same information is entered three times.

  • Doctors wait for reports.

  • Staff perform unnecessary paperwork.

Lean thinking asks:

\"Which steps actually create value for the patient, and which steps are waste?\"

2. Why was Lean created?

Lean originated from the Toyota Production System (TPS).

After World War II, Japan had:

  • Limited resources.

  • Limited money.

  • High competition.

Toyota needed a way to:

  • Produce high-quality products.

  • Reduce waste.

  • Use resources efficiently.

Toyota developed a system focused on:

  • Continuous improvement.

  • Employee involvement.

  • Eliminating unnecessary activities.

This became known globally as Lean Manufacturing.

Later, Lean concepts moved into:

  • Software development.

  • Healthcare.

  • Product management.

  • Startups.

  • AI development.

3. Lean mindset

A Lean thinker always asks:

Question 1:

\"Does this activity create customer value?\"

If yes:

Continue.

If no:

Remove or reduce it.

Question 2:

\"Can we deliver faster with less waste?\"

Question 3:

\"How can we improve continuously?\"

4. Lean principles

Lean has five fundamental principles.

Principle 1: Identify Value

Meaning

Understand what customers actually value.

Not everything a company builds creates value.

Example

Healthcare app:

Customers value:

✅ Easy appointment booking\ ✅ Fast doctor access\ ✅ Accurate medical information

Customers do not value:

❌ Complicated registration\ ❌ Unnecessary screens\ ❌ Extra features nobody uses

Product Manager perspective

A Product Manager must always ask:

\"Will this feature solve a real user problem?\"

Principle 2: Map the Value Stream

Meaning

Understand the complete process from idea to customer delivery.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Current process:

Case received

↓

Manual data entry

↓

Medical review

↓

Coding

↓

Quality check

↓

Submission

Lean analysis asks:

Where is time wasted?

Where are delays?

Where are unnecessary steps?

Value Stream Mapping

A visual representation of:

  • Activities.

  • Waiting time.

  • Handoffs.

  • Delays.

  • Bottlenecks.

Example:

Traditional PV process:

Case received

(2 hours waiting)

↓

Manual entry

(4 hours)

↓

Medical review

(1 day waiting)

↓

Coding

(3 hours)

Lean improvement:

AI extraction

↓

↓

Result:

Processing time reduced.

Principle 3: Create Flow

Meaning

Make work move smoothly without interruptions.

Example:

Bad flow:

Developer starts 10 features.

Nothing finishes.

Good Lean flow:

Complete one feature.

Release it.

Move to next feature.

Relationship with Kanban:

Kanban supports Lean by improving workflow flow.

Principle 4: Establish Pull

Meaning

Work should be created based on actual demand, not assumptions.

Example:

Traditional approach:

\"We think users need 20 features.\"

Build everything.

Later discover users use only 5 features.

Waste created.

Lean approach:

Build small feature.

Measure usage.

Improve based on feedback.

This is the foundation of:

  • MVP.

  • Product experimentation.

  • Startup methodology.

Principle 5: Pursue Perfection

Meaning

Continuous improvement.

Lean never says:

\"We are finished.\"

It asks:

\"How can we improve?\"

Examples:

  • Faster delivery.

  • Better quality.

  • Lower cost.

  • Better user experience.

5. The 8 wastes of Lean

Lean identifies activities that do not create value.

Remember:

DOWNTIME

1. Defects

Errors requiring correction.

Example:

AI model extracts wrong patient information.

Impact:

  • Rework.

  • Delays.

  • Cost increase.

2. Overproduction

Creating more than needed.

Example:

Building 20 dashboard features when users need only 5.

3. Waiting

Idle time.

Examples:

  • Waiting for approval.

  • Waiting for data.

  • Waiting for testing.

4. Non-utilized talent

Not using people\'s skills.

Example:

A pharmacovigilance expert is only used for testing but not involved in requirement design.

5. Transportation

Unnecessary movement of information.

Software example:

Multiple systems requiring manual data transfer.

6. Inventory

Too much unfinished work.

Example:

50 incomplete backlog items.

7. Motion

Unnecessary effort.

Example:

Users clicking through 10 screens for a simple task.

8. Extra Processing

Doing unnecessary work.

Example:

Entering the same patient data into multiple systems.

Solution:

AI extraction.

Result:

  • Faster processing.

  • Reduced errors.

  • More analyst time for complex cases.

Lean is a methodology focused on maximizing customer value by eliminating waste and continuously improving processes.

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Extreme Programming (XP) is.

  • History of XP.

  • XP values and principles.

  • When XP should be used.

1. What is Extreme Programming (XP)?

Simple definition

Extreme Programming (XP) is an Agile software development framework focused on delivering high-quality software through strong engineering practices, continuous feedback, and frequent releases.

In simple words:

Scrum helps teams decide what to build and when to build it. XP focuses on building it correctly with high technical quality.

Simple analogy

Imagine building a hospital.

Scrum answers:

  • Which departments should be built first?

  • What should be delivered in the next phase?

XP answers:

  • Are the electrical systems safe?

  • Are materials high quality?

  • Are construction standards followed?

Both focus on successful delivery, but XP emphasizes quality of construction.

2. Why was XP created?

In traditional software development:

Teams often faced problems:

  • Requirements changed frequently.

  • Bugs appeared late.

  • Testing happened at the end.

  • Developers worked separately.

  • Releases were slow.

XP was created to solve these problems by introducing:

  • Continuous testing.

  • Frequent releases.

  • Close collaboration.

  • Better coding practices.

3. History of Extreme Programming

XP was created by:

Kent Beck

during the late 1990s.

It was first used in a project called:

Chrysler Comprehensive Compensation System (C3 Project)

The project faced problems with traditional development approaches.

Kent Beck introduced XP practices to:

  • Improve software quality.

  • Increase developer collaboration.

  • Deliver faster.

The book:

\"Extreme Programming Explained\"

was published by Kent Beck in 1999.

4. Why is it called \"Extreme\" Programming?

The idea:

Take good software development practices and apply them to the extreme.

Examples:

Normal practice:

\"Test software.\"

XP:

\"Write tests continuously before coding.\"

Normal practice:

\"Review code.\"

XP:

\"Two developers work together continuously.\"

Normal practice:

\"Integrate changes.\"

XP:

\"Integrate code multiple times every day.\"

5. XP Values

XP is built around five major values.

1. Communication

Meaning

Team members communicate frequently instead of relying only on documents.

Example:

Developer talks directly with Product Owner to clarify requirements.

Healthcare example:

Developer discusses workflow directly with pharmacovigilance experts instead of guessing requirements.

2. Simplicity

Meaning

Build the simplest solution that solves the current problem.

Avoid unnecessary complexity.

Example:

Do not build 50 AI features before proving users need the basic feature.

3. Feedback

Meaning

Get feedback quickly.

Sources:

  • Automated tests.

  • Customers.

  • Users.

  • Team members.

4. Courage

Meaning

Teams should be willing to:

  • Refactor bad code.

  • Remove unnecessary features.

  • Challenge incorrect assumptions.

5. Respect

Meaning

Team members respect each other\'s skills and contributions.

6. Core XP Practices

Now we learn the most important XP practices.

1. Pair Programming

What is it?

Two developers work together on the same code.

One developer:

Driver

Writes code.

Other developer:

Navigator

Reviews and guides.

They switch roles regularly.

Benefits

  • Fewer bugs.

  • Better knowledge sharing.

  • Better code quality.

Healthcare example:

One developer writes AI extraction logic.

Another developer reviews:

  • Data privacy.

  • Accuracy.

  • Error handling.

2. Test-Driven Development (TDD)

What is TDD?

Developers write tests before writing the actual code.

Process:

Write Test

↓

Write Code

↓

Run Test

↓

Improve Code

Called:

Red → Green → Refactor

Example:

Requirement:

\"The system should identify adverse drug reactions.\"

First create tests:

Input:\ Patient case with nausea after medication.

Expected output:

Adverse event detected.

Then develop the feature.

3. Continuous Integration (CI)

Meaning

Developers frequently merge their code into a shared repository.

Benefits:

  • Problems discovered early.

  • Fewer integration issues.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance platform:

Developer A updates AI extraction.

Developer B updates dashboard.

CI automatically tests whether both changes work together.

4. Continuous Testing

Testing happens continuously.

Includes:

  • Unit testing.

  • Integration testing.

  • Automated testing.

5. Refactoring

Meaning

Improving code structure without changing functionality.

Example:

Old code:

Slow and difficult to maintain.

Refactor:

Cleaner and faster.

6. Small Releases

XP encourages releasing small improvements frequently.

Example:

Instead of:

One major release every year.

Release:

Small improvements every week.

7. Collective Code Ownership

Meaning:

Any developer can improve any part of the code.

Benefits:

  • No dependency on one person.

  • Better collaboration.

8. Coding Standards

Teams follow common coding practices.

Benefits:

  • Easier maintenance.

  • Better collaboration.

XP Roles

XP does not have exactly the same roles as Scrum.

Typical roles:

Role Responsibility

Customer Defines requirements and priorities

Programmer Develops software

Tester Creates and runs tests

Coach Guides XP practices

Tracker Tracks progress and metrics

When should XP be used?

XP is suitable when:

1. Requirements change frequently

Example:

AI products.

2. Quality is critical

Examples:

  • Healthcare systems.

  • Banking applications.

  • Medical software.

3. Technical complexity is high

Examples:

  • AI systems.

  • Data platforms.

  • Large applications.

4. Fast feedback is required

Example:

Startup products.

When XP may not be suitable

XP may be difficult when:

  • Team members are distributed across many locations.

  • Organization cannot support frequent collaboration.

  • Developers are unwilling to adopt engineering practices.

  • The project requires heavy documentation instead of rapid iteration.

Healthcare example

Electronic Health Record System

XP practices:

Pair programming:

Two developers review patient data workflows.

TDD:

Test prescription validation before development.

Continuous integration:

Ensure updates don\'t break existing hospital functions.

Feature:

XP approach:

Step 1

Write tests:

Input:

Patient report:

\"Patient developed rash after taking drug X.\"

Expected:

System identifies:

  • Drug name.

  • Adverse event.

  • Patient details.

Step 2

Develop AI extraction.

Step 3

Run automated tests.

Step 4

Refactor and improve accuracy.

AI Product example

AI Medical Chatbot

XP practices:

Pair programming:

AI engineer + backend engineer collaborate.

TDD:

Test chatbot responses.

Continuous integration:

Every model update is tested.

Small releases:

Release improvements weekly.

Common mistakes

Mistake 1:

\"XP is only about coding.\"

Wrong.

XP improves:

  • Communication.

  • Collaboration.

  • Quality.

  • Feedback.

Mistake 2:

\"XP replaces Scrum.\"

Wrong.

Many teams combine:

Scrum + XP.

This is common.

Mistake 3:

\"Testing happens after development.\"

Wrong.

XP promotes testing continuously.

Best practices

  • Automate testing wherever possible.

  • Encourage collaboration.

  • Release small improvements frequently.

  • Maintain coding standards.

  • Refactor continuously.

  • Use feedback loops.

Answer:

Lesson 23: Crystal Framework -- People-Centric Agile Approach and When to Use It

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Crystal Agile is.

1. What is Crystal?

Simple definition

Crystal is an Agile framework that focuses on people, communication, collaboration, and adapting the process based on project characteristics.

Simple meaning:

The team matters more than the process.

Crystal believes:

A small team building a simple app should not follow the same process as a large team building a life-critical medical system.

Simple analogy

Imagine two medical situations:

Situation 1:

A small clinic creates a simple appointment booking app.

Team:

  • 5 people.

  • Low risk.

  • Simple requirements.

They need:

  • Fast communication.

  • Minimal documentation.

Situation 2:

A pharmaceutical company develops an AI system that detects adverse drug reactions.

Team:

  • 100+ people.

  • Regulatory requirements.

  • Patient safety concerns.

They need:

  • More documentation.

  • More controls.

  • More communication structure.

Crystal says:

\"Do not use the same process for both.\"

2. Why was Crystal created?

Traditional software methods had problems:

  • Too many rules.

  • Too much documentation.

  • Same process for every project.

  • Slow decision-making.

Agile experts realized:

Different projects have different needs.

A banking system and a small mobile app cannot be managed identically.

Crystal was created to provide:

  • Flexibility.

  • Human-centered collaboration.

  • Appropriate processes.

3. History of Crystal

Crystal was created by:

Alistair Cockburn

in the 1990s.

He studied successful software teams and found:

Successful teams depended heavily on:

  • Communication.

  • Trust.

  • Collaboration.

  • Frequent delivery.

Not just processes.

Crystal became one of the original Agile approaches and influenced the Agile movement.

4. Core philosophy of Crystal

Crystal follows this idea:

\"People, interaction, and communication create successful software.\"

The framework emphasizes:

1. People over processes

Good teams can overcome process limitations.

2. Frequent delivery

Deliver working software regularly.

3. Close communication

The closer the team works together, the better the outcome.

4. Continuous improvement

Teams regularly improve how they work.

5. Crystal Family

Crystal is not one single method.

It is a family of methods.

Different colors represent different levels of complexity and risk.

Crystal Colors

1. Crystal Clear

For:

  • Small teams.

  • Low-risk projects.

Typical:

  • 1--6 people.

Example:

Small startup developing a simple mobile app.

2. Crystal Yellow

For:

  • Small-medium teams.

  • Moderate complexity.

Typical:

  • 7--20 people.

Example:

Healthcare dashboard development.

3. Crystal Orange

For:

  • Larger projects.

  • More complexity.

Typical:

  • 20--80 people.

Example:

Hospital management platform.

4. Crystal Red

For:

  • Very large and complex projects.

Example:

Enterprise healthcare systems.

5. Crystal Diamond / Sapphire

For:

Very high-risk systems.

Examples:

  • Aircraft software.

  • Medical devices.

  • Nuclear systems.

Crystal classification principle

Crystal considers:

Team size

More people = more communication challenges.

System criticality

More risk = more controls needed.

Example:

A toy shopping app:

Low risk.

↓

Crystal Clear.

AI system making clinical decisions:

High risk.

↓

More rigorous Crystal approach.

6. Crystal Properties

Crystal has seven important properties.

Property 1: Frequent Delivery

Teams should deliver working software regularly.

Example:

Every few weeks deliver a usable feature.

Healthcare example:

Release:

Patient registration.

Then:

Appointment booking.

Then:

Prescription module.

Property 2: Reflective Improvement

Teams regularly ask:

\"What can we improve?\"

Similar to:

Scrum Retrospective.

Property 3: Osmotic Communication

This is a unique Crystal concept.

Meaning:

Information naturally flows between team members.

Example:

Team members sitting together can hear discussions and share knowledge naturally.

Modern example:

A Slack channel where developers, BA, and product managers continuously communicate.

Property 4: Personal Safety

Team members should feel safe to:

  • Raise concerns.

  • Admit mistakes.

  • Suggest improvements.

Healthcare example:

A developer should be comfortable saying:

\"The AI model accuracy is not sufficient.\"

Property 5: Focus

Team members should have:

  • Clear priorities.

  • Protected time.

  • Clear goals.

Property 6: Easy Access to Expert Users

The team should communicate directly with real users.

Example:

PV analysts provide feedback directly to the product team.

Property 7: Technical Environment

Teams need proper tools:

  • Development environment.

  • Testing tools.

  • Collaboration tools.

1. What is DSDM?

Simple definition

Dynamic Systems Development Method (DSDM) is an Agile framework that focuses on delivering business solutions quickly while maintaining strong governance, collaboration, and quality.

Simple meaning:

DSDM helps organizations build the right solution, at the right time, with strong business involvement.

Simple analogy

Imagine a pharmaceutical company building a:

Drug Safety Management System

Many people are involved:

  • Pharmacovigilance team.

  • Regulatory department.

  • IT team.

  • Quality assurance.

  • Compliance team.

  • Management.

A simple development approach may fail because:

  • Requirements are complex.

  • Regulations are strict.

  • Many stakeholders are involved.

DSDM provides:

  • Clear roles.

  • Strong communication.

  • Prioritization.

  • Governance.

2. Why was DSDM created?

Before Agile:

Organizations faced problems:

  • Projects took years.

  • Requirements changed.

  • Users received software too late.

  • Business teams were disconnected from developers.

However, some organizations also needed:

  • More structure.

  • More governance.

  • More predictability.

DSDM was created to combine:

Agile flexibility + business discipline

3. History of DSDM

DSDM was created in:

1994

by a consortium of organizations in the UK.

The goal:

Create a standard Agile approach for Rapid Application Development (RAD).

It became one of the earliest Agile frameworks.

Later:

DSDM became known as:

Agile Project Framework

4. Core philosophy of DSDM

The main idea:

\"Time and resources are fixed, but scope can change.\"

This is opposite to traditional projects where:

Fixed:

  • Scope.

Flexible:

  • Time and cost.

Traditional Waterfall

Fixed scope

↓

Estimate time

↓

Estimate cost

DSDM

Fixed:

  • Time.

  • Cost.

  • Quality.

Flexible:

  • Features.

Example:

A healthcare app must launch in 3 months.

Instead of delaying launch:

DSDM says:

Deliver the most valuable features first.

Move less important features later.

5. DSDM Principles

DSDM has eight principles.

Principle 1: Focus on Business Need

Everything should deliver business value.

Question:

\"Why are we building this?\"

Example:

Don\'t build AI extraction because AI is trendy.

Build it because:

\"It reduces manual pharmacovigilance processing time.\"

Principle 2: Deliver on Time

Time-boxing is critical.

Example:

Release must happen on:

30 September.

Features are adjusted to meet the deadline.

Principle 3: Collaborate

Business and technical teams work together.

Example:

PV expert works directly with developers.

Principle 4: Never Compromise Quality

Fast delivery does not mean poor quality.

Especially important in:

  • Healthcare.

  • Finance.

  • Safety systems.

Principle 5: Build Incrementally

Deliver in small pieces.

Example:

Release:

Version 1:

ICSR creation.

Version 2:

AI extraction.

Version 3:

Signal detection.

Principle 6: Develop Iteratively

Build → Test → Feedback → Improve.

Principle 7: Demonstrate Control

Maintain:

  • Visibility.

  • Governance.

  • Tracking.

Principle 8: Communicate Continuously

Frequent communication prevents misunderstanding.

6. DSDM Lifecycle

DSDM has multiple phases.

Phase 1: Feasibility

Question:

\"Should we build this?\"

Activities:

  • Business analysis.

  • Risk assessment.

  • Initial requirements.

Example:

Should we build AI pharmacovigilance software?

Phase 2: Foundations

Create:

  • Business vision.

  • Architecture.

  • Initial roadmap.

  • Priorities.

Phase 3: Exploration

Understand user needs.

Activities:

  • Workshops.

  • Prototypes.

  • User feedback.

Phase 4: Engineering

Build the solution.

Activities:

  • Development.

  • Testing.

  • Integration.

Phase 5: Deployment

Release to users.

Activities:

  • Training.

  • Rollout.

  • Support.

7. MoSCoW Prioritization

One of the most important DSDM concepts.

MoSCoW helps prioritize requirements.

M = Must Have

Critical requirements.

Without them, solution fails.

Example:

Pharmacovigilance system:

Must have:

  • Case creation.

  • User login.

  • Audit trail.

S = Should Have

Important but not mandatory.

Example:

Advanced reporting.

C = Could Have

Nice-to-have features.

Example:

Custom dashboard themes.

W = Won\'t Have Now

Not included in current release.

Example:

Voice assistant feature.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Priority Feature

Must Have Case Workflow

Should Have AI Extraction

Could Have Voice Commands

Won\'t Have Blockchain Integration

Answer:

DSDM is an Agile framework that focuses on delivering business solutions quickly while maintaining governance, collaboration, and quality.

Q4. Why is DSDM useful for healthcare projects?

Because healthcare projects require collaboration among multiple stakeholders, regulatory compliance, predictable delivery, and strong governance.

Lesson 25: SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) -- Enterprise Agile, Agile Release Train, PI Planning, and Portfolio Management

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What SAFe is.

  • Why SAFe was created.

  • History of SAFe.

  • SAFe levels.

  • Agile Release Train (ART).

  • PI Planning.

  • SAFe roles.

  • Lean Portfolio Management.

  • SAFe vs Scrum.

  • When to use SAFe.

  • Healthcare, pharma, and AI examples.

1. What is SAFe?

Simple definition

SAFe (Scaled Agile Framework) is a framework that helps large organizations apply Agile practices across multiple teams while maintaining alignment, governance, and business strategy.

Simple meaning:

Scrum works well for one team. SAFe helps hundreds of teams work together toward one business goal.

Simple analogy

Imagine building a hospital information system.

A small team:

  • 8 developers.

  • 1 Product Owner.

  • 1 Scrum Master.

Can use Scrum.

But a global healthcare platform may need:

  • 500 developers.

  • Multiple products.

  • Security teams.

  • Compliance teams.

  • Data science teams.

  • Regulatory experts.

Scrum alone may not be enough.

SAFe provides coordination.

2. Why was SAFe created?

Large organizations faced problems:

  • Many Agile teams worked independently.

  • Teams built conflicting features.

  • Business strategy was disconnected from development.

  • Dependencies caused delays.

  • Leadership lacked visibility.

Example:

Team A builds patient records.

Team B builds billing.

Team C builds analytics.

Without coordination:

  • Integration problems.

  • Duplicate work.

  • Delayed releases.

SAFe solves this by connecting:

Business strategy → Portfolio → Programs → Teams

3. History of SAFe

SAFe was created by:

Dean Leffingwell

around 2011.

It combines ideas from:

  • Agile.

  • Scrum.

  • Lean.

  • Systems thinking.

  • Product development flow.

SAFe is maintained by:

Scaled Agile

4. SAFe Core Values

SAFe has four core values:

1. Alignment

Everyone understands:

  • Business goals.

  • Priorities.

  • Roadmap.

Example:

All teams know the goal:

\"Reduce pharmacovigilance case processing time by 50%.\"

2. Built-in Quality

Quality is not added at the end.

Quality is built into every step.

Examples:

  • Automated testing.

  • Security reviews.

  • Compliance checks.

3. Transparency

Everyone can see:

  • Progress.

  • Risks.

  • Dependencies.

4. Program Execution

The organization focuses on delivering working solutions.

5. SAFe Levels

SAFe has different configurations.

Level 1: Team Level

Focus:

Individual Agile teams.

Similar to Scrum.

Team members:

  • Developers.

  • Product Owner.

  • Scrum Master.

Level 2: Program Level

Multiple teams work together.

Main concept:

Agile Release Train (ART)

Level 3: Large Solution Level

For very large systems.

Example:

National healthcare platform.

Level 4: Portfolio Level

Connects:

Business strategy → Investment → Execution

Best practices

  • Connect strategy with execution.

Q1. What is SAFe?

SAFe is a scaled Agile framework that helps large organizations apply Agile practices across multiple teams while maintaining alignment, governance, and business strategy.

Lesson 26: LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum) -- Scaling Scrum Without Adding Heavy Complexity

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What LeSS is.

  • Why LeSS was created.

  • History of LeSS.

  • LeSS principles.

  • LeSS structure.

  • LeSS roles.

  • LeSS events.

  • LeSS vs SAFe.

  • When to use LeSS.

  • Healthcare, pharmacovigilance, and AI examples.

1. What is LeSS?

Simple definition

LeSS (Large-Scale Scrum) is a framework for applying Scrum principles to multiple teams working on one product while keeping the process as simple as possible.

Simple meaning:

LeSS is Scrum expanded to multiple teams without adding unnecessary management layers.

Simple analogy

Imagine building a hospital information system.

Traditional scaling approach:

Create separate departments:

  • Appointment team.

  • Billing team.

  • Patient records team.

  • Analytics team.

Each has:

  • Separate priorities.

  • Separate managers.

  • Separate goals.

Problem:

Teams optimize their own area instead of the whole hospital system.

LeSS approach:

All teams work toward:

One product goal:

\"Build the best hospital information system.\"

One:

  • Product Backlog.

  • Product Owner.

  • Product vision.

2. Why was LeSS created?

When organizations scaled Scrum, they often created problems:

  • Too many managers.

  • Too many meetings.

  • Separate priorities.

  • Complex processes.

  • Teams working in isolation.

LeSS creators believed:

Many organizations were scaling Agile by adding more layers instead of improving collaboration.

LeSS focuses on:

  • Simplicity.

  • Transparency.

  • Whole product thinking.

  • Customer value.

3. History of LeSS

LeSS was created by:

Bas Vodde

and

Craig Larman

They developed LeSS based on:

  • Scrum.

  • Lean thinking.

  • Systems thinking.

The framework became popular for organizations wanting lightweight Agile scaling.

4. LeSS Philosophy

LeSS follows these ideas:

1. More teams, one product

Multiple teams should work on the same product.

Not separate products.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Wrong approach:

Team A owns AI extraction.

Team B owns reporting.

Team C owns dashboard.

Each creates separate priorities.

LeSS approach:

All teams contribute to one product:

\"AI Drug Safety Platform.\"

2. Simplify organizational structure

Reduce:

  • Managers.

  • Handoffs.

  • Approval layers.

3. Customer focus

The goal is:

Deliver customer value faster.

4. Whole-product thinking

Teams are not feature factories.

They are product builders.

5. Continuous improvement

Teams continuously improve.

5. Types of LeSS

LeSS has two versions:

1. Basic LeSS

For:

2--8 Scrum teams.

Each team:

  • 4--8 members.

Total:

Approximately 10--50 people.

2. LeSS Huge

For:

More than 8 teams.

Hundreds of people.

Example:

Global pharmaceutical platform.

6. LeSS Structure

Traditional Scrum:

One Product

|

One Scrum Team

LeSS:

One Product

|

One Product Owner

|

--------------------------------

Team 1 Team 2 Team 3

Scrum Scrum Scrum

Team Team Team

Important:

There is:

  • One Product Owner.

  • One Product Backlog.

  • One Product Goal.

7. LeSS Roles

LeSS keeps Scrum roles.

Product Owner

Responsibilities:

  • Owns Product Backlog.

  • Defines product vision.

  • Maximizes value.

Scrum Masters

Multiple Scrum Masters may support multiple teams.

Responsibilities:

  • Improve Scrum adoption.

  • Remove organizational obstacles.

  • Coach teams.

Developers

Multiple teams develop the product.

Important difference:

LeSS does NOT introduce many additional roles.

Unlike SAFe, it avoids:

  • Program managers.

  • Release train engineers.

  • Extra coordination roles.

8. LeSS Events

LeSS uses Scrum events but adapts them.

Sprint Planning

Large-scale planning has two parts:

Sprint Planning Part 1

All teams:

  • Understand goals.

  • Select backlog items.

Sprint Planning Part 2

Each team:

  • Plans technical implementation.

Daily Scrum

Each team conducts its own Daily Scrum.

Sprint Review

Important difference:

A single Sprint Review.

All teams demonstrate the product together.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Team 1 demonstrates:

AI extraction.

Team 2 demonstrates:

Signal detection.

Team 3 demonstrates:

Reporting.

Stakeholders see the complete product.

Sprint Retrospective

Teams improve their own process.

9. LeSS Product Backlog

One of the most important concepts:

One Product Backlog

Not:

  • Team backlog.

  • Department backlog.

  • Feature backlog.

Example:

Wrong:

AI team backlog.

Reporting team backlog.

Dashboard team backlog.

Correct:

One backlog:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform backlog.

This is a very important interview topic.

Philosophy Scale Scrum simply Scale Agile with structure

Complexity Lightweight More structured

Product One PO Product managers + POs Owner

Governance Less More

Best for Organizations wanting Large enterprises needing simplicity coordination

Example:

Startup growing to 50 developers

LeSS may fit.

Why?

Need:

  • Simple scaling.

  • Less bureaucracy.

Global pharma company

SAFe may fit.

Why?

Need:

  • Compliance.

  • Governance.

  • Portfolio management.

Aspect Scrum LeSS

Backlog One One

LeSS works well when:

1. Multiple teams build one product

Example:

Healthcare platform.

2. Organization wants simplicity

3. Teams can collaborate closely

4. Product ownership is strong

When NOT to use LeSS?

Avoid when:

  • Organization requires heavy governance.

  • Regulatory controls dominate.

  • Teams are completely independent.

  • Management wants many reporting layers.

\"Complete drug safety workflow.\"

Not:

\"My module only.\"

Teams:

AI model team.

Backend team.

Mobile team.

Analytics team.

LeSS approach:

All teams focus on:

\"Improve patient assistant experience.\"

Common mistakes

Mistake 1:

\"LeSS means adding more Scrum teams.\"

Wrong.

LeSS changes organizational thinking.

Mistake 2:

\"Every team owns a separate feature.\"

Wrong.

Teams collaborate on the whole product.

Mistake 3:

\"Scaling means adding managers.\"

Wrong.

LeSS reduces unnecessary hierarchy.

Best practices

  • Maintain one Product Backlog.

  • Have one Product Owner.

  • Focus on customer value.

  • Encourage cross-functional teams.

  • Remove unnecessary coordination layers.

  • Improve organizational design.

Interview questions

Q1. What is LeSS?

Answer:

LeSS is a framework that applies Scrum principles to multiple teams while maintaining simplicity and reducing unnecessary complexity.

Q2. Difference between SAFe and LeSS?

Answer:

SAFe provides a structured enterprise scaling approach with additional roles and governance, while LeSS scales Scrum by keeping the framework lightweight and simple.

Q3. How many Product Owners exist in LeSS?

Answer:

One Product Owner owns one Product Backlog for the entire product.

Q4. What is the main principle of LeSS?

Answer:

Scale Scrum principles, not complexity.

  2. What is the main philosophy of LeSS?

  3. How many Product Backlogs exist in LeSS?

  4. Difference between SAFe and LeSS?

  5. When would you choose LeSS?

Practical assignment

Product:

Summary

LeSS teaches:

\"Scaling Agile does not mean adding more complexity.\"

Important concepts:

✅ One Product Owner\ ✅ One Product Backlog\ ✅ Multiple Scrum teams\ ✅ Whole product thinking\ ✅ Simplicity over bureaucracy

For a Product Manager or Business Analyst, LeSS helps you understand how large products can be built collaboratively without creating unnecessary management layers.

Key takeaways

  • LeSS = Large-Scale Scrum.

  • Created by Bas Vodde and Craig Larman.

  • Scales Scrum to multiple teams.

  • Keeps Agile lightweight.

  • Uses one Product Backlog and one Product Owner.

  • Focuses on customer value and simplicity.

  • Different from SAFe because SAFe adds structure while LeSS minimizes complexity.

1. What is Nexus?

Simple definition

Nexus is a Scrum scaling framework designed to help 3--9 Scrum teams work together on one product while managing dependencies and integration challenges.

Simple meaning:

Nexus helps multiple Scrum teams build one integrated product without breaking Scrum.

Simple analogy

Imagine building a large hospital management system.

You have:

Team 1:\ Patient Registration

Team 2:\ Doctor Portal

Team 3:\ Billing System

Team 4:\ Analytics

Each team works separately.

The problem:

At the end:

  • Patient data does not connect.

  • Billing does not understand registration.

  • Reports are incorrect.

The issue is not individual team performance.

The issue is:

Integration.

Nexus focuses on solving this.

2. Why was Nexus created?

When organizations scaled Scrum, common problems appeared:

Problem 1: Dependencies

Team A waits for Team B.

Example:

AI team waits for data engineering team.

Problem 2: Integration failures

Each team builds successfully, but the complete product fails.

Problem 3: Multiple priorities

Teams optimize their own goals.

Problem 4: Poor visibility

Nobody understands the complete system.

Nexus was created to solve these problems.

3. History of Nexus

Nexus was created by:

Ken Schwaber

in 2015.

Ken Schwaber is also one of the creators of Scrum.

Nexus is maintained by:

Scrum.org

4. Nexus Philosophy

Nexus follows:

\"Use Scrum as the foundation, then add only what is needed to manage integration.\"

Important idea:

Do not create unnecessary complexity.

5. Nexus Principles

Principle 1: One Product

All teams work on:

One product.

Not:

Separate products.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Wrong:

AI team has one product.

Reporting team has another.

Correct:

Everyone contributes to one drug safety platform.

Principle 2: One Product Backlog

Nexus uses:

One Product Backlog.

Owned by:

Product Owner.

Example:

Backlog:

Epic:

AI Case Processing

Features:

  • Data extraction.

  • Medical coding.

  • Signal detection.

Principle 3: Integration is everyone\'s responsibility

Integration is not only testers\' job.

Every team must ensure:

Their work fits the complete product.

6. Nexus Structure

Nexus consists of:

3--9 Scrum Teams

Each team:

  • Developers.

  • Scrum Master.

  • Product Owner.

Plus:

Nexus Integration Team

This is the unique part.

3. Organization wants Scrum scaling

Without heavy frameworks.

4. Teams are technically connected

When NOT to use Nexus?

Avoid when:

  • Teams work on unrelated products.

  • Only one Scrum team exists.

  • Organization requires heavy portfolio governance.

Healthcare Example

Hospital AI Platform

Teams:

Team 1:

Patient data.

Team 2:

AI diagnosis assistant.

Team 3:

Doctor dashboard.

Team 4:

Analytics.

Nexus ensures:

Patient data →

AI model →

Doctor dashboard →

Reports

work as one system.

Pharmacovigilance Example

AI Drug Safety Platform

Teams:

Team 1:

Case Intake

Team 2:

AI Extraction

Team 3:

MedDRA Coding

Team 4:

Signal Detection

Without Nexus:

Each module works separately.

With Nexus:

Complete workflow:

Case received

↓

AI extracts adverse event

↓

Medical coding happens

↓

Signal detected

↓

Regulatory report generated

AI Product Example

AI Medical Chatbot

Teams:

AI model team.

Backend team.

Mobile team.

Security team.

Nexus focuses on:

  • Model integration.

  • Data pipelines.

  • User experience.

  • Security.

Common mistakes

Mistake 1:

\"Nexus is another Scrum replacement.\"

Wrong.

Nexus extends Scrum.

Mistake 2:

\"Integration happens at the end.\"

Wrong.

Integration happens continuously.

Mistake 3:

\"One team owns integration.\"

Wrong.

Everyone owns integration.

Best practices

  • Maintain one product vision.

  • Integrate frequently.

  • Identify dependencies early.

  • Use automation.

  • Collaborate continuously.

  • Build complete increments.

Interview Questions

Q1. What is Nexus?

Answer:

Nexus is a Scrum scaling framework that helps multiple Scrum teams work together by focusing on integration and dependency management.

Q2. Who created Nexus?

Answer:

Ken Schwaber created Nexus in 2015.

Q3. What is Nexus Integration Team?

Answer:

A team responsible for helping Scrum teams integrate their work and improve integration practices.

Q4. Difference between Nexus and LeSS?

Answer:

Nexus focuses on integration challenges, while LeSS focuses on scaling Scrum with minimal organizational complexity.

Q5. Difference between Nexus and SAFe?

Answer:

Nexus is lightweight and Scrum-focused, while SAFe provides enterprise-level scaling with portfolio management.

Mini Quiz

Answer these:

  1. What problem does Nexus mainly solve?

  2. Who created Nexus?

  3. How many Scrum teams does Nexus support?

  4. What is the Nexus Integration Team?

  5. How is Nexus different from SAFe?

Practical Assignment

Design Nexus structure for:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Create:

Product:

AI Drug Safety Platform

Teams:

Create 4 Scrum teams.

Example:

  1. Case Management

  2. AI Extraction

  3. Medical Coding

  4. Signal Detection

Define:

  1. Three integration challenges.

  2. How Nexus Integration Team solves them.

  3. How Sprint Review would work.

  4. How you ensure one integrated product.

Summary

Nexus teaches:

\"Multiple teams are successful only when they deliver one integrated product.\"

Key concepts:

✅ One Product Backlog\ ✅ One Product Owner\ ✅ Multiple Scrum Teams\ ✅ Nexus Integration Team\ ✅ Continuous Integration\ ✅ Integrated Increment

Key Takeaways

  • Nexus = Scrum scaling framework.

  • Created by Ken Schwaber.

  • Focuses on integration.

  • Best for 3--9 Scrum teams.

  • Lightweight compared to SAFe.

  • More integration-focused than LeSS.

  • Useful for complex healthcare and AI platforms.

Lesson 28: Spotify Model -- Squads, Tribes, Chapters, Guilds, and Autonomous Agile Teams

Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Spotify Model is.

  • Why Spotify created this model.

  • History.

  • Squad structure.

  • Tribes.

  • Chapters.

  • Guilds.

  • How autonomy works.

  • Spotify Model vs Scrum.

  • Spotify Model vs SAFe.

  • Healthcare and AI examples.

1. What is Spotify Model?

Simple definition

Spotify Model is an Agile organizational approach that organizes people into autonomous, cross-functional teams while maintaining alignment through communities and shared practices.

Simple meaning:

Small teams decide how to build things, but everyone moves toward the same company vision.

Simple analogy

Imagine a pharmaceutical company developing an AI Drug Safety Platform.

Traditional structure:

Everyone reports through departments:

IT Department

↓

Development Team

↓

Testing Team

↓

Business Team

Problems:

  • Slow decisions.

  • Too many approvals.

  • Teams work separately.

Spotify approach:

Create autonomous teams:

AI Extraction Squad

Signal Detection Squad

Analytics Squad

User Experience Squad

Each squad owns a product area.

2. Why was Spotify Model created?

Spotify grew rapidly.

Problems appeared:

  • Too many people.

  • Communication challenges.

  • Slow decision-making.

  • Too many dependencies.

They needed:

  • Speed.

  • Innovation.

  • Team ownership.

  • Scalability.

The goal:

Keep the feeling of a small startup while becoming a large organization.

3. History of Spotify Model

The model became famous after engineering leaders at Spotify shared their organizational approach around 2012.

Important note:

Spotify Model was never officially released as a framework.

Many organizations copied parts of it.

4. Core Principles of Spotify Model

Principle 1: Autonomy

Teams decide:

  • How to work.

  • Which tools to use.

  • How to solve problems.

Example:

AI team decides:

  • Which ML framework.

  • Which testing approach.

  • Which architecture.

Principle 2: Alignment

Autonomy does not mean everyone does whatever they want.

Teams align through:

  • Company goals.

  • Product strategy.

  • Vision.

Example:

Company goal:

\"Reduce drug safety processing time by 60%.\"

Every squad contributes toward this.

Principle 3: Cross-functional teams

Teams contain different skills.

Example:

AI Product Squad:

  • Developer.

  • Data scientist.

  • UX designer.

  • QA engineer.

  • Product Owner.

  • Business Analyst.

Principle 4: Continuous improvement

Teams regularly improve their processes.

5. Spotify Organizational Structure

The main components:

  1. Squads

  2. Tribes

  3. Chapters

  4. Guilds

1. Squads

The most important concept.

What is a Squad?

A small autonomous cross-functional team.

Similar to:

A Scrum Team.

Typical size:

5--10 people.

Example:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Case Processing Squad

Members:

  • Developer.

  • BA.

  • QA.

  • Pharmacovigilance expert.

  • Product Owner.

Responsibility:

Own case processing experience.

Squad characteristics:

A squad has:

  • Mission.

  • Goal.

  • Autonomy.

  • Ownership.

2. Tribes

What is a Tribe?

A group of related squads working toward a larger mission.

Example:

Healthcare AI Tribe:

Contains:

Squad 1:

AI Extraction

Squad 2:

Signal Detection

Squad 3:

Analytics

Squad 4:

Reporting

Purpose:

Coordination between squads.

3. Chapters

What is a Chapter?

People with similar skills across squads.

Example:

Developers across squads form:

Engineering Chapter.

Other chapters:

  • Data Science Chapter.

  • QA Chapter.

  • UX Chapter.

  • Business Analyst Chapter.

Purpose:

Share:

  • Knowledge.

  • Standards.

  • Best practices.

4. Guilds

What is a Guild?

A voluntary community of interest.

Anyone can join.

Example:

AI Guild:

Members discuss:

  • Machine learning.

  • Prompt engineering.

  • AI ethics.

Healthcare example:

Healthcare AI Guild:

Discuss:

  • FDA regulations.

  • Medical AI safety.

  • Data privacy.

Spotify Model Diagram

Tribe

----------------------------

Squad Squad Squad

| | |

Chapter Chapter Chapter

\ | /

Guild

6. Squad vs Scrum Team

They look similar but are different.

Aspect Squad Scrum Team

Framework Organizational model Agile framework

Scrum roles Optional Defined

Sprint Optional Required

Autonomy High Moderate

Goal Product ownership Sprint delivery

7. Spotify Model vs SAFe

Aspect Spotify SAFe

Philosophy Autonomy Alignment + governance

Structure Squads/Tribes ARTs/Portfolio

Management Lightweight More structured

Best for Innovative companies Large enterprises

8. Spotify Model vs LeSS

Aspect Spotify LeSS

Focus Organization design Scrum scaling

Teams Squads Scrum teams

Backlog Depends One Product Backlog

Goal Autonomy Simplify Scrum

9. When to use Spotify Model?

Useful when:

1. Innovation is important

Example:

AI products.

2. Teams need autonomy

3. Organization has many products

4. Fast experimentation is required

When NOT to use Spotify Model?

Avoid when:

  • Organization needs strict command-and-control.

  • Regulatory environment requires heavy governance.

  • Teams lack maturity.

Healthcare Example

Digital Health Platform

Organization structure:

Patient Care Tribe

Squads:

  • Appointment Squad.

  • Telemedicine Squad.

  • Patient Portal Squad.

AI Healthcare Tribe

Squads:

  • AI Diagnosis.

  • AI Chatbot.

  • Analytics.

Compliance Chapter

Ensures:

  • HIPAA compliance.

  • Data security.

  • Quality standards.

Pharmacovigilance Example

AI Drug Safety Organization

Drug Safety Tribe

Squads:

ICSR Squad

Owns:

Case processing.

AI Extraction Squad

Owns:

NLP extraction.

Signal Detection Squad

Owns:

Safety signals.

Reporting Squad

Owns:

Regulatory reports.

Chapters:

  • Pharmacovigilance experts.

  • Data scientists.

  • Engineers.

Guild:

\"Healthcare AI Safety Guild\"

AI Product Example

AI Medical Assistant

Squads:

Conversation Squad

Owns chatbot experience.

AI Model Squad

Owns model performance.

Data Squad

Owns training data.

Safety Squad

Owns:

AI risks and compliance.

Common mistakes

Mistake 1:

\"Spotify Model is a replacement for Scrum.\"

Wrong.

It is an organizational structure.

Mistake 2:

\"Autonomous teams need no alignment.\"

Wrong.

Autonomy requires strong vision.

Mistake 3:

\"Copy Spotify structure exactly.\"

Wrong.

Every organization must adapt.

Best practices

  • Create clear team missions.

  • Maintain strong product vision.

  • Encourage knowledge sharing.

  • Reduce unnecessary dependencies.

  • Build cross-functional teams.

  • Balance autonomy and alignment.

Interview Questions

Q1. What is Spotify Model?

Answer:

Spotify Model is an organizational approach that uses autonomous cross-functional teams called squads supported by tribes, chapters, and guilds.

Q2. What is a Squad?

Answer:

A squad is a small autonomous cross-functional team responsible for a specific product area.

Q3. Difference between Chapter and Guild?

Answer:

A Chapter is a group of people with the same expertise inside an organization, while a Guild is a voluntary community sharing knowledge and interests.

Q4. Is Spotify Model a framework?

Answer:

No. It is an organizational model, not a formal Agile framework.

Mini Quiz

Answer these:

  1. What is the main purpose of Spotify Model?

  2. What is a Squad?

  3. Difference between Tribe and Chapter?

  4. Is Spotify Model an Agile framework?

  5. How can Spotify Model help AI product development?

Practical Assignment

Design Spotify Model for your:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Create:

Tribe:

Example:\ \"AI Drug Safety Tribe\"

Squads:

Create 5 squads.

Chapters:

Create 4 skill communities.

Guild:

Create 2 knowledge-sharing groups.

Explain:

  • What autonomy each squad has.

  • How squads stay aligned.

  • How BA/Product Manager works inside this model.

Summary

Spotify Model focuses on:

✅ Autonomous teams\ ✅ Cross-functional squads\ ✅ Knowledge sharing\ ✅ Innovation\ ✅ Fast decision-making

Important concepts:

  • Squad → Product team.

  • Tribe → Group of squads.

  • Chapter → Skill community.

  • Guild → Interest community.

Key Takeaways

  • Spotify Model is an organizational model, not a framework.

  • Created from Spotify\'s engineering practices.

  • Focuses on autonomy and alignment.

  • Useful for innovative products.

  • Very relevant for AI product organizations.

  • Should be adapted, not blindly copied.
