MODULE 6 -- Agile Metrics

Lesson 76: Why Agile Metrics Matter (Foundation)

Role Perspective:\ As a future Business Analyst / Product Analyst / Product Manager / AI Product Manager, understanding metrics is critical because Agile is not only about \"delivering faster\"; it is about delivering the right value and continuously improving.

1. Concept: What are Agile Metrics?

Simple Definition

Agile Metrics are measurements used by Agile teams to understand progress, performance, quality, flow, and improvement.

They help answer questions like:

  • Are we delivering value?

  • Are we improving?

  • Are we predictable?

  • Are we building quality products?

  • Are customers happy?

Example:

A Pharmacovigilance team is developing an:

AI Adverse Event Detection Platform

Management asks:

\"Are we progressing well?\"

A weak answer:

\"We completed 50 user stories.\"

A better Agile answer:

  • Average cycle time reduced from 10 days to 5 days

  • Case processing accuracy increased from 85% to 95%

  • Release predictability improved from 60% to 90%

  • User satisfaction increased

These are metrics.

2. Why Agile Metrics Exist

The Problem

Without metrics, teams rely on opinions.

Example:

Product Owner:

\"The team is slow.\"

Developer:

\"We are working very hard.\"

Manager:

\"Why is release delayed?\"

Everyone has a different opinion.

Metrics create a common reality.

Metrics help answer:

1. Where are we?

Example:

How much work is completed?

2. Where are we going?

Example:

Can we release the product by December?

3. What is blocking us?

Example:

Why are user stories waiting 15 days?

4. How can we improve?

Example:

Why are defects increasing every sprint?

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine you are driving a car.

Without metrics:

You don\'t know:

  • Speed

  • Fuel level

  • Engine temperature

You may reach the destination, or you may fail.

Dashboard gives information:

Speed 80 km/hr

Fuel 50%

Temperature Normal

Distance 100 km

Agile metrics are the dashboard of a product team.

4. Technical Explanation

Agile metrics generally fall into four categories:

Agile Metrics

|

------------------------------------------------

| | | |

Delivery Flow Quality Value

Metrics Metrics Metrics Metrics

Category 1: Delivery Metrics

Measure:

\"Are we completing planned work?\"

Examples:

  • Velocity

  • Sprint Completion

  • Sprint Predictability

  • Burndown Chart

Example:

Sprint Goal:

Complete AI case extraction module.

Planned:

20 story points

Completed:

18 story points

Sprint completion:

90%

Category 2: Flow Metrics

Measure:

\"How smoothly does work move through the system?\"

Examples:

  • Cycle Time

  • Lead Time

  • Throughput

  • WIP

Example:

AI model improvement request:

Day 1:\ Created

Day 5:\ Developer starts

Day 10:\ Testing

Day 12:\ Released

Flow metrics measure this journey.

Category 3: Quality Metrics

Measure:

\"Are we building a reliable product?\"

Examples:

  • Escaped Defects

  • Bug Rate

  • Test Coverage

  • Production Issues

Healthcare example:

AI Pharmacovigilance system:

A defect causes:

Wrong MedDRA coding suggestion.

Quality metric detects:

  • Number of errors

  • Severity

  • Root cause

Category 4: Value Metrics

Measure:

\"Are users getting benefits?\"

Examples:

  • User satisfaction

  • Adoption rate

  • Revenue

  • Time saved

  • Business outcomes

Example:

Before AI:

PV associate reviews:

100 cases/day

After AI:

300 cases/day

Value improvement:

3x productivity.

5. Metrics vs KPIs

Many people confuse these.

Metric

Any measurement.

Example:

Number of user stories completed.

KPI (Key Performance Indicator)

A metric directly linked to business goals.

Example:

Goal:

Reduce drug safety case processing time.

KPI:

Average processing time reduced by 40%.

Comparison:

Metric KPI

Measures something Measures important business outcome

Many metrics exist Few important KPIs

Team-focused Business-focused

6. Good Agile Metrics vs Bad Agile Metrics

Good Metrics

Help improvement.

Examples:

✅ Cycle time\ ✅ Customer satisfaction\ ✅ Defect rate\ ✅ Release frequency

Bad Metrics

Create unhealthy behavior.

Examples:

❌ Number of hours worked\ ❌ Number of lines of code\ ❌ Number of meetings attended\ ❌ Number of tickets closed

Example:

If developers are measured by:

\"Number of tickets completed\"

They may close easy tickets instead of solving important problems.

7. Agile Metrics in Scrum

A Scrum team commonly uses:

Product Backlog

|

↓

Sprint Planning

|

↓

Sprint Execution

|

↓

Sprint Review

|

↓

Metrics Analysis

|

↓

Retrospective Improvement

Metrics support continuous improvement.

8. Healthcare Example

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Business Goal:

Reduce manual case processing.

Metrics:

Delivery:

Velocity:\ 30 story points/sprint

Flow:

Cycle Time:\ 7 days/story

Quality:

AI extraction accuracy:\ 96%

Value:

Case processing time:

Before:\ 30 minutes/case

After:\ 10 minutes/case

9. AI Product Example

AI Medical Assistant

Important metrics:

Model Performance

  • Accuracy

  • Precision

  • Recall

  • Hallucination rate

Product Metrics

  • Daily active users

  • User retention

  • Task completion rate

Agile Metrics

  • Release frequency

  • Cycle time

  • Defect rate

10. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1:

Using metrics to punish teams.

Wrong:

\"Your velocity dropped, explain.\"

Better:

\"Why did velocity change? What can improve?\"

Mistake 2:

Optimizing one metric.

Example:

Increase velocity.

Result:

Teams create smaller stories.

Velocity increases but value decreases.

Mistake 3:

Tracking too many metrics.

A dashboard with 100 metrics creates confusion.

11. Best Practices

Good Agile metrics should be:

Simple

Everyone understands them.

Transparent

Visible to the team.

Actionable

They should lead to improvement.

Balanced

Include:

  • Speed

  • Quality

  • Value

12. Jira Example

Jira provides Agile reports:

Dashboard

--------------------------------

Sprint Burndown

Remaining Work ↓

Velocity Chart

Sprint 1: 35 points

Sprint 2: 42 points

Sprint 3: 40 points

Cumulative Flow Diagram

Cycle Time Report

--------------------------------

13. Interview Questions

Q1. Why are Agile metrics important?

Answer:

Agile metrics provide visibility into team performance, product delivery, quality, and improvement opportunities. They help teams make data-driven decisions.

Q2. Should velocity be used to compare teams?

Answer:

No. Velocity is a team-specific planning metric. Comparing velocity between teams creates unhealthy competition.

Q3. What is the difference between metric and KPI?

Answer:

A metric measures any activity, while a KPI measures progress toward an important business objective.

14. Mini Quiz

Answer these:

Q1.

Agile metrics mainly help teams:

A) Punish poor performers\ B) Improve decision-making\ C) Avoid planning

Q2.

Which is a Flow Metric?

A) Cycle Time\ B) Revenue\ C) Customer Rating

Q3.

Velocity should be:

A) Compared between teams\ B) Used for team forecasting\ C) Used to judge developers

Q4.

Which is a Value Metric?

A) Number of meetings\ B) Customer satisfaction\ C) Lines of code

15. Practical Assignment

For your portfolio project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Create a metrics dashboard.

Define:

Delivery Metrics:

Flow Metrics:

Quality Metrics:

Value Metrics:

16. Lesson Summary

Today we learned:

  • What Agile metrics are

  • Why they exist

  • Four categories of metrics

  • Metrics vs KPIs

  • Good vs bad metrics

  • How metrics help Product Managers and Business Analysts

Key Takeaways

Remember:

  1. Metrics are a product team\'s health dashboard.

  2. Metrics should improve decisions, not punish people.

  3. Velocity measures capacity, not value.

  4. Business outcomes matter more than activity.

  5. Good Agile teams measure delivery + flow + quality + value.

Lesson 77: Velocity (Advanced Understanding)

Role Perspective:\ As a Business Analyst / Product Analyst / Product Manager, velocity helps you understand how much work a team can realistically deliver, forecast releases, and identify improvement opportunities.

A common interview mistake is saying:

\"Velocity measures developer productivity.\"

This is incorrect.

Velocity measures team delivery capacity, not individual performance.

1. Concept: What is Velocity?

Simple Definition

Velocity is the amount of work a Scrum team completes during a Sprint, usually measured in Story Points.

Formula:

Velocity = Total Story Points Completed in a Sprint

Example:

Sprint duration:

2 weeks

Team committed:

40 Story Points

Completed:

35 Story Points

Velocity:

35 Story Points

2. Why Velocity Exists

The Problem

A Product Owner asks:

\"When can we release our AI Pharmacovigilance Platform?\"

The team says:

\"We don\'t know.\"

Velocity helps create a forecast.

Example:

Product Backlog:

300 Story Points

Team velocity:

30 points/sprint

Forecast:

300 ÷ 30 = 10 Sprints

If one Sprint = 2 weeks:

10 × 2 = 20 weeks

Approximate release:

5 months

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine you run a restaurant.

Every day you prepare meals.

Day 1:

100 meals

Day 2:

120 meals

Day 3:

110 meals

Your average capacity:

≈110 meals/day

You can predict:

\"How many meals can we prepare next week?\"

Velocity works similarly.

4. Technical Explanation

Velocity uses:

Story Points

Not:

❌ Hours\ ❌ Lines of code\ ❌ Number of tasks

Example:

Sprint 1:

User Story Points

Login 3

Patient Profile 5

Case Upload 8

Dashboard 13

Completed:

3 + 5 + 8 + 13

= 29 Story Points

Velocity:

29

5. How Velocity is Calculated

Example: AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Sprint 1

Completed:

  • User Authentication → 5

  • PDF Upload → 8

  • Case Database → 13

Velocity:

5 + 8 + 13 = 26

Sprint 2

Completed:

  • MedDRA Search → 8

  • Case Validation → 5

  • Reporting Module → 13

Velocity:

8 + 5 + 13 = 26

Sprint 3

Completed:

  • Signal Detection → 13

  • Dashboard → 8

Velocity:

21

Average Velocity:

(26 + 26 + 21) ÷ 3

= 24.3

≈ 24 Story Points/Sprint

6. Velocity Chart

A Jira Velocity Chart looks like:

Story Points

50 |

40 |

30 | █

20 | █ █ █

10 |

---------------------

S1 S2 S3

Committed

Completed

It shows:

  • Planned work

  • Completed work

  • Team consistency

7. Velocity and Product Management

Product Managers use velocity for:

Release Forecasting

Question:

\"When will Feature X be available?\"

Example:

Backlog:

Feature:

AI Signal Detection

Remaining:

120 points

Team velocity:

30 points

Forecast:

120 / 30

= 4 Sprints

8. Velocity in Healthcare Example

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Case Processing Platform

Product Backlog:

Feature Points

ICSR Upload 8

AI Extraction 13

MedDRA Coding 13

Duplicate Detection 8

Signal Detection 21

Total:

63 points

Team velocity:

20 points/sprint

Forecast:

63 ÷ 20

≈ 4 Sprints

9. Velocity in AI Product Development

AI products are uncertain.

Example:

Building:

Medical AI Chatbot

Some stories:

  • Create UI → predictable

  • Integrate LLM → uncertain

  • Improve accuracy → highly uncertain

Velocity helps absorb uncertainty.

Example:

Sprint 1:

20 points

Sprint 2:

25 points

Sprint 3:

28 points

Team learns and improves forecasting.

10. Velocity vs Capacity

This is a common interview trap.

Q1. What is velocity?

Answer:

Q2. Can velocity be compared between teams?

Q3. What happens if velocity suddenly drops?

Lesson 78: Cycle Time (Deep Dive)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Analyst • Product Manager • AI Product Manager

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what Cycle Time is.

  • Differentiate Cycle Time from Lead Time (a very common interview topic).

  • Identify bottlenecks using Cycle Time.

  • Use Cycle Time to improve delivery.

  • Interpret Cycle Time reports in Jira.

  • Apply Cycle Time to Healthcare, Pharmacovigilance, and AI products.

1. Concept

What is Cycle Time?

Simple Definition

Cycle Time is the time it takes to complete work after the team starts working on it.

It answers the question:

\"Once we start working on something, how long does it take until it is finished?\"

2. Why Does Cycle Time Exist?

Imagine you\'re a Product Manager.

A stakeholder asks:

\"Once the development team starts working on the AI Duplicate Detection feature, how long will it take to finish?\"

Velocity won\'t answer that because Velocity measures how much work is completed in a Sprint.

Cycle Time answers how long a single work item takes.

Without Cycle Time:

  • Delivery becomes unpredictable.

  • Stakeholders lose confidence.

  • Bottlenecks remain hidden.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine ordering a pizza.

Timeline:

6:00 PM Order placed

6:20 PM Chef starts making pizza

6:45 PM Pizza ready

7:00 PM Delivered

Cycle Time begins when the chef starts cooking.

6:20 PM → 6:45 PM

Cycle Time = 25 minutes

Notice that waiting before cooking is not part of Cycle Time.

Done

Cycle Time begins when the work item enters:

In Progress

Cycle Time ends when it reaches:

Done

Formula:

Cycle Time = Done Date − Start Date

What is Lead Time?

Simple Definition

Imagine you request a new feature:

Lesson 80: Flow Efficiency (Deep Dive)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Analyst • Product Manager • AI Product Manager • Scrum Master

Flow Efficiency is one of the most powerful---but least understood---Agile metrics.

Elite organizations like Amazon, Microsoft, and Spotify focus not just on working faster, but on reducing waiting time. This is where Flow Efficiency becomes valuable.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what Flow Efficiency is.

  • Calculate Flow Efficiency.

  • Identify waste in Agile processes.

  • Improve delivery speed without increasing workload.

  • Apply Flow Efficiency to Healthcare, Pharmacovigilance, and AI products.

  • Interpret Flow Efficiency alongside Lead Time and Cycle Time.

1. Concept

What is Flow Efficiency?

Simple Definition

Flow Efficiency measures how much of the total time a work item is actually being worked on versus waiting.

It answers:

\"How much of the elapsed time was productive work?\"

2. Why Does Flow Efficiency Exist?

Imagine a user story takes 10 days to finish.

You might think:

\"It took 10 days of work.\"

But when you investigate:

  • Developers worked only 3 days.

  • The story spent 7 days waiting:

    • Waiting for approvals.

    • Waiting for testing.

    • Waiting for another team.

    • Waiting for deployment.

Flow Efficiency reveals this hidden waste.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Suppose you visit a hospital for a blood test.

Timeline:

9:00 AM Arrive

9:20 AM Registration

9:50 AM Waiting

10:10 AM Blood Sample (5 minutes)

10:15 AM Waiting

11:00 AM Doctor Review (10 minutes)

11:10 AM Leave

Total Time:

2 hours 10 minutes (130 minutes)

Actual medical work:

  • Blood sample = 5 minutes

  • Doctor review = 10 minutes

Total active work:

15 minutes

Most of your visit was spent waiting.

This is exactly what Flow Efficiency measures.

4. Technical Explanation

Formula:

Flow Efficiency = (Active Working Time ÷ Total Elapsed Time) × 100%

Example:

User Story:

Total elapsed time:

10 days

Actual work:

4 days

Calculation:

(4 ÷ 10) × 100

= 40%

Flow Efficiency:

40%

Meaning:

The work item spent 60% of its time waiting.

Legend:

  • █ = Active work

  • ░ = Waiting

Even though the story took 5 days, only 2 days involved actual work.

17. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1

Assuming low Flow Efficiency means developers are slow.

Reality:

The process may be inefficient.

Mistake 2

Trying to increase working hours.

Better approach:

Reduce waiting.

Mistake 3

Ignoring dependency queues.

Many delays happen outside the development team.

18. Best Practices

✔ Track waiting reasons.

✔ Reduce handoffs.

✔ Review bottlenecks every Sprint Retrospective.

✔ Improve automation.

✔ Measure trends, not one-off numbers.

19. Interview Questions

Q1. What is Flow Efficiency?

Answer:

Flow Efficiency measures the percentage of total elapsed time during which work is actively being performed on a work item.

Q2. How is Flow Efficiency calculated?

Answer:

Flow Efficiency = (Active Working Time ÷ Total Elapsed Time) × 100%.

Q3. What causes low Flow Efficiency?

Answer:

Waiting for approvals, dependencies, code reviews, testing, or deployment.

Q4. How can a Product Manager improve Flow Efficiency?

Answer:

By reducing waiting time, prioritizing effectively, removing bottlenecks, and supporting process improvements rather than simply increasing team workload.

Key Takeaways

  1. Flow Efficiency measures how much time is spent working versus waiting.

  2. High waiting time is usually a process problem, not a people problem.

Lesson 81: Escaped Defects (Deep Dive)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Analyst • Product Manager • Scrum Master • QA • AI Product Manager

If Velocity tells you how fast you\'re delivering, Escaped Defects tell you whether you\'re delivering quality.

A team can have excellent Velocity and terrible quality. High-performing Agile teams optimize both speed and quality.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Escaped Defects are.

  • Why they matter.

  • How to measure them.

  • How to reduce them.

  • The role of BAs, Product Managers, Scrum Masters, Developers, and QA.

  • Real Healthcare and AI examples.

  • Interview scenarios and Jira usage.

1. Concept

What is an Escaped Defect?

Simple Definition

An Escaped Defect is a bug that was not found during development or testing and reaches the customer or production environment.

In simple words:

A defect that \"escaped\" your quality process.

2. Why Does This Metric Exist?

Imagine your team says:

\"We delivered every Sprint on time.\"

Great!

But one week later:

Customers complain:

  • Login doesn\'t work.

  • AI gives incorrect answers.

  • Reports are missing data.

The team delivered quickly, but poor quality.

Escaped Defects help answer:

\"How many problems reached our users?\"

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a pharmaceutical company manufactures tablets.

Quality checks happen before shipping.

If damaged tablets reach pharmacies:

The quality process failed.

The damaged tablets are like Escaped Defects.

4. Technical Explanation

Typical software flow:

Requirements

│

▼

Development

│

▼

Code Review

│

▼

Testing

│

▼

Release

│

▼

Customer

If a bug is found:

  • During Development ✅

  • During Testing ✅

It is not an escaped defect.

If the customer finds it after release ❌

It is an Escaped Defect.

5. Example

Feature:

AI PDF Upload

Bug:

Large PDF files fail to upload.

Timeline:

Development

↓

Testing

↓

Release

↓

Customer uploads 50MB PDF

↓

System crashes

This bug escaped testing.

Therefore:

Escaped Defect = Yes

6. Formula

There are different ways organizations measure Escaped Defects.

Method 1: Count

Example:

Production bugs this Sprint:

Method 2: Percentage

Formula:

Escaped Defect Rate =

(Production Defects ÷ Total Defects) × 100%

Example:

Total defects found:

100

Production defects:

8

Calculation:

8 ÷ 100 × 100

= 8%

Escaped Defect Rate:

8%

7. Healthcare Example

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Feature:

Automatic MedDRA Coding

Bug:

\"Nausea\"

as

\"Vomiting\"

The testing team missed it.

PV Associates discover the issue after release.

Impact:

  • Incorrect safety database.

  • Incorrect regulatory submissions.

  • Potential compliance risk.

This is a High-Severity Escaped Defect.

8. AI Product Example

Project:

Medical AI Chatbot

Question:

\"Can I take Drug A and Drug B together?\"

The AI incorrectly answers:

\"Yes\"

The correct answer should have warned about a serious interaction.

The bug was not detected before release.

Consequences:

  • Patient safety risk.

  • Loss of user trust.

  • Possible legal issues.

This is a Critical Escaped Defect.

9. Types of Escaped Defects

Functional

Feature doesn\'t work.

Example:

Login button fails.

Performance

System is too slow.

Example:

Dashboard loads in 60 seconds.

Security

Sensitive data exposed.

Example:

Patient records visible without authorization.

Usability

Confusing interface.

Example:

Users cannot find the Submit button.

Data

Incorrect calculations.

Example:

Wrong dosage displayed.

AI

Incorrect AI predictions.

Example:

Hallucinated medical advice.

10. Severity vs Priority

These are often confused.

Severity

How serious is the impact?

Examples:

  • System crash

  • Data loss

  • Wrong diagnosis

Priority

How quickly should we fix it?

Examples:

  • High

  • Medium

  • Low

Example:

Typo on homepage.

Severity:

Low

Priority:

High (because every customer sees it)

11. Root Cause Analysis

Instead of asking:

\"Who made the mistake?\"

Ask:

\"Why did this defect escape?\"

Possible reasons:

  • Poor requirements.

  • Missing acceptance criteria.

  • Incomplete testing.

  • Lack of automation.

  • Last-minute changes.

  • Communication gaps.

  • AI model limitations.

13. Role Responsibilities

Reduce defects by:

  • Writing clear requirements.

  • Defining acceptance criteria.

  • Clarifying business rules.

  • Validating stakeholder expectations.

Focus on:

  • Prioritizing defect fixes.

  • Balancing new features vs quality.

Scrum Master

Ensure:

  • Root Cause Analysis during Retrospectives.

  • Process improvements.

  • Better collaboration.

Developers

Responsibilities:

  • Unit testing.

  • Code reviews.

  • Following coding standards.

QA Engineers

Responsibilities:

  • Test planning.

  • Regression testing.

  • Exploratory testing.

  • Automation.

16. Common Causes

  • Incomplete requirements.

  • Ambiguous acceptance criteria.

  • Insufficient testing.

  • Manual testing only.

  • Tight deadlines.

  • Lack of regression testing.

  • Weak code reviews.

  • Poor communication.

17. How to Reduce Escaped Defects

Better User Stories

Clear requirements reduce misunderstandings.

Strong Acceptance Criteria

Developers know exactly what \"done\" means.

Automated Testing

Run regression tests every release.

Code Reviews

Catch issues early.

Shift Left Testing

Start testing earlier.

Frequent Releases

Smaller releases reduce risk.

Root Cause Analysis

Improve the process after each escaped defect.

18. Healthcare Best Practices

For healthcare software:

  • Clinical validation.

  • Regulatory review.

  • Audit trails.

  • Data verification.

  • Medical SME testing.

  • Risk-based testing.

Quality is not optional.

19. AI Product Considerations

AI products require additional validation:

  • Hallucination testing.

  • Bias testing.

  • Safety testing.

  • Prompt testing.

  • Model evaluation.

  • Human review for critical decisions.

Some AI errors are not traditional software bugs, but they still affect users and should be monitored.

20. Interview Questions

Q1. What is an Escaped Defect?

Answer:

A defect discovered by users after the software has been released to production.

Q2. Why is it important?

Answer:

It measures the effectiveness of the development and testing process and highlights quality issues that reached customers.

Q3. How can a Business Analyst reduce Escaped Defects?

Answer:

By gathering complete requirements, writing clear user stories, defining strong acceptance criteria, and validating business rules with stakeholders.

Q4. What should a Scrum Team do after a critical escaped defect?

Answer:

Fix the issue, perform Root Cause Analysis, discuss it in the Retrospective, and implement process improvements to prevent recurrence.

Today we learned:

  • How they differ from defects found during testing.

  • Why they are a key quality metric.

  1. Escaped Defects are bugs discovered after release.

  2. Quality is a shared responsibility across the Scrum Team.

Lesson 82: Sprint Predictability (Deep Dive)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Analyst • Product Manager • Scrum Master • Product Owner • Engineering Manager

Sprint Predictability answers one of the most important business questions:

\"Can this team reliably deliver what they plan?\"

Managers don\'t expect perfection---they value consistency and reliable forecasting.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Sprint Predictability is.

  • Why it\'s more important than high Velocity.

  • How to calculate it.

  • Why teams miss Sprint Goals.

  • How Product Managers use Predictability.

  • How Scrum Masters improve it.

  • How Jira measures Sprint Predictability.

1. Concept

What is Sprint Predictability?

Simple Definition

Sprint Predictability measures how consistently a Scrum Team delivers the work it committed to during Sprint Planning.

It answers:

\"Did we deliver what we said we would?\"

2. Why Does Sprint Predictability Exist?

Imagine you are a Product Manager.

You tell the CEO:

\"The AI Duplicate Detection feature will be ready this Sprint.\"

Sprint ends.

Feature is only 50% complete.

Now:

  • Customers wait.

  • Release plans change.

  • Stakeholders lose confidence.

The issue isn\'t just that work is unfinished---it\'s that the forecast was unreliable.

Sprint Predictability helps improve trust.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a courier company.

Every day they promise:

\"We will deliver 100 packages.\"

Scenario A:

Day Promised Delivered

Monday 100 99

Tuesday 100 101

Wednesday 100 98

Very predictable.

Scenario B:

Day Promised Delivered

Monday 100 45

Tuesday 100 140

Wednesday 100 70

Average deliveries may still be close to 100, but customers cannot rely on them.

Consistency matters.

4. Technical Explanation

Formula:

Sprint Predictability (%) =

(Completed Story Points ÷ Committed Story Points) × 100

Example:

Sprint Planning:

Committed:

40 Story Points

Sprint End:

Completed:

36 Story Points

Calculation:

36 ÷ 40 × 100

= 90%

Sprint Predictability:

90%

5. Another Example

Sprint Commitment:

50 Story Points

Completed:

50 Story Points

Predictability:

50 ÷ 50 ×100

=100%

Excellent predictability.

Now another Sprint:

Committed:

60

Completed:

30

Predictability:

30 ÷60 ×100

=50%

This indicates unreliable planning or execution.

│

▼

Committed

40 Points

│

▼

Sprint Work

│

▼

Completed

36 Points

│

▼

Predictability

7. Why Predictability Matters More Than Velocity

Consider two teams.

Team Alpha

Velocity:

60

Predictability:

45%

Team Beta

Velocity:

35

Predictability:

95%

Which team would a Product Manager prefer?

Usually Team Beta.

Why?

Because reliable forecasting enables:

  • Better release planning.

  • Better stakeholder communication.

  • Better customer commitments.

A fast but unpredictable team creates planning problems.

  • AI PDF Upload

  • MedDRA Search

  • Duplicate Detection

Questions to investigate:

  • Were requirements unclear?

  • Did priorities change?

  • Were developers unavailable?

  • Were stories underestimated?

  • Were there external dependencies?

Discussion:

10. What Affects Sprint Predictability?

Unrealistic Sprint Planning

Taking too much work.

Poor Estimation

Story Points don\'t reflect actual complexity.

Scope Changes

New work added mid-Sprint.

Team Absence

Unexpected leave.

Dependencies

Waiting for another team.

Technical Debt

Unexpected refactoring.

Production Support

Developers pulled away for urgent incidents.

Velocity Predictability

Measures completed work Measures forecasting accuracy

Story Points Percentage

Velocity:

40

Higher Velocity doesn\'t necessarily mean better performance.

12. Sprint Goal vs Sprint Predictability

Suppose the Sprint Goal is:

\"Enable AI to extract patient demographics.\"

Stories:

  • PDF Upload

  • Patient Name Extraction

  • Age Detection

  • Gender Detection

If only PDF Upload is completed:

Story completion may look acceptable.

Sprint Goal is not achieved.

Modern Scrum emphasizes Sprint Goal achievement, not just Story Point completion.

13. How Scrum Masters Improve Predictability

  • Better Sprint Planning.

  • Remove blockers quickly.

  • Protect the Sprint from unnecessary scope changes.

  • Improve estimation skills.

  • Facilitate Retrospectives.

  • Encourage smaller user stories.

14. How Product Owners Improve Predictability

  • Prioritize effectively.

  • Clarify requirements.

  • Avoid changing priorities during the Sprint.

  • Prepare backlog items before Sprint Planning.

15. How Business Analysts Improve Predictability

Business Analysts contribute by:

  • Writing complete user stories.

  • Defining clear acceptance criteria.

  • Resolving stakeholder questions early.

  • Reducing requirement ambiguity.

Better requirements reduce surprises.

16. Jira Example

A Scrum Master may notice frequent mid-Sprint additions and discuss this during the Retrospective.

17. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1

Trying to achieve 100% every Sprint.

Reality:

Unexpected events happen.

A consistent range (for example, around 85--100%) is often healthier than forcing perfection.

Mistake 2

Adding work during the Sprint.

Frequent additions reduce predictability.

Mistake 3

Overcommitting.

Teams sometimes commit to impress stakeholders.

Result:

Missed Sprint Goals.

Mistake 4

Measuring individuals.

Sprint Predictability belongs to the team, not to a single developer.

18. Best Practices

✔ Use historical Velocity during Sprint Planning.

✔ Keep stories small.

✔ Avoid changing Sprint scope.

✔ Prepare backlog items before Sprint Planning.

✔ Analyze missed commitments during Retrospectives.

✔ Focus on delivering the Sprint Goal.

19. Interview Questions

Q1. What is Sprint Predictability?

Answer:

Sprint Predictability measures how consistently a Scrum Team delivers the work it committed to during Sprint Planning.

Q2. Why is Sprint Predictability important?

Answer:

It builds trust with stakeholders, improves forecasting, and supports more reliable release planning.

Q3. Can a team have high Velocity but poor Predictability?

Answer:

Yes. A team may complete a lot of work overall but frequently miss what it originally committed to.

Q4. How can Sprint Predictability be improved?

Answer:

By improving estimation, keeping user stories small, reducing scope changes, preparing the backlog well, and removing impediments quickly.

22. Lesson Summary

Today we learned:

  • What Sprint Predictability is.

  • How to calculate it.

  • Why consistency is more valuable than occasional high output.

  • The relationship between Velocity, Sprint Goals, and Predictability.

  • How each Agile role contributes to improving predictability.

Key Takeaways

  1. Sprint Predictability measures how reliably a team delivers its Sprint commitment.

  2. Reliable teams are easier to plan around than simply fast teams.

  3. Stable Sprint scope and good backlog preparation improve predictability.

  4. Focus on achieving the Sprint Goal, not just maximizing Story Points.

  5. Use Sprint Predictability to improve planning---not to blame the team.

Lesson 83: Burndown Chart (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Owner • Scrum Master • Product Manager • Engineering Manager

The Burndown Chart is one of the most recognized Agile charts.

However, many people know how to look at it but not how to interpret it. In interviews, you\'re often shown a Burndown Chart and asked:

What is a Burndown Chart?

Simple Definition

A Burndown Chart is a graph that shows how much work remains in the Sprint over time.

Imagine you\'re halfway through a two-week Sprint.

\"Are we likely to finish all planned work?\"

Without a Burndown Chart:

With a Burndown Chart:

  • You can see the trend.

  • You can identify risks early.

  • You can take corrective action before the Sprint ends.

Instead of remaining distance, it tracks remaining work.

Using the Burndown Chart to judge individual developers.

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Owner • Product Manager • Scrum Master • Engineering Manager

Many experienced Product Managers prefer Burnup Charts over Burndown Charts because they clearly show both progress and scope changes.

If your CEO asks:

\"Why isn\'t the release finished yet?\"

Learning Objectives

1. Concept

What is a Burnup Chart?

Simple Definition

A Burnup Chart is a graph that shows:

  1. How much work has been completed (Completed Work Line)

  2. How much total work exists (Total Scope Line)

A Burnup Chart shows:

Lesson 85: Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD) (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Manager • Scrum Master • Engineering Manager • Agile Coach

If the Burndown Chart tells you \"Are we finishing work?\", the Cumulative Flow Diagram tells you \"How is work flowing through the system?\"

Companies like Amazon, Microsoft, Spotify, Atlassian, and many large healthcare organizations use CFDs to identify bottlenecks before they become major problems.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what a Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD) is.

  • Read every part of a CFD.

  • Identify bottlenecks.

  • Detect excessive Work in Progress (WIP).

  • Understand the relationship between CFD, Lead Time, Cycle Time, and Throughput.

  • Use CFDs in Jira and Azure DevOps.

  • Answer CFD interview questions confidently.

1. Concept

What is a Cumulative Flow Diagram?

Simple Definition

A Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD) is a chart that shows how work moves through different stages of your workflow over time.

Unlike a Burndown Chart, which focuses on remaining work, a CFD shows:

  • How much work is waiting.

  • How much work is in progress.

  • How much work is completed.

  • Whether work is flowing smoothly.

2. Why Does CFD Exist?

Imagine your Product Manager says:

\"We completed only 15 stories this Sprint.\"

The next question is:

\"Why?\"

Possible reasons:

  • Too much work waiting.

  • Testing is overloaded.

  • Code reviews are delayed.

  • Developers started too many tasks.

A CFD helps answer these questions visually.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a hospital emergency department.

Patients move through stages:

Registration

↓

Doctor Assessment

↓

Lab Tests

↓

Treatment

↓

Discharge

If many patients are waiting for lab tests, the queue grows.

This indicates a bottleneck in the lab---not that doctors are working slowly.

A CFD works exactly the same way for software delivery.

4. Technical Explanation

A CFD tracks the number of work items in each workflow state.

Example workflow:

To Do

↓

In Progress

↓

Code Review

↓

Testing

↓

Done

Each stage is represented by a colored band (or layer) on the chart.

The height of each band shows how many items are in that stage.

5. Anatomy of a CFD

Number of Work Items

40 |████████████████████████ Done

35 |██████████████████ Testing

30 |██████████████ Code Review

25 |██████████ In Progress

20 |██████ To Do

+------------------------------------>

Week1 Week2 Week3 Week4 Week5

Each colored layer represents one workflow stage.

The total height represents all work items in the system.

Wide Band

Warning.

Too much work is waiting in testing.

Possible causes:

  • Too few testers.

  • Manual testing delays.

  • Complex regression testing.

  • Are requirements causing rework?

  • Is QA overloaded?

10. What Can a CFD Tell You?

Bottlenecks

Stable Flow

Good sign.

In Progress

14. CFD and Throughput

A flat \"Done\" band suggests work is not being completed.

During Sprint Reviews or Retrospectives, the Scrum Team can discuss:

  • Which stage is growing?

  • Why is work waiting?

  • How can we improve flow?

18. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1

Looking only at the \"Done\" band.

You should examine every stage.

Mistake 2

Ignoring growing queues.

Large queues often mean hidden delays.

Mistake 3

Treating a CFD as a productivity chart.

A CFD measures flow, not individual performance.

Mistake 4

Trying to maximize WIP.

Starting more work rarely improves delivery.

Finishing work does.

19. Best Practices

✔ Limit Work in Progress.

✔ Monitor bottlenecks regularly.

✔ Keep workflow stages clearly defined.

✔ Automate repetitive steps where possible.

✔ Review CFDs during Retrospectives.

✔ Combine CFDs with Lead Time and Throughput metrics.

20. Interview Questions

Q1. What is a Cumulative Flow Diagram?

Answer:

A CFD is a visualization showing the number of work items in each workflow stage over time, helping teams understand flow and identify bottlenecks.

Q2. What does a widening band indicate?

Q3. Why is a CFD useful?

Answer:

It helps teams monitor flow, identify delays, manage WIP, and improve overall delivery efficiency.

Q4. How does a CFD differ from a Burndown Chart?

Answer:

A Burndown Chart shows remaining work over time, while a CFD shows how work is distributed across workflow stages and highlights bottlenecks.

Lesson 86: Throughput (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Manager • Scrum Master • Agile Coach • Engineering Manager

Throughput answers one simple but powerful question:

\"How many work items does the team complete in a given period?\"

Unlike Velocity, Throughput doesn\'t care about Story Points. It focuses on finished work, making it especially useful in Kanban, Lean, DevOps, and AI product teams.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what Throughput is.

  • Calculate Throughput.

  • Differentiate Throughput from Velocity.

  • Use Throughput for forecasting.

  • Understand its role in Scrum and Kanban.

  • Learn the basics of Monte Carlo Forecasting.

  • Apply Throughput to Healthcare and AI projects.

  • Answer common interview questions.

1. Concept

What is Throughput?

Simple Definition

Throughput is the number of work items completed in a specific period of time.

It answers:

\"How many items did we finish?\"

Notice that Throughput measures count, not size.

2. Why Does Throughput Exist?

Imagine two Scrum teams.

Team A

Completed:

  • 8 User Stories

Team B

Completed:

  • 16 User Stories

At first glance, Team B seems faster.

But what if:

  • Team A completed eight large stories.

  • Team B completed sixteen very small stories.

Throughput only tells you how many items were completed, not how complex they were.

That is why Throughput and Velocity are complementary metrics.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a pharmacy.

During one day:

  • 150 prescriptions are filled.

The pharmacist doesn\'t measure:

  • How complex each prescription was.

They simply measure:

How many prescriptions were completed today?

That is Throughput.

4. Technical Explanation

Formula:

Throughput = Number of Completed Work Items

Time period examples:

  • Per day

  • Per week

  • Per Sprint

  • Per month

Example

Sprint:

2 weeks

Completed:

Work Item Status

Login Done

Dashboard Done

Reports Done

PDF Upload Done

AI Extraction Done

Throughput:

5 work items

5. Throughput vs Velocity

Throughput Velocity

Counts completed items Counts Story Points completed

Doesn\'t consider complexity Reflects estimated complexity

Common in Kanban Common in Scrum

Easier to calculate Requires estimation

Useful for flow Useful for Sprint planning

Example

Sprint A:

Story Story Points

Login 3

Dashboard 8

Reports 5

Throughput:

3 stories

Velocity:

16 Story Points

Both metrics describe the same Sprint from different perspectives.

6. Healthcare Example

Project:

Hospital Management System

Completed this week:

  • Patient Registration

  • Appointment Booking

  • Billing

  • Lab Results

  • Doctor Schedule

Throughput:

5 features

Even if one feature was much larger than another, Throughput simply counts completed items.

7. Pharmacovigilance Example

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Completed this Sprint:

  • Duplicate Detection

  • MedDRA Coding

  • WHO Drug Coding

  • PDF Upload

  • Audit Trail

  • User Management

Throughput:

6 completed work items

The Product Manager can compare this with previous Sprints to understand delivery trends.

8. AI Product Example

Project:

Medical AI Chatbot

Completed:

  • Prompt Improvement

  • Response Logging

  • Feedback Screen

  • Hallucination Detection

  • Voice Input

Throughput:

5 completed features

If the team consistently completes around five items per Sprint, that becomes useful for forecasting.

9. Throughput Trend

Suppose a team\'s Throughput over six Sprints is:

Sprint Throughput

1 5

2 6

3 5

4 7

5 6

6 5

Average Throughput:

(5 + 6 + 5 + 7 + 6 + 5) ÷ 6

= 5.67

You might forecast that the team will complete around 5--6 items per Sprint, assuming work items are of similar size.

10. Throughput and Forecasting

Suppose your backlog contains:

40 user stories.

Average Throughput:

5 stories per Sprint.

Estimated number of Sprints:

40 ÷ 5 = 8 Sprints

Remember:

This is an estimate, not a guarantee.

Changes in scope, team capacity, or story size can affect the outcome.

11. Introduction to Monte Carlo Forecasting

Many modern Agile tools use Monte Carlo Simulation for forecasting.

Instead of asking:

\"Exactly when will we finish?\"

It asks:

\"Based on our historical delivery, what is the most likely completion window?\"

Simple Analogy

Imagine tossing a coin thousands of times.

You can\'t predict the next toss with certainty.

But you can estimate probabilities.

Monte Carlo uses the same idea with historical delivery data.

Example

Historical Throughput:

  • Sprint 1 = 5

  • Sprint 2 = 6

  • Sprint 3 = 4

  • Sprint 4 = 7

  • Sprint 5 = 5

Instead of saying:

\"The release will finish in exactly 8 Sprints.\"

Monte Carlo may estimate:

  • 70% probability: Finished within 8 Sprints.

  • 90% probability: Finished within 9 Sprints.

This helps Product Managers communicate uncertainty more honestly.

12. Scrum vs Kanban

Scrum

Primary metric:

Velocity

Secondary metric:

Throughput

Kanban

Primary metric:

Throughput

Because Kanban teams often do not estimate Story Points, Throughput becomes one of the main measures of delivery.

13. Jira Example

Jira dashboards can show:

Sprint Completed Issues

Sprint 1 12

Sprint 2 14

Sprint 3 13

Sprint 4 15

A Scrum Master can identify trends:

  • Stable Throughput

  • Increasing Throughput

  • Declining Throughput

The focus should be on understanding why, not simply expecting higher numbers every Sprint.

14. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1

Comparing Throughput between different teams.

Different teams:

  • Build different products.

  • Handle different complexity.

  • Define work items differently.

Direct comparisons are often misleading.

Mistake 2

Ignoring work item size.

Completing:

  • 10 tiny tasks

is not necessarily better than completing:

  • 3 large, high-value features.

Mistake 3

Chasing higher Throughput.

Teams may split work into many tiny tickets just to increase the metric.

This creates misleading data.

Mistake 4

Using Throughput to evaluate individuals.

Throughput is a team metric, not a personal performance measure.

15. Best Practices

✔ Track Throughput over multiple Sprints.

✔ Combine Throughput with Lead Time and Cycle Time.

✔ Keep work items reasonably consistent in size.

✔ Use Throughput for forecasting, not competition.

✔ Discuss unusual changes during Retrospectives.

16. Interview Questions

Q1. What is Throughput?

Answer:

Throughput is the number of work items completed during a specific period of time.

Q2. How does Throughput differ from Velocity?

Answer:

Throughput counts completed work items, while Velocity measures completed Story Points.

Q3. Why is Throughput important in Kanban?

Answer:

Kanban often doesn\'t use Story Points, so Throughput provides a simple measure of delivery and supports forecasting.

Q4. Can Throughput alone measure team performance?

Answer:

No. It should be interpreted alongside metrics such as Lead Time, Cycle Time, quality metrics, and business value delivered.

17. Mini Quiz

Q1.

Throughput measures:

A. Story Points

B. Completed work items

C. Team size

Q2.

A team completes 8 user stories this Sprint.

Their Throughput is:

A. 8 Story Points

B. 8 work items

C. 16 work items

Q3.

Which framework relies more heavily on Throughput?

A. Kanban

B. Scrum

C. Waterfall

Q4.

True or False:

Throughput should be used to compare individual developer performance.

18. Practical Assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, assume the following completed work items over five Sprints:

Sprint Completed Items

1 6

2 5

3 7

4 6

5 8

Now answer:

  1. What is the average Throughput?

  2. If 36 user stories remain, how many Sprints would you estimate are needed?

  3. What factors could make your estimate inaccurate?

  4. Would you communicate this as a fixed date or as a forecast range? Why?

19. Lesson Summary

Today we learned:

  • What Throughput is.

  • How it differs from Velocity.

  • Why Throughput is central to Kanban.

  • How Throughput supports forecasting.

  • The basics of Monte Carlo Forecasting.

  • Healthcare, Pharmacovigilance, and AI examples.

  • Best practices and common pitfalls.

Key Takeaways

  1. Throughput counts completed work items over time.

  2. It complements Velocity by focusing on quantity rather than estimated effort.

  3. Throughput is a core metric in Kanban and Lean environments.

  4. Historical Throughput helps forecast future delivery, especially when work items are similarly sized.

  5. Use Throughput to improve planning---not to compare teams or individuals.

Lesson 87: Work in Progress (WIP) (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Manager • Scrum Master • Agile Coach • Engineering Manager

One of the biggest mistakes Agile teams make is starting too much work instead of finishing work.

High-performing companies like Amazon, Microsoft, Spotify, Toyota, and many healthcare organizations focus on limiting Work in Progress (WIP) because it improves flow, quality, and predictability.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Understand what Work in Progress (WIP) is.

  • Learn why limiting WIP improves delivery.

  • Understand Little\'s Law (in simple terms).

  • Use WIP limits in Kanban and Scrum.

  • Relate WIP to Lead Time, Cycle Time, Throughput, and Flow Efficiency.

  • Apply WIP concepts to Healthcare, Pharmacovigilance, and AI products.

  • Answer common interview questions.

1. Concept

What is Work in Progress (WIP)?

Simple Definition

Work in Progress (WIP) is the amount of work that has been started but not yet completed.

Think of WIP as unfinished work.

2. Why Does WIP Exist?

Imagine a developer starts:

  • Login

  • Dashboard

  • Reports

  • Notifications

  • AI Module

All at the same time.

After one week:

Nothing is finished.

Customers receive zero value.

Now imagine another developer:

  • Starts Login.

  • Finishes Login.

  • Starts Dashboard.

  • Finishes Dashboard.

Customers begin receiving usable features much sooner.

This is why Agile emphasizes finishing before starting more work.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine you\'re cooking dinner.

Scenario A:

You start:

  • Rice

  • Curry

  • Chapati

  • Dessert

  • Soup

Everything is half done.

Dinner isn\'t ready.

Scenario B:

You prepare:

  1. Rice ✔

  2. Curry ✔

  3. Chapati ✔

  4. Soup ✔

  5. Dessert ✔

The meal is ready sooner, with less confusion.

The second approach keeps WIP low.

4. Technical Explanation

Example Kanban Board:

+------------+---------------+-----------+------+

| To Do | In Progress | Testing | Done |

+------------+---------------+-----------+------+

| Login | Dashboard | Reports | PDF |

| Billing | AI Search | | |

| Audit | | | |

+------------+---------------+-----------+------+

Here:

  • In Progress = 2 items

  • Testing = 1 item

Current WIP = 3

5. Why High WIP is Dangerous

Imagine:

To Do

↓

Development

↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓↓

20 Stories

↓

Testing

↓

Done

Developers start many stories.

Testing becomes overloaded.

Nothing gets completed.

Result:

  • Longer Lead Time.

  • Lower Flow Efficiency.

  • Poor Sprint Predictability.

  • Increased defects.

6. Low WIP Example

Development

Story 1

↓

Testing

↓

Done

↓

Story 2

Only a few items are active.

Benefits:

  • Faster completion.

  • Easier tracking.

  • Better quality.

  • Reduced context switching.

7. Healthcare Example

Project:

Hospital Management System

Poor WIP:

The team starts:

  • Patient Registration

  • Billing

  • Appointments

  • Pharmacy

  • Insurance

All remain incomplete.

Doctors cannot use any feature.

Better approach:

Complete:

  • Patient Registration

Release it.

Then continue with Billing.

Users receive value sooner.

8. Pharmacovigilance Example

Project:

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Instead of building all modules simultaneously:

  • Login

  • MedDRA Coding

  • WHO Drug Coding

  • Duplicate Detection

  • Signal Detection

The team finishes:

  • Login

  • PDF Upload

  • Basic MedDRA Coding

First.

This enables early user feedback and reduces integration risk.

9. AI Product Example

Project:

Medical AI Chatbot

Poor WIP:

Working simultaneously on:

  • Voice Input

  • Translation

  • Image Analysis

  • Hallucination Detection

  • Analytics

None are finished.

Better WIP:

Finish:

  • Hallucination Detection

Deploy.

Gather feedback.

Then begin Voice Input.

10. WIP Limits

Kanban introduces WIP Limits.

Example:

In Progress (Limit = 3)

✔ Login

✔ Dashboard

✔ Reports

No more work may enter this column until one item leaves.

This encourages teams to finish existing work before starting new work.

11. Why WIP Limits Improve Delivery

Benefits include:

  • Shorter Lead Time.

  • Better Flow Efficiency.

  • Higher Throughput.

  • Fewer defects.

  • Less multitasking.

  • Better collaboration.

12. Little\'s Law (Simple Explanation)

Little\'s Law is a foundational concept in Lean and Kanban.

Formula

Lead Time = WIP ÷ Throughput

Where:

  • Lead Time = Time from request to completion.

  • WIP = Number of items in progress.

  • Throughput = Number of items completed per unit of time.

Example

Suppose:

  • WIP = 20 stories

  • Throughput = 5 stories per week

Lead Time:

20 ÷ 5 = 4 weeks

Now reduce WIP:

  • WIP = 10

  • Throughput = 5

Lead Time:

10 ÷ 5 = 2 weeks

Reducing WIP often reduces Lead Time.

Note: Little\'s Law assumes a relatively stable system with consistent arrival and completion rates. It\'s a useful guide, not an exact prediction for every project.

13. Relationship with Other Metrics

Metric Relationship with WIP

Lead Time Higher WIP often increases Lead Time

Cycle Time Excessive WIP can increase Cycle Time

Throughput Moderate WIP can support stable Throughput, but excessive WIP often hurts it

Flow Efficiency Lower WIP generally improves Flow Efficiency

Sprint Lower WIP often improves Predictability Predictability

14. WIP in Scrum

Scrum does not require formal WIP limits.

However, Scrum Teams often apply the same principle:

Instead of:

10 stories started

1 finished

Aim for:

3 stories started

3 stories finished

This supports the Sprint Goal and creates more frequent progress.

15. Jira Example

Jira Kanban Board:

In Progress (Limit = 4)

Login

Dashboard

Reports

AI Search

When four items are already in progress:

No new work should enter until one is completed.

Some teams configure Jira to highlight WIP limit violations.

16. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1

Believing busy people mean productive teams.

Reality:

Many active tasks can hide slow delivery.

Mistake 2

Starting new work whenever someone becomes free.

Sometimes it\'s better to help finish existing work.

Mistake 3

Ignoring bottlenecks.

If Testing is overloaded, adding more work to Development usually makes the problem worse.

Mistake 4

Using WIP limits as rigid rules.

WIP limits should encourage healthy flow, not prevent urgent work when exceptions are justified.

17. Best Practices

✔ Finish work before starting new work.

✔ Set realistic WIP limits.

✔ Keep user stories small.

✔ Swarm on blocked work (have team members collaborate to finish it).

✔ Monitor bottlenecks regularly.

✔ Review WIP during Daily Scrums.

18. Interview Questions

Q1. What is Work in Progress (WIP)?

Answer:

WIP is the number of work items that have been started but are not yet completed.

Q2. Why are WIP limits important?

Answer:

They help reduce multitasking, improve flow, shorten Lead Time, and encourage teams to finish work before starting more.

Q3. What is Little\'s Law?

Answer:

Little\'s Law relates Lead Time, Work in Progress, and Throughput:

Lead Time = WIP ÷ Throughput (under stable system conditions).

Q4. Does Scrum require WIP limits?

Answer:

No. WIP limits are a core Kanban practice, but Scrum Teams often adopt similar principles to improve flow.

19. Mini Quiz

Q1.

WIP stands for:

A. Work in Progress

B. Work Improvement Plan

C. Weekly Improvement Process

Q2.

High WIP usually leads to:

A. Shorter Lead Time

B. More multitasking and longer Lead Time

C. Automatically higher Velocity

Q3.

According to Little\'s Law, if Throughput stays the same and WIP decreases, Lead Time will generally:

A. Increase

B. Decrease

C. Stay exactly the same in every situation

Q4.

True or False:

A team should always start as many tasks as possible to maximize productivity.

20. Practical Assignment

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform, imagine this Kanban board:

Stage Items

To Do 12

Development 8

Testing 7

Done 5

Answer:

  1. What is the current WIP?

  2. Which stage appears to be the bottleneck?

  3. If the Development WIP limit is 5, what action should the team take?

  4. As a Scrum Master or Product Manager, what process improvements would you suggest?

21. Lesson Summary

Today we learned:

  • What Work in Progress (WIP) is.

  • Why limiting WIP improves delivery.

  • The basics of Little\'s Law.

  • The relationship between WIP and other Agile metrics.

  • How WIP limits work in Kanban and can benefit Scrum teams.

  • Practical examples from Healthcare, Pharmacovigilance, and AI products.

Key Takeaways

  1. WIP is work that has started but is not yet finished.

  2. High WIP often creates delays, bottlenecks, and lower quality.

  3. Limiting WIP improves flow, focus, and predictability.

  4. Little\'s Law links WIP, Throughput, and Lead Time.

  5. Successful Agile teams prioritize finishing work over starting more work.

Lesson 88: Interpreting Agile Metrics & Charts Together (Advanced Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Manager • Scrum Master • Agile Coach

In real organizations, nobody looks at one metric alone.

A senior Agile professional does not say:

\"Velocity decreased, so the team is bad.\"

Instead, they connect multiple signals:

Velocity + Burndown + CFD + Lead Time + Cycle Time + Throughput + Quality Metrics

and understand the complete story.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will learn:

  • Why one Agile metric is never enough.

  • How to combine metrics for decision-making.

  • How Scrum Masters analyze team health.

  • How Product Managers use metrics for forecasting.

  • How to interpret common chart patterns.

  • Healthcare and AI product examples.

  • Interview-level scenario analysis.

1. Concept

What does \"Interpreting Metrics Together\" mean?

It means:

Instead of asking:

\"What does this one chart show?\"

We ask:

\"What story are all metrics telling together?\"

Example:

Velocity decreased.

Is that bad?

Not necessarily.

Maybe:

  • Story quality improved.

  • Defects reduced.

  • Team spent time fixing technical debt.

One metric alone can mislead.

2. Why Does This Exist?

Agile metrics are signals, not answers.

A metric tells you:

\"Something is happening.\"

It does not automatically tell:

\"Why it is happening.\"

The Agile professional investigates the reason.

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine a patient\'s health report.

Doctor does not look only at:

  • Temperature

They check:

  • Blood pressure

  • Heart rate

  • Blood tests

  • Symptoms

  • Medical history

One value is not enough.

Agile metrics work the same way.

4. Agile Metrics Relationship Map

BUSINESS VALUE

|

|

Product Outcomes

|

--------------------------------

| |

Delivery Flow Quality

| |

| |

Velocity Escaped Defects

Throughput Test Quality

Cycle Time

Lead Time

|

|

WIP

|

|

CFD

5. Scenario 1: Velocity Decreased

Situation

Previous Sprint:

Velocity = 40 points

Current Sprint:

Velocity = 25 points

A manager says:

\"The team performance dropped.\"

Should we agree?

No.

Let\'s investigate.

Check Other Metrics

Burndown

Healthy?

✅ Yes

Work finished continuously.

Escaped Defects

Reduced:

20 → 5

Good.

Cycle Time

Reduced:

8 days → 4 days

Good.

Interpretation

The team may have delivered better quality with smaller stories.

Velocity reduction is not necessarily a problem.

6. Scenario 2: Velocity Increased But Customers Are Unhappy

Situation:

Velocity:

50 → 70 points

Looks good.

But:

Customer complaints increased.

Why?

Check:

Escaped Defects

Increased:

5 → 30

Problem.

Customer Satisfaction

Decreased.

Interpretation:

The team optimized output, not value.

They delivered more but poorer-quality features.

7. Scenario 3: Burndown Chart Is Flat

Observation:

Remaining Work

50

50

50

48

48

45

Looks bad.

Now check CFD.

CFD shows:

Testing column growing.

Meaning:

Development

████

Testing

██████████████████

Problem:

Testing bottleneck.

Solution:

  • Add QA support.

  • Improve automation.

  • Reduce batch size.

8. Scenario 4: Throughput Decreased

Previous:

10 items/Sprint

Current:

5 items/Sprint

Is this bad?

Check:

Story Size

Maybe stories became larger.

Cycle Time

Reduced:

10 days → 5 days

Meaning:

Stories are completed faster.

Interpretation:

Throughput dropped because the team changed work sizing.

Not necessarily a problem.

9. Scenario 5: High WIP Problem

Metrics:

CFD

Development band increasing.

↓

Cycle Time

Increasing.

↓

Lead Time

Increasing.

↓

Throughput

Decreasing.

Complete story:

The team is starting too much work.

Solution:

Reduce WIP.

Focus on finishing.

10. Product Manager Perspective

A Product Manager asks different questions.

Not:

\"Did developers complete enough points?\"

Instead:

\"Are we delivering customer value?\"

They look at:

Delivery Metrics

  • Velocity

  • Throughput

  • Cycle Time

Product Metrics

  • User adoption

  • Conversion

  • Retention

  • Customer satisfaction

Business Metrics

  • Revenue

  • Cost reduction

  • Market growth

11. Healthcare Product Example

Product

AI Pharmacovigilance Platform

Metrics:

Velocity

45 → 35

Looks negative.

But:

Escaped Defects:

15 → 3

↓

Compliance Issues:

8 → 1

↓

Regulatory Approval Time:

Reduced.

Interpretation:

The team slowed down intentionally to improve safety.

In healthcare, quality is more important than speed alone.

12. AI Product Example

Product

Medical AI Assistant

Metrics:

Throughput increased

10 models tested/month

↓

20 models tested/month

Looks good.

But:

AI Accuracy

92% → 85%

Problem.

More output, lower quality.

Need balance.

13. Agile Health Dashboard Example

A mature Agile dashboard might contain:

Delivery

Metric Purpose

Velocity Sprint capacity

Throughput Delivery rate

Cycle Time Speed

Lead Time Customer waiting time

Flow

Metric Purpose

WIP Work overload

CFD Bottlenecks

Flow Efficiency Waste

Quality

Metric Purpose

Escaped Defects Production quality

Test Coverage Engineering quality

Product

Metric Purpose

Adoption Usage

Retention Customer value

Satisfaction Experience

14. Common Metric Traps

Trap 1

\"More Velocity = Better Team\"

Wrong.

Velocity is only capacity.

Trap 2

\"More Features = More Value\"

Wrong.

Users may not need those features.

Trap 3

\"100% Resource Utilization\"

Wrong.

Fully occupied teams create bottlenecks.

Trap 4

\"Compare Teams Using Velocity\"

Wrong.

Velocity is team-specific.

15. Interview Questions

Q1. Why should Agile teams avoid using one metric alone?

Answer:

Because individual metrics provide incomplete information. Multiple metrics together provide a more accurate view of delivery, quality, and business value.

Q2. Velocity decreased. How would you analyze this?

Answer:

I would check:

  • Story size changes.

  • Quality metrics.

  • Defects.

  • Cycle time.

  • Throughput.

  • Team capacity.

I would avoid immediately concluding performance problems.

Q3. What metrics would you show to executives?

Answer:

Executives usually need:

  • Delivery predictability.

  • Business value delivered.

  • Release progress.

  • Quality trends.

  • Customer outcomes.

Not only Story Points.

Q4. How do you identify bottlenecks?

Answer:

I analyze:

  • CFD.

  • WIP.

  • Cycle Time.

  • Lead Time.

  • Throughput trends.

16. Mini Quiz

Q1.

Velocity decreases but defects also decrease significantly. Is this automatically bad?

A. Yes

B. No

Q2.

A growing Testing column in CFD indicates:

A. Testing bottleneck

B. Faster development

C. More customers

Q3.

Which metric measures customer waiting time?

A. Lead Time

B. Velocity

C. Story Points

Q4.

True or False:

A good Agile leader uses metrics to improve systems, not punish people.

17. Practical Assignment

Analyze this AI Pharmacovigilance project:

Metric Previous Current

Velocity 50 40

Throughput 8 items 7 items

Cycle Time 10 days 6 days

Defects 20 5

Customer Satisfaction 80% 92%

Answer:

  1. Is the team improving or declining?

  2. Which metrics are most important here?

  3. How would you explain this to management?

18. Summary

Today we learned:

  • Metrics must be interpreted together.

  • No single Agile metric tells the complete story.

  • Delivery speed, quality, flow, and business value must be balanced.

  • Senior Agile professionals look for patterns, not individual numbers.

Key Takeaways

  1. Metrics are signals, not judgments.

  2. Velocity alone does not measure success.

  3. Combine flow, quality, and value metrics.

  4. Use metrics to improve the system.

  5. Great Agile leaders ask \"Why?\" behind every number.

Lesson 1: Product Vision (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Product Manager • Product Owner • Business Analyst • AI Product Manager

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Product Vision is.

  • Why every successful product needs a vision.

  • Difference between Vision, Mission, Strategy, and Roadmap.

  • How Product Managers create a Product Vision.

  • How to write a Product Vision Document.

  • Real examples from Amazon, Google, healthcare, and AI products.

  • How to create a Product Vision for your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

1. Concept: What is Product Vision?

Simple Definition

A Product Vision is a clear statement describing:

\"What future we want to create for our customers through our product.\"

It explains:

  • Why the product exists.

  • Who it helps.

  • What problem it solves.

  • What impact it creates.

A Product Vision is the North Star of the product.

Every decision should connect back to it.

2. Why Does Product Vision Exist?

Imagine a company says:

\"Let\'s build a healthcare AI platform.\"

The team asks:

Developer:

\"What features should we build?\"

Designer:

\"What should the user experience look like?\"

Business team:

\"What problem are we solving?\"

Regulatory team:

\"What compliance requirements matter?\"

Without a vision, everyone moves in different directions.

Without Vision

Product Team

↓

Feature A

↓

Feature B

↓

Feature C

No clear destination

With Vision

PRODUCT VISION

↓

Product Strategy

↓

Roadmap

↓

Features

↓

User Stories

↓

Development

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine planning a journey.

Your destination:

\"I want to reach Mumbai.\"

That is your Vision.

Your route:

Highway → Ahmedabad → Vadodara → Mumbai

That is your Strategy.

Your stops:

Fuel stop, hotel, sightseeing

That is your Roadmap.

Your daily driving tasks:

Take highway exit, fill fuel, check GPS

Those are your Tasks.

4. Technical Explanation

A Product Vision usually answers five questions:

Question Answer

Who? Target users

What? Product solution

Why? Problem being solved

How? Differentiation

Impact? Expected outcome

5. Product Vision Formula

A common Product Vision template:

For [target customer] who [customer need/problem], our product [solution] that [key benefit]. Unlike [current alternatives], we provide [unique value].

Example:

For pharmacovigilance professionals who spend significant time manually processing adverse event cases, our AI platform automates case extraction, coding, and validation to reduce processing time while improving regulatory compliance.

6. Vision vs Mission vs Strategy vs Roadmap

This is a very common interview topic.

Product Vision

Question:

Where are we going?

Example:

Make drug safety monitoring faster and safer through AI.

Product Mission

Question:

Why do we exist every day?

Example:

Help healthcare organizations identify and manage safety risks effectively.

Product Strategy

Question:

How will we achieve the vision?

Example:

  • Build AI extraction capability.

  • Integrate regulatory databases.

  • Automate case processing.

Product Roadmap

Question:

When will we deliver things?

Example:

Q1:

Case Management

Q2:

AI Coding

Q3:

Signal Detection

Visual:

VISION

|

↓

MISSION

|

↓

STRATEGY

|

↓

ROADMAP

|

↓

FEATURES

|

↓

USER STORIES

7. Who Creates Product Vision?

Usually:

Product Manager

Owns the vision.

Product Owner

Translates vision into backlog decisions.

Business Analyst

Provides:

  • User insights.

  • Business requirements.

  • Process understanding.

Stakeholders

Provide:

  • Business goals.

  • Regulatory needs.

  • Customer expectations.

8. When is Product Vision Created?

Usually:

New Product

Before development starts.

Example:

Building an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.

Existing Product

When:

  • Market changes.

  • Customer needs change.

  • Technology changes.

Example:

Traditional PV software → AI-powered PV platform.

9. Product Vision Example: Amazon

Amazon is known for a customer-centric approach.

A simplified interpretation of Amazon\'s product thinking:

Build products and services that make customer experiences simpler, faster, and more convenient.

The vision guides decisions like:

  • One-click buying.

  • Prime delivery.

  • Recommendation systems.

10. Product Vision Example: Healthcare

Problem

Pharmacovigilance teams process thousands of adverse event reports manually.

Problems:

  • Slow processing.

  • Human errors.

  • High operational cost.

Product Vision

\"To create an intelligent pharmacovigilance platform that uses AI to accelerate adverse event processing, improve data quality, and help healthcare organizations ensure patient safety.\"

11. AI Product Vision Example

For your AI Pharmacovigilance Platform:

Current State

Case Received

↓

Manual Data Entry

1. Concept: What is a Business Case?

Simple Definition

A Business Case is a document that explains:

\"Why should the organization invest money, time, and resources into this initiative?\"

It answers:

  • What problem are we solving?

  • Why solve it now?

  • What benefits will we get?

  • How much will it cost?

  • Is the investment worthwhile?

2. Why Does a Business Case Exist?

Imagine you are a Product Manager.

You go to leadership and say:

\"I want to build an AI Pharmacovigilance Platform.\"

Leadership asks:

  • How much will it cost?

  • What problem does it solve?

  • How much money will it save?

  • What risks exist?

  • What is the expected return?

A Business Case provides these answers.

Without Business Case:

Idea

↓

Build Product

↓

Hope it succeeds

With Business Case:

Problem

↓

Analysis

↓

Investment Decision

↓

Build Product

↓

Lesson 7: NFR (Non-Functional Requirements) (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Manager • Product Owner • Solution Analyst • AI Product Manager

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) are.

  • Why NFRs are as important as features.

  • Difference between Functional and Non-Functional Requirements.

  • Types of NFRs.

  • How to write good NFRs.

  • Healthcare and Pharmacovigilance NFR examples.

  • AI Product NFR considerations.

  • How NFRs are tested and tracked.

  • Interview questions.

1. Concept: What are Non-Functional Requirements (NFR)?

Simple Definition

A Non-Functional Requirement describes:

\"How well a system should perform its functions.\"

Functional requirements tell:

What the system does.

NFRs tell:

How the system should behave.

Example:

Functional Requirement:

\"The system shall allow users to upload safety reports.\"

Non-Functional Requirements:

\"The system shall process uploaded reports within 10 seconds.\"

\"The system shall encrypt patient data.\"

\"The system shall support 10,000 concurrent users.\"

2. Why Do NFRs Exist?

Imagine building a hospital application.

The system has:

✅ Patient registration\ ✅ Appointment booking\ ✅ Medical records

But:

  • It crashes during peak hours.

  • Patient data is exposed.

  • Pages load slowly.

  • No backup exists.

The features work, but the product fails.

NFRs prevent this.

Without NFR

Build Features

↓

System Works

↓

Users Suffer

↓

Performance/Security Problems

With NFR

Features

+

Performance

+

Security

+

Reliability

+

Compliance

↓

Successful Product

3. Real-Life Analogy

Buying a car.

Functional Requirements:

  • Car should move.

  • Car should have brakes.

  • Car should have air conditioning.

Non-Functional Requirements:

  • Mileage should be 20 km/litre.

  • Safety rating should be high.

  • Should start in cold weather.

  • Should last 10 years.

The car\'s functions work, but quality determines user satisfaction.

4. Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements

Very Important Interview Question.

Functional Requirement Non-Functional Requirement

What system does How system performs

Features Quality attributes

User actions System characteristics

Business capability Technical quality

Example: Login Example: Login response \< 2 seconds

Example:

Functional:

\"The system shall generate safety reports.\"

Non-Functional:

\"The system shall generate reports within 5 seconds.\"

5. Types of Non-Functional Requirements

Major categories:

Non-Functional Requirements

|

|

--------------------------------

| | | |

Performance Security Reliability Scalability

Usability Compliance Availability Maintainability

6. Performance Requirements

Meaning:

How fast the system responds.

Examples:

  • Page loading time.

  • API response time.

  • Report generation speed.

Healthcare Example:

Requirement:

\"Patient medical history should load within 3 seconds.\"

Pharmacovigilance Example:

\"The system should extract data from a safety report within 30 seconds.\"

7. Security Requirements

Meaning:

Protect information from unauthorized access.

Especially critical in healthcare.

Examples:

  • Authentication.

  • Authorization.

  • Encryption.

  • Audit logs.

Pharmacovigilance Example:

Requirement:

\"Only authorized PV users can access adverse event cases.\"

Another:

\"All patient information must be encrypted during storage and transmission.\"

8. Scalability Requirements

Meaning:

Ability to handle growth.

Example:

Today:

10,000 cases/month.

Future:

1 million cases/month.

System should support growth.

AI Platform Example:

Year 1:

100 users

↓

Year 5:

10,000 users

System should continue working.

9. Availability Requirements

Meaning:

How often system should be operational.

Usually measured as uptime.

Example:

99.9% availability.

Meaning:

System downtime should be minimal.

Healthcare Example:

Emergency systems cannot be unavailable.

10. Reliability Requirements

Meaning:

System should work consistently without failures.

Examples:

  • Data should not be lost.

  • Transactions should complete correctly.

  • Recovery should be possible.

Pharmacovigilance Example:

A submitted safety case should never disappear.

11. Usability Requirements

Meaning:

How easy the system is to use.

Examples:

  • Simple navigation.

  • Clear messages.

  • Accessibility support.

Healthcare Example:

A doctor should complete patient registration without training.

12. Maintainability Requirements

Meaning:

How easily the system can be modified and maintained.

Examples:

  • Clean architecture.

  • Documentation.

  • Modular design.

AI Product Example:

AI model should be replaceable without rebuilding the entire system.

13. Compliance Requirements

Extremely important in healthcare.

Examples:

Pharmacovigilance systems require:

  • Data integrity.

  • Audit trail.

  • Regulatory compliance.

Example Requirement:

\"The system shall maintain complete audit history of all case modifications.\"

14. AI Product Specific NFRs

AI systems have additional requirements.

1. AI Accuracy

Example:

\"AI extraction accuracy should exceed 95%.\"

2. Explainability

Users should understand AI decisions.

Example:

AI suggests:

\"Drug X associated with headache.\"

System should show:

Why?

Based on:

  • Previous cases.

  • Literature.

  • Data patterns.

3. Bias Control

AI should avoid unfair outcomes.

Example:

Medical AI should perform consistently across patient groups.

4. Human Oversight

Important in healthcare.

Example:

AI suggestion:

↓

Human medical reviewer approval

↓

Final submission

5. Model Monitoring

AI performance can change.

Need:

  • Accuracy monitoring.

  • Drift detection.

  • Retraining.

15. Pharmacovigilance Platform NFR Example

Product:

AI ICSR Processing Platform

Performance

NFR-001:

The system shall process uploaded safety documents within 30 seconds.

Security

NFR-002:

The system shall encrypt patient data.

Availability

NFR-003:

The system shall maintain 99.9% uptime.

Audit

NFR-004:

The system shall maintain complete user activity logs.

Scalability

NFR-005:

The system shall support 50,000 cases per month.

AI Accuracy

NFR-006:

AI extraction accuracy should be above 95%.

16. How to Write Good NFRs

A good NFR should be:

Specific

Bad:

\"The system should be fast.\"

Good:

\"The dashboard should load within 3 seconds.\"

Measurable

Bad:

\"System should be secure.\"

Good:

\"All data transmission should use encryption.\"

Testable

QA team should verify it.

Realistic

Don\'t demand impossible targets.

17. NFR and Testing

Each NFR requires testing.

Example:

NFR:

\"System supports 10,000 users.\"

Testing:

Load testing.

NFR:

\"Response time below 2 seconds.\"

Testing:

Performance testing.

NFR:

\"Data encrypted.\"

Testing:

Security testing.

18. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1:

Ignoring NFR until the end.

Wrong:

Build first, optimize later.

Mistake 2:

Using vague words.

Examples:

  • Fast.

  • Secure.

  • Reliable.

Need measurable values.

Mistake 3:

Ignoring compliance.

Healthcare cannot ignore:

  • Privacy.

  • Audit.

  • Security.

Mistake 4:

Only thinking about current users.

Always consider future growth.

19. Best Practices

✔ Define NFRs early.

✔ Make them measurable.

✔ Review with engineering.

✔ Include regulatory needs.

✔ Link NFRs with testing.

✔ Prioritize critical quality attributes.

20. Interview Questions

Q1. What are Non-Functional Requirements?

Answer:

NFRs define the quality attributes and constraints of a system, such as performance, security, scalability, and reliability.

Q2. Difference between functional and non-functional requirements?

Answer:

Functional requirements describe system capabilities; non-functional requirements describe how effectively the system performs those capabilities.

Q3. Give healthcare NFR examples.

Answer:

  • Patient data encryption.

  • Audit trail.

  • High availability.

  • Fast response time.

  • Regulatory compliance.

Q4. Why are NFRs important?

Answer:

Because a system can have all required features but still fail if it is slow, insecure, unreliable, or difficult to use.

Today we learned:

  • NFRs define system quality.

  • Functional requirements explain what; NFRs explain how well.

  • Healthcare systems require strong security and compliance.

  • AI systems require accuracy, explainability, and monitoring.

  • Good NFRs are measurable and testable.

Key Takeaways

Lesson 8: User Stories & Acceptance Criteria (Masterclass)

Role Perspective: Business Analyst • Product Owner • Product Manager • Scrum Master • AI Product Manager

Note: We covered User Stories and Acceptance Criteria in depth in Module 4 (Product Backlog Mastery). This lesson revisits them from the Agile Documentation perspective---how they are documented, linked to BRD/PRD/FRD, and used in Jira and Sprint Planning.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

  • What a User Story is.

  • Why Agile uses User Stories instead of large requirement documents.

  • How User Stories fit into Agile documentation.

  • Story structure.

  • INVEST principle (revision).

  • Acceptance Criteria.

  • Given--When--Then format.

  • Epic → Feature → Story hierarchy.

  • Healthcare and AI examples.

  • Jira documentation.

  • Common interview questions.

1. What is a User Story?

Simple Definition

A User Story is a short description of a requirement from the user\'s perspective.

Instead of writing:

\"Implement document upload functionality using API X.\"

Agile says:

\"As a PV Specialist, I want to upload a safety report so that I can begin case processing.\"

The focus shifts from technology to user value.

2. Why Do User Stories Exist?

Before Agile, teams often wrote 300-page requirement documents.

Problems:

  • Difficult to read.

  • Difficult to update.

  • Stakeholders rarely read them.

  • Developers misunderstood requirements.

Agile introduced User Stories to make requirements:

  • Small

  • Clear

  • Easy to discuss

  • Easy to prioritize

Traditional Documentation

Requirement Document

Page 1

Page 2

Page 3

...

Page 300

Agile Documentation

Epic

↓

Feature

↓

User Story

↓

Acceptance Criteria

↓

Sprint

3. Real-Life Analogy

Imagine opening a restaurant.

Instead of saying:

\"Build a restaurant.\"

Break it into user needs:

Customer:

\"I want to reserve a table.\"

Chef:

\"I want to receive orders digitally.\"

Manager:

\"I want daily sales reports.\"

Each becomes a User Story.

4. Standard User Story Format

Every User Story follows this template:

As a \<user role>,

I want \<goal>,

So that \<business value>.

Example

As a Pharmacovigilance Specialist,

I want to upload adverse event reports,

So that I can process new safety cases efficiently.

5. Anatomy of a Good User Story

Example:

As a PV Specialist,

I want AI to extract patient information,

So that I reduce manual data entry.

Breakdown:

Role

  • PV Specialist

Goal

  • Extract patient information

Benefit

  • Reduce manual effort

6. Epic → Feature → User Story

Epic

↓

Feature

↓

User Story

↓

Task

Example:

↓

AI Data Extraction

↓

↓

Extract Adverse Event

↓
